Help me complete and structure a type hierarchy. I'm formalizing "the organization of language" as one evolutionary tree rooted at the Word, generated by exactly three operators: aggregate (one -> many), refine (one -> same, with validation), specialize (one -> further specified). Full context and my current type sketch are attached.
Please give a structured, substantive answer to three questions: (1) What types am I MISSING for completeness in the organization of language? (2) Propose a precise type hierarchy that unifies the EVOLUTION ordering (how a thing grows: chapter -> book -> subject -> library) with the INHERITANCE ordering (is-a: Cover <: Chapter, Subject <: Book, Library <: Subject). (3) Is "reference/pointer" a fourth operator beside the three, or is it derivable from refine?
Also weigh this analogy and tell me whether it dissolves the evolution-vs-inheritance tension: all living eukaryotes descend from a single-celled ancestor yet are multicellular, so the one-to-many (aggregate) step does NOT sever inheritance from the ancestor. Does aggregation itself act as a mode of inheritance -- the many descending from the one?
Aim for depth over breadth. I'll evaluate your answer against my own framework.

This is a genuinely good formal object you've got, and the three operators are sharper than most attempts at this. Before the three questions, one refinement to the operator definitions, because it makes all three answers fall out cleanly — and it exposes where your current sketch is quietly inconsistent.
A sharper cut of the three operators
Distinguish them by what they do to a type's extension (its set of values) versus its intension (its identity/role), and by where the membership test lives:
operatorcarrierextension (value set)intension (role)membership decidable from…
aggregatenew (X[])brand new—a functor; not a subtype relation at all
refinesamenarrowed to a subsetunchangedthe value's own local structure
specializesame (often + fields)unchanged (or enriched)new role/positionhow the value is used in a larger structure
The load-bearing addition is the last column. ␀0␀ adds a predicate that is locally checkable (a Sentence is a complete Expression — you can verify that from the expression alone). ␀1␀ adds a role — a position/use, not an internal-structure constraint (any Expression can be a Title; nothing about the expression changes, only what it names). Most of your specialize nodes also smuggle in a refinement (a Cover must contain Title/Author/Synopsis/ToC), so practically specialize = refine + a role tag. Refine is the purely extensional skeleton of specialize.
Hold onto the local-vs-global distinction — it answers Q3 by itself.
Q1 — What you're missing
I'll skip the long tail (Clause between phrase and sentence; the fact that Word is a chosen cut, not a bottom — it's really refine(aggregate(Grapheme)), "a sequence of graphemes that is a lexeme," and the tree extends downward if you ever want it to). The high-value gaps are four clusters:
1. The reference *co-structure* — your biggest gap, and it's exactly your stated purpose. You have Reference (the source end of an edge) but not the sink end. Heading is noted as "also a reference target," which means target-hood is its own concept you haven't typed. You need an Anchor / Label (a named, addressable target) as the dual of Reference. An edge has two typed endpoints; you've modeled half.
Then notice your reference-collections form a symmetry that reveals two more missing types:
TableOfContents = references down into own parts, keyed by position
(missing) Index = references down into own parts, keyed by Term
Citations = references out, to external sources
…but Citations points out to nothing typed. You're missing the Source / Work node (the external target) and Bibliography = aggregate(Source). Right now Citation (the in-text pointer) and the source record it resolves to are conflated. They're different objects on different sides of the edge.
For a library that "represents the identity of a formal theory and its evolution," the structure that matters most — the theory's dependency graph, Definitions depending on Definitions, Theorems on Lemmas — isentirely reference edges. The thing you're most missing is the typed edge and its relation-kinds (defines, depends-on, proves, refines, cites). That's not a footnote; for your purpose it's the spine. (See Q3.)
2. A whole class of non-prose blocks. List = aggregate(ListItem) where ListItem = specialize(Paragraph); plus Figure, Table, Equation, CodeBlock, Caption = specialize(Expression) bound to a Figure, Quotation = specialize(Paragraph) + Reference(source), Footnote = specialize(Paragraph) reached via a Reference. Footnote and Quotation are the cleanest worked examples of "a content node that only exists at the intersection of aggregate and the reference edge" — more grist for Q3.
3. The identity/version layer — also dead-center on your purpose. You say the library represents "the identity of a formal theory and its evolution," but nothing in the sketch carries identity across change. You need the $-membrane made into a type: a Work (the persistent abstract identity) versus its Editions/Versions (the concrete representations that change). This is a solved ontology — FRBR: Work → Expression → Manifestation → Item. Your Library/Subject/Book tower is the upper bibliographic ontology, partly reinvented (note FRBR's "Expression" collides with your phrase-level Expression — worth disambiguating before it bites you). Pull from FRBR/BIBFRAME for the bibliographic half and from RST (Rhetorical Structure Theory) / TEI / DocBook for the rhetorical half. They give you external correctness checks.
4. The uniform "Head" you already half-discovered. You wrote that a Cover is "the self-describing head a container grows." That's a recursion you've only instantiated at one scale. The pattern is: every container, at every scale, grows a Head that is a smaller copy of its own descriptive content — Title (one expression) for a Chapter, Heading (one title) for a Section, Synopsis (one paragraph) for the body, Cover (one chapter) for a Book. These are the same role at different scales — the η-image (singleton embedding) of the container's descriptive content into itself. Name it once (Head) and let Title/Heading/Cover be its instances, rather than four ad-hoc specialize nodes.
One thing to exclude explicitly: Page, Folio, running head — these are representation artifacts (the $ membrane), not content nodes. Since you compile to HTML, state the exclusion so nobody adds them.
Q2 — Unifying evolution and inheritance
Here is the inconsistency, stated plainly, because it's the whole game:
You claim is-a for the top of the spine (Subject <: Book, Library <: Subject) but not for the bottom (you never say Book <: Chapter or Chapter <: Section). Structurally these rungs are identical. Book = aggregate(Chapter); Subject (= a body of Books) is aggregate(Book) by the same logic. If a Book is not a Chapter (it's a sequence of chapters — correct), then a Subject is not a Book either, and Library <: Subject <: Book is simply false under the aggregate reading. The top three rungs only feel special because there the element type and container type converge (a subject's parts are books, and you still want to call the whole "book-like writing"). That convergence is an illusion produced by stopping the recursion and renaming the levels.
So you have a fork, and you're standing on both tines:
Aggregate reading (your labels: Book = aggregate(Chapter)): distinct carriers at each level. No is-a up the spine. What you do get is the list monad's η (every Chapter is a one-chapter Book — lower embeds into higher, faithfully) and μ (a Library of subjects flattens lossily toward a Book). Under this reading the only faithful subtype runs lower <: higher (Chapter <: Book via singleton) — the opposite of what you wrote, and the downward direction you wrote is the lossy μ coercion, not real subtyping.
Refinement reading: one recursive carrier Container = aggregate(Content or Container), and Subject/Library are Containers satisfying nested uniformity predicates ("all my children are themselves Containers-of-Containers"). Under this reading Library <: Subject <: Book is genuine (nested subsets) — but then consistency forces Book <: Chapter <: Section too, which you'd have to accept.
My recommendation: don't pick either tine — recognize they're the same object and use the fixed point. Let F(X) = NonemptySeq(Content + X) be the container/aggregate functor (with leaves). Your whole spine above the leaf is the initial algebra μF: the type of all finite content-trees. Chapter, Book, Subject, Library are not different kinds — they are depth strata of one type μF.
Now Lambek's lemma does the unification you've been circling as "a duality." The initial algebra's structure map α : F(μF) → μF is an isomorphism:
text
μF  ≅  F(μF)
Read left-to-right and right-to-left:
␀0␀ (the carrier) is the inheritance / is-a view: there is one kind, the recursive Container; every node is the same type. "A Library is the same kind of thing as a Book" is true because they're both μF.
␀0␀ (the unfolding) is the evolution / grows-by-aggregate view: a thing is an aggregate of (sub)things of the same kind. "A Library is a sequence of Subjects, each a sequence of Books…" — the growth tower.
They are not two hierarchies in tension, and not merely dual. They are the two sides of a single isomorphism on a single recursive type. The evolution ladder and the inheritance ladder are the same ladder because μF ≅ F(μF) says "to be the whole" and "to be an aggregate of (parts that are wholes)" are literally the same type. Your "dynamic inheritance where an instance is re-revealed as a higher type at runtime" is then precisely the structure map: η lifts a Chapter into a one-chapter Book, and accreting siblings is the rest of α⁻¹. That's the runtime re-reveal, pinned.
Concretely, the type hierarchy I'd write:
text
Atom:        Word                              -- the chosen cut
Spine:       μF, F(X) = Seq(Content + X)        -- ONE recursive type;
             Expression…Sentence…Paragraph…    -- Section/Chapter/Book/Subject/Library
             are strata + local refinements of μF, not separate kinds
Heads:       Head (= η-image of a node's own descriptive content)
             ↳ Title, Heading, Synopsis, Cover  -- same role, four scales
Decorations: specialize-nodes hanging OFF spine nodes (roles), orthogonal axis
Edges:       Reference (source) ←→ Anchor (sink)  -- the graph layer (Q3)
Identity:    Work / Edition                       -- the $-membrane, across-time identity
The crucial structural recommendation: separate the growth spine (built by ␀0␀ + local ␀1␀) from the role-decorations (␀2␀), which hang off the spine as an orthogonal axis. Title/Author/Citation/Synopsis aren't rungs on the ladder; they're roles attached to rungs. Once you do that, the spine is a clean μF, and Lambek does the unification for free.
Q3 — Is reference a fourth operator?
As a type: yes, it's a refinement. Reference = refine(Name) = { n : Name | resolves(n) }. You have this right.
As a structure: no — and this is where the local-vs-global column pays off. Your three operators all produce types whose membership is decidable from local data: a Sentence's completeness (the expression itself), a Book's bookhood (its own chapters).␀0␀ is not local. It is decidable only against the entire library. That global-relational character is exactly what a pointer is. So reference is not a fourth member of the node-forming family; it is the introduction of edges on top of the nodes — a different ontological level.
The sharp consequence: aggregate, refine, and specialize, applied to anything, can only ever build a tree (a containment hierarchy — every node has one parent, membership is local). The instant you add reference, the structure becomes a graph (tree + cross-edges, nodes addressable from elsewhere). No composition of three tree-builders produces a cross-edge; that's a structural jump they cannot make. Your TableOfContents, Citations, and the Index I added are the proof that the graph layer is already load-bearing in your model — and the fact that you typed only the source end (Reference) and left the sink end (Anchor) implicit is the residue of treating edges as if they were nodes.
So: reference-the-type derives from ␀0␀; reference-the-relation does not derive from anything in the family — it is the primitive edge that turns your tree into a graph, and its signature is that its validity is global rather than local. Don't list it as a fourth operator beside three peers; list it as the first relation over the three node-operators. Different tier.
The eukaryote analogy
First, a factual correction, because you'll want it right: it is not true that all living eukaryotes are multicellular. Unicellular eukaryotes are everywhere — yeasts, amoebae, ciliates, most protists. Multicellularity arose independently many times (animals, land plants, fungi, brown algae, several others) and is polyphyletic. The accurate claim is the weaker one: all eukaryotes share a single-celled common ancestor (LECA), and multicellular eukaryotes are built from cells that each still carry the ancestral cell-level machinery.
Now the load-bearing part. Your analogy quietly runs three different relations together, and separating them changes the verdict:
Phylogenetic descent (lineage → lineage, over time) — your evolution axis.
Part-of composition (organism made of cells) — your aggregate axis.
Type is-a (a human cell is-a eukaryotic cell) — your inheritance axis.
Here's the catch: relation 3 holds of the cells, not the organism. A human is not a cell. A human is made of cells that are-a eukaryotic cell. So:
Aggregation does not make the composite is-a the element. A book is-not-a chapter exactly as a human is-not-a cell. What aggregation does is preserve the elements' inheritance and carry it up by composition — the is-a lives at the part level, threaded through to every leaf.
So, read carefully, the eukaryote case cuts against "aggregation is a mode of inheritance" for the whole. It does not license aggregate(X) <: X.
But — and this is why the analogy is still worth keeping — it does dissolve your tension, by a different mechanism, and it's the same mechanism as Q2. What survives aggregation is (a) the atom preserved at every depth (every aggregate bottoms out in Words / every organism bottoms out in cells — the base case is present at every scale), and (b) fixpoint self-similarity (μF ≅ F(μF): the whole is the same kind as its parts). "The many descending from the one" is true in the precise sense that every node bottoms out in the atom, and the whole is self-similar to its parts — not in the sense that the composite inherits-from the element. The grain of truth is Lambek, not subtyping.
So my bottom line on your seed: the intuition that evolution and inheritance are "the same ladder seen two ways" is right, and stronger than you framed it — they're isomorphic via the fixed point, not merely dual. But the bridge is not "aggregation is inheritance." Aggregation is the functor; inheritance up the spine is the fixed-point iso; and the only thing aggregation literally inherits is the atom, carried to every leaf. Keep the conclusion, swap the mechanism.
One place to pressure-test me: I've assumed your library is finite (initial algebra, least fixed point). If you ever want lazily-infinite or self-referential structures — a Library that contains itself, a Term defined circularly — you'd move to the final coalgebra νF, where Lambek still gives the iso but the "evolution" reading becomes unfolding rather than construction. Worth knowing which fixed point you're standing on before you commit the type.

Designing .public — a compiler for a library that validates a knowledge graph
You have no context on this project. This document gives you all of it.
Doug is the person whose design this is. Where his wording carries the idea better than a paraphrase would, he is quoted directly and marked ␀0␀. Everything unquoted is our reading of it, and may be wrong — say so where you think it is.
0. What this is
We are building a compiler for a library. Not a software library — an actual one: books, chapters, sections, subjects, authors, a card catalogue. Books are written as TypeScript classes in a reactive framework; the compiler turns a directory of them into a published site, and — more importantly — into a validated knowledge graph.
Doug: "Library semantics establish the soundness of a knowledge graph — a knowledge graph is just an abstraction of a library and I am choosing canonical semantics which are suggestive."
Nodes and edges are what is left of books and references when you take the words away, and taking the words away is what makes a graph hard to reason about: nothing about a node tells you what it would be for that node to be wrong. A dangling edge is an abstraction. A reference to a book that is on no shelf is something anyone can see is wrong.
So the vocabulary is not decoration over a graph. It is the graph's semantics, and soundness is defined in terms of it.
This is a working method, not a naming style, and it has already earned its keep. Doug asserted a card catalogue was necessary; the engineering team objected on complexity grounds; the domain settled it — real and digital libraries do not carry a catalogue by accident. His account of why that mattered:
Doug: "It is not cute one-word names, it is the usage of canonical semantics of a domain to steer us in the direction of me being able to tell you I am sure the catalogue is necessary because real and digital libraries wouldn't have one if they weren't, and you did object, and my use of canonical semantics made that not hypothetical — in the context of libraries you are telling me there should be no catalogue. You are obviously wrong."
And the corollary, which governs every naming decision below:
Doug: "If any one obscures by being short, you have failed. But if you make something that has no short name, you are deviating from the domain! Naming is a semantic constraint satisfaction problem, and the answer isn't obscurity. It is allowing your design to change to accommodate the missing semantics to stay IN the domain."
1. The needs of the system
Stated as needs rather than features, because the architecture should fall out of these.
N1 — Referential integrity across the whole library. Every reference from anywhere to anywhere must be correct, and correctness must be decidable rather than hoped for.
N2 — Reference must survive a change of layout. Today a book renders as one page with its chapters as sections. We want to be able to decide tomorrow that chapters are their own pages, or are routed, and have that change one rule instead of every cross-reference in the corpus.
Doug: "What if we want chapters to be through the router rather than on a page, or maybe we want chapters to each be their whole page? If the catalogue system handles this, we should be able to easily change this without much fuss as long as the catalogue is used to fetch the reference." And: "So even the table needs to go through the catalogue for its chapters."
N3 — Local validation of structure, at a level static analysis cannot reach.
Doug: "The catalogue system makes referential life easy and the specification system allows things to be locally validated so that it gets hit when necessary. And specification isn't in ␀0␀. We compile because it's a property of the library. We are specifying at a level static analysis fails at. This app exists across JavaScript runtimes. No runtime type system can hold it." And: "I want something static-like for web development that goes beyond TypeScript. I want a library specification."
N4 — Realtime development feedback. A person editing a book must see the result immediately and be told immediately when they have broken something.
Doug: "Support for hot reload is obviously ESSENTIAL… restarting a server is death."
N5 — Speed, as a first-order requirement rather than a nice-to-have. Doug's standard, given this week while we were fixing an unrelated tool, and it applies here exactly:
Doug: "1 second of blink and 10 seconds of wait is a whole universe." "I shouldn't be waiting noticeable amounts of time for anything so if you HAVE to wait, wait 250." "You should never wait blind, so the absence of a confirmation is the do-and-check is just proof that you are blind." "Running is from the time I ask to the time it happens."
That last one is the measure. Not the build's internal wall clock — the interval between a person changing something and seeing the consequence.
N6 — It must not be a maze.
Doug: "No branching codebases that have exponential complexity on figuring out what they do."
N7 — Failure must be loud.
Doug: "You guys don't like to throw exceptions. I love exceptions so all bugs like that are on you."
We have just spent a day proving him right in a different codebase: three separate functions returned a falsy value on failure, every caller discarded it, and one of them had been reporting failure on everysuccess for months without anyone noticing.
2. The anchors — what the design is judged against
A1. The catalogue refuses by non-membership alone.
Doug: "With the catalogue, you can have dictionary lookup speed and you can have names validated at runtime. If the catalogue controls the link generation, all links are guaranteed to be right, right?" "The catalogue refuses by non-membership alone."
The argument, which we believe holds: a table of contents works because a book holds its own chapters — that data is local. A reference from one book to another needs what is not local. With no shared index, every book must reach every other book to check a name — a cycle, an N² load, and exactly the coupling that makes incremental compilation impossible. So the catalogue is not an optimisation of lateral reference; it is what makes lateral reference possible at all.
And once it exists, validation collapses into membership: a reference is not checked after it is written, it is generated from the catalogue, so a reference that would be wrong cannot be written.
A2. One set of cards.
Doug: "A library has a catalogue right? You don't want to have catalogue cards written EVERYWHERE and check them all. Make one set of cards."
A3. Identity, not address. The catalogue holds which book, which chapter, which key; the address is derived. This is what makes N2 possible and it is the property that earns the whole system.
A4. The mention is the essence.

3. What cannot give — the library semantics
The vocabulary is fixed, and the design bends to it rather than the other way round. If a piece of the design has no natural word from the library domain, the design is wrong and must change until it does. Reaching for a longer, more mechanical name is the failure mode, because obscurity hides the drift.
The fixed pieces:
Book, chapter, section, paragraph — the containment levels.
Subject, title, author — the three ways a library is entered.
Catalogue (a book that catalogues books) and card catalogue (the index you look things up in). These are different things and the model currently collides them under one class name, which we regard as a defect.
Mention and reference — a mention means the thing and carries no path; a reference is a mention that also knows where.
Synopsis — the short description. Doug's ruling on where they go: "everything at section scale should have a summary or has one made. I don't think the direct mention should carry one of those."
Cover, table of contents — views over a book, not stored data.
The query surface, which is canonical rather than invented:
Doug: "The catalogue would have subject, title, author queries because each one has a unique book — we need to make unique the author one. And then from those you should be able to query chapter and mention, from chapter to section (yes let's have standard section ones). This is a comprehensive catalogue. I would say it should provide a tagline for each thing."
Size is roughly N books × M chapters.
The authoring syntax, just settled. Doubling declares; single refers:
Doug: "You are missing the ␀0␀ versus ␀1␀. ␀2␀ and ␀3␀ would be refers to. ␀4␀ and ␀5␀ would be referred to as (mentioned as)."
writtenmeans
[[great]]this is referred to as "great" — a declaration; the key is the copy
[[This is Important]](important)says "This is Important", keyed as important
[great]refers to whatever is referred to as "great"
[Doug](MY Library Log)says "Doug", refers to MY Library Log
Note this is the inverse of MediaWiki, where [[…]] is the link. The reasoning: declaring is the rarer, more deliberate act, and doubling should mark deliberateness. We parse our own markup deliberately — "it's not markdown, WE should be parsing that" — so the syntax is free to move.
A mention in prose is never casual:
Doug: "That isn't casual. That will get converted into a mention by the compiler, and a reference should be able to go there."

text

4. What can give — the implementation layer
Everything below the semantics is negotiable, and Doug has asked specifically for plugin architectures to be considered rather than a bespoke compiler:
Doug: "Please ask, for each feature, where it exists at in the pipeline. What are we modifying or emitting as part of the build and where is the most elegant insertion point? Yes, research plugin architectures including Babel, Vite, layers — great stuff. Consider TypeScript too… Do research to talk about what it looks like to do this as more of a plugin architecture to an existing web compiler."
And on where validation can happen:
Doug: "And remember as an anchor, support for hot reload is obviously ESSENTIAL, and if we need to read certain things by parsing and consuming the page itself rather than running something, we can validate the library in code too." "Validating by compiler, or by an app that runs a primitive lightweight version of the thing so that it can be efficiently inspected are both parts of the plan. I am fine with either or both as needed."
What is currently there. A bespoke nine-phase compiler: configure · inventory · assemble · specify · resolve · bundle · render · proof · record. It runs on Vite/Rollup. render spawns one Node process per page, serially, for isolation — 28 of 42 seconds. A one-property change to how a page looks costs about 42 seconds to see.
The constraint that shapes everything about the implementation:
Doug: "If we are careful, all the static links could be validated at build time and even substituted in. We still want a catalogue abstraction, and we want to find a way, at build time, for the system to be able to request parts of the catalogue, so it can provide dynamic services. No API needed."
So: a reference an author wrote is resolved during the build and emitted as a finished link. Ordinary prose costs nothing at runtime — a resolved reference is just a link. The catalogue survives as something that hands out parts for genuinely dynamic work. Nothing is shipped whole and looked up.
Why a compile is required at all, and why neither obvious alternative works.
Static analysis cannot reach the values. A title is inside a print() method. A theme value sits behind a getter, and one chain has 126 of them. A chapter's document does not exist until it is printed. A parser sees the shape, not the library.
No runtime holds the whole thing. The browser loads exactly one book. The prerenderer loads one book per process. The build's own process holds only what it imported. No runtime ever has all the pieces in front of it at once — and the property we care about is precisely how the pieces relate.
So the compile is the only moment the library exists as one object, and the library specification sits in a third position: TypeScript checks the code that builds the library, a runtime type system checks one process's objects, and the library specification checks the library.
Also negotiable, and Doug has proposed changes to both:
The type declarations.
Doug: *"We currently make an interface and a typeof and all of that, and keep things loosely coupled. I think we need a way of relying on dependency injection to swap out types, optimizing that in $Chemistry, to avoid having to have such loosely coupled polymorphism. We aren't using that system. We should compress everything just to the $ types. The type system can then be used to specify the sort of multiple inheritance that it affords by adding types to add validation, but it doesn't need us to create types for everything."

5. What is worth optimizing
All of it, and the reason is N4 and N5 together: it has to be fast and provide realtime code feedback, which means the budget is a human's attention span, not a CI job's.
Specifically:
The edit-to-see loop. Currently ~42s. It must be sub-second for the common case.
Catalogue construction. It is global by nature and must be rebuildable on every change. This is the hardest tension in the design.
The specification pass. Currently walks 33,158 writings. The grammar restructure removes most of them; what remains is local and therefore incremental by construction.
Process isolation. One Node process per page is ~1.5s of fixed cost paid and discarded, six times.
Reference resolution. Must be a dictionary lookup, not a search.

Above all: think about this holistically, across levels. Not asking about: CSS, styling, the rendering layer, or TypeScript ergonomics. Prose is fine — no need to produce documents. We want prior art, failure stories, cross-level consequences, and the names of things we should go read.

Read all three as one brief. Before the numbered questions, the cross-level findings you asked for first — because most of your nine questions turn out to be three questions wearing nine hats, and the hats matter less than the heads underneath.
The spine: one dependency graph, every input tracked
The single most load-bearing decision in this whole design is not in your list as its own item — it's smeared across 6.1, 6.7, and 6.8, and until it's settled those three can't be answered independently. It is this ruling: everything the build reads to produce a unit's output must be a tracked input in one dependency graph — props, injected services, and catalogue lookups included, and lookups counted whether they hit or miss.
Here's why those three questions are one. Doug found that a bond constructor re-runs on children but not props — "props are a second input channel that bypasses the bond entirely." That is not merely a reactivity quirk. In an incremental compiler it is a correctness-fatal untracked input. Incrementality (salsa, red-green, everything in 6.1) rests on exactly one assumption: a unit's output is a pure function of its tracked dependencies. If output can depend on a prop the graph doesn't see, then early cutoff will skip re-evaluation when it shouldn't, and serve stale output silently. That is the worst possible failure under N7 — not a loud exception, a quiet green light over a broken reference. So the props/children asymmetry (6.8) isn't a substrate detail that happens to also be a bug; it is the incremental engine's foundation, cracked.
Same with DI (6.7). If a service is resolved inside a constructor and captured in a field, then (a) the incremental graph doesn't see the dependency on that service, and (b) — your explicit worry — when the constructor re-runs on a children-change it re-resolves, but when a prop changes it doesn't re-run at all, so a prop-driven service swap is missed. The DI-capture hazard and the props-bypass bug are the same defect seen from two levels.
So the established position on 6.8 is unambiguous and it decides 6.7 and enables 6.1: a component's output must be a function of all its inputs; privileging one channel is a latent-bug generator. React's "children is just another prop" is the principled stance for correctness. The props/children asymmetry is defensible only as a performance optimization, and only if it's an emergent consequence of fine-grained tracking ("props didn't change, so the prop-dependent sub-computation was cut off") rather than a structural rule ("props don't trigger bonds"). Right now you have the structural rule, which is why it's wrong. The fix is not "also re-run bonds on props" bluntly — that throws away the perf win — it's to make every input a tracked read at fine grain, so the thing that skips work is early cutoff, not channel-blindness.
This is also the right answer to 6.7's "compare React/Vue/Solid/Svelte." Angular's inject()-only-in-injection-context is the right constraint, and the runInInjectionContext story is the cautionary tale you're about to re-live: binding injection to construction time was too restrictive the moment injection was needed in lifecycle hooks or after re-construction, so they had to bolt on a way to re-establish the context later. Vue's provide/inject and Svelte's getContext have the identical construction-time-capture hazard (resolved at setup/init, not reactively). Solid is the one to study, because resolution there is a reactive read inside the tracking scope, not a construction-time snapshot — which decouples "when you resolve" from "when you construct." That decoupling is exactly what you need: make DI resolution a tracked dependency in the same graph as everything else, and you get correct re-resolution and the incremental engine can see the DI edge. Doug's instinct — "the DI container just works anywhere, it just needs to inherit the scoping" plus a suspicion of props — is pointing straight at Solid's model without naming it. The hierarchical injector maps perfectly onto book → chapter → section scope; the thing to import is reactive resolution, not construction-time resolution.
So: settle the dependency model first. One graph, all inputs, hits and misses. Everything incremental, every DI question, and the props question hang off it, and N7 is violated until it's true.
Two rulings that cannot both be true
(1) "Resolved references bake to plain links" (Part 2) vs. N2 (a layout change touches one rule).
I flagged this between parts; now I can name the resolution in your own vocabulary. A3 says the catalogue holds identity and the address is derived. Part 2 says the reference is resolved at build and "substituted in… just a link." Read literally — substitute the URL into every referring page — N2 dies: change the routing rule and every page with a baked URL is stale, so N2 becomes recompile-the-corpus, and the corpus recompile is your 42-second problem.
But there's a domain word missing, and Doug's own method produces it. A real library already separates these two things: the catalogue card holds identity (author, title, key); the call number is what tells you which shelf. Re-shelving the stacks does not reprint the cards — because the card holds the call number, and the shelf location is derived from the call number by the shelving rule. Your design is missing the call number. Identity and address are collided (which is the same collision you already named between Catalogue and card catalogue, one level up). The moment you split them, the conflict dissolves without a runtime API:
Evaluation (books → identities + content + which identities they reference) is expensive and content-dependent.
Address derivation (identity → URL, via the routing rule) is cheap and route-dependent.
Bake addresses into the HTML — Doug's right that a shipped reference should be a plain link — but bake them in aseparate, late pass that is a pure function of identity and the routing rule, and that does not re-evaluate the books. Then a layout change (N2) invalidates only that late pass: a dictionary map over references, not the per-page evaluation. "One rule, whole corpus follows" becomes cheap because re-deriving addresses is cheap; re-evaluating books is what's expensive, and a routing change doesn't touch it. Concretely this means your pipeline needs a seam — … resolve(identity) → [derive-address] → render — and I'd bet the current 42s render entangles address-derivation inside the per-page process, which is precisely why layout changes cost a full render. Pull address-derivation out of evaluation and make it a late function of the call number. That is the whole of N2, and it's Doug's identity-not-address anchor made mechanical.
This is also where FRBR (6.2) stops being decorative. The reason a reference can survive re-layout is that it points at the Work/Expression (the persistent thing), and layout only changes the Manifestation (the rendered page). N2 is literally the statement "references bind to Work, not Manifestation." Your conflation — a "book" is a source file, a rendered page, and a card at once — is the same identity/address collision at the bibliographic level. The card is a Work/Expression record; the call number/URL is a Manifestation property. Until they're separateobjects, you will keep discovering references that broke on a layout change, and no amount of catalogue discipline will save you, because the catalogue entry itself is carrying an address it shouldn't own.
(2) "Always refuse" (A5) vs. references that point *outside* the library.
A5 — a reference that doesn't resolve fails the build, every build — is sound for intra-library references and unsound the instant a reference points at something you don't control. You have Citations (references out). You cannot guarantee an external work resolves; holding external citations to A5 means either the build breaks on things outside your authority, or you've quietly weakened A5 without admitting which references are exempt.
The domain already solved this: a library holds a catalogue card for a work it does not own (the union-catalogue / ILL record). So the fix stays in-domain: an external citation resolves not to the external thing but to your card describing it — a Source record you do control. Citation (the in-text pointer) and the Source (the thing it resolves to) are different objects on different sides of the edge, and you're currently conflating them. Add Source and Bibliography = aggregate(Source), and A5 becomes true again by construction: every reference resolves to a catalogue member, and external-ness is a property of the member, not a hole in the guarantee. This is the single cleanest way to keep A5 total. Xanadu is the cautionary tale here (more below): "every link always resolves" is affordable only for a closed corpus, and the way you keep your corpus closed while still citing the world is to pull the world's identity inside as Source cards.
The process-isolation chain, and what forces it
render spawns one Node process per page, serially — 28 of 42 seconds, and 1.5s of that is pure startup paid and discarded six times. Ask why isolation is needed, because I suspect the answer indicts the substrate, not the pages. You isolate presumably because evaluating a book mutates shared module/global state or because the DI container is a singleton whose registrations leak between books. If so, then:
process isolation (compiler) ← forced by → global mutable DI state (substrate) ← which also breaks → cross-edit memoization ← which N5 incrementality requires.
A fresh process has no warm salsa cache, so per-page processes make fine-grained incrementality impossible — you throw away the memoized catalogue every time. This is not a parallelize-the-processes problem; the processes shouldn't exist. Fix the substrate so evaluation is side-effect-contained — lexically scoped injectors, no global mutable registry (the Solid-shaped DI above gives you exactly this) — and you can evaluate N books in one warm process, keep the catalogue hot across edits, and get incrementality. If you genuinely need isolation against runaway loops or crashes, the ladder from cheapest to most-isolated is: same-realm-with-scoped-DI → vm.createContext (shared heap, separate globals) → worker_threads (own event loop) → child_process (what you have, the most expensive rung). Since this is authors' own trusted content, not untrusted code, I'd argue you're paying for isolation you don't need, and the real win is upstream: scoped DI removes the reason to isolate. This is 6.4's "isolate evaluations of independent units inside one process" — and the concrete mechanism is in the plugin answer below.
What to settle, in order
The dependency model — one graph, all inputs tracked, hits and misses. (Enables 6.1; decides 6.7, 6.8; is the precondition for N7 not lying.)
Split identity from address — add the call number; make Work/Expression vs Manifestation two objects. (Enables N2 cheaply; resolves conflict 1; un-collides your Catalogue/card catalogue defect at the same stroke.)
Declare the corpus boundary — closed, with external identities pulled in as Source cards. (Makes A5 total; resolves conflict 2.)
Everything else is engineering on top of these three.
6.1 — incremental construction of a global index
Your framing is right that this is "a global index that must be correct," not "a DAG of independent outputs," and that distinction eliminates half your candidates. Bazel/Buck are the wrong tool: their action graph assumes declared, static inputs known before a target runs. Here the dependency set is discovered by evaluation — you don't know which catalogue entries a book references until you've evaluated its print() — and it includes absence (a reference is broken because a key isn't there). Bazel cannot express "rebuild this because a name that didn't exist now does." Nix is content-addressed caching — same "inputs known up front" limitation, process-granular. TypeScript project references are project-granular and don't do name-level cutoff. Salsa / rustc's red-green is the right frame, because queries discover their dependencies as they run, and salsa tracks them per-revision with early cutoff.
The three things to get right, in order of how badly they'll bite:
Depend on the entry, not the catalogue. If every reference depends on "the catalogue," any edit anywhere invalidates every reference — the exact N² coupling A1 exists to kill, resurrected in the incremental layer. Reference-to-great must depend only on catalogue-entry-␀1␀. Salsa does this with interned keys and per-key revisions. This is the whole game.
Track negative/absence dependencies. "I looked up great and it wasn't there" must be recorded as a real dependency, or you'll miss your own stated case — "an added name flips a distant reference from failing to passing." When great is added, only the references with a recorded negative dependency on great re-run. Make-style and timestamp systems famously cannot do this; it's the reason they can't detect "a file that didn't exist now exists." Salsa can.
The firewall query. This is the pattern that saves you from your other big cost: a reference should depend on the target's identity and address-identity, not its body. Editing the prose of chapter A must not re-validate references pointing at A. In rustc this is the query that extracts a signature so that body edits don't invalidate dependents. For you: interpose a query that yields "does key K exist and what is its call number," and let references depend on that, not on the chapter's content. Then prose edits are local and references are stable.
Early cutoff is the right frame; its failure modes are (1) output-equality checks as expensive as recompute (cutoff buys nothing), (2) non-deterministic evaluation — if print() reads a clock, a global, or has order-dependence, red-green lies — which loops straight back to the spine finding: untracked or impure inputs make the whole scheme unsound, silently. rust-analyzer is salsa in production if you want a reference implementation.
6.2 + 6.5 — library science, and why they're one question
You're right that you're badly underusing this, and two of your questions collapse together. Authority control (unique author) and validated aliases (rename a key without breaking references) are the same mechanism: a canonical record with a set of variant forms and "see" cross-references. "The author query is unique" does not mean "the string is unique" — it means "the string resolves to exactly one authority record." An author is just a referrable thing whose card is an authority record carrying variant name-forms. Build the validated alias (6.5) and you get authority control (6.2) for free; they are one feature. The minimal honest version for hundreds of records: a small authority file, each entry an opaque id + a set of forms, and a build rule that refuses collisions and alias cycles. That's LCNAF/VIAF/ISNI/ORCID in miniature — ORCID is the one to look at for the "opaque id resolves human-facing variant forms" shape.
On opaque vs meaningful identity (6.5): your hand-written meaningful ids (the-semantics-of-books#the-mention) are self-documenting but encode a classification that will change — move the-mention out of that essay and the id lies or breaks. Wikidata chose Q42 opacity precisely to survive reorganization. The synthesis: store opaque, stable identity; let the meaningful name be a *label* (an access point) that resolves to the opaque id. But your authoring syntax references by meaningful key ([great]) — which it must, for ergonomics; nobody authors [Q42]. So the resolution is: authors write names, names resolve through the authority/alias layer to stable ids, and renaming makes the old name a "see" reference to the same id rather than deleting it. The failure mode to design against is silent alias chains (A→B→C) that rot; the build should refuse cycles and can warn on multi-hop. This is a 301 redirect that fails the build if its target is gone — the validated version of what the web does unsafely.
FRBR/IFLA-LRM — covered above; it's the backbone of conflict 1. The extra thing a real record carries that you haven't mentioned: relator codes (the role a person plays — author vs editor vs illustrator vs translator). Your "author" is really a relator; if Ana illustrates and Doug writes, "author" under-describes. And uniform title — the Work-level canonical title distinct from the title-as-printed — is exactly the Title/Heading distinction you're circling, and it's what a reference should bind to.
Ranganathan and pre- vs post-coordination — you are choosing a side. [[great]] fixes the key at declaration: that's pre-coordination. Pre-coordination makes the declaration the authority (good — it's what makes refuse-by-membership work) but makes faceted discovery rigid: if you later want to reach a thing by a combination of facets (subject × author × period), pre-coordinate keys can't compose and you'd re-cut headings. Post-coordination (tags combined at query time, à la LCSH's later drift) buys discovery flexibility at the cost of the membership guarantee. Given A1/A5, pre-coordination is the right choice for you — but name it, so nobody expects Ranganathan-style faceted queries to fall out of a system deliberately built to refuse anything not declared. Your subject/title/author "drawers" are access points, not facets; that's fine, just don't mistake three access points for a classification.
6.3 — two-sided references that refuse
Additions to your list, then the failure stories, which are what you actually asked for.
Belongs on the list: CTS-URN (you named it — it's your best prior art, see below), DOI/Handle (opaque id + resolver indirection = identity-outlives-location, the 6.5 pattern shipped at scale),ARK (persistence with an explicit commitment statement — the institution promising the id will resolve, which is the social half your build can't provide),W3C Web Annotation selectors (TextQuoteSelector: point into content by quote + prefix/suffix with a positional fallback — the robustness pattern you need for 6.6's deep citations), and language-server find-references / go-to-definition as a live two-sided system worth imitating for dev-time feedback.
Which got error reporting right, and wrong:
MediaWiki ␀0␀ renders a visible inline "cite error" at the point of use in the output. Right, because the error is loud and located (N7).
Sphinx nitpicky fails the build on an unresolved xref. Right, because it honors A5.
LaTeX ␀0␀ is the antipattern and the best failure story you'll get: an undefined reference renders as?? and emits a warning buried in a ten-thousand-line log nobody reads. Papers ship to publication with ?? and [?] in them regularly. That is precisely N7's quiet-failure death — a falsy return discarded by every caller — at document scale. Design against it explicitly: your unresolved reference must fail the build (A5) and be visible at the point of use if it ever renders at all.
TEI XPointer is the scale failure: scheme-based pointing into arbitrary structure was so complex almost nobody implemented the full spec, and the community retreated to xml:id — pointing only at explicitly declared anchors. The lesson lands directly on you: only allow references to declared anchors ([[]]), never to computed or positional locations. You've mostly chosen this — except the ToC ("references down to own parts") is positional, and it is the one place your refuse-by-membership guarantee leaks (see 6.9).
Obsidian/Roam block refs: the failure story is opaque per-block ids invisible in the text, so moving a block between files silently strips the anchor; and "unlinked mentions" is the post-coordinate shadow of your pre-coordinate mentions.
Xanadu: the design is the cautionary tale. Bidirectional, always-resolving, version-stable transclusion with no dangling links is so strong a guarantee it never shipped at scale. That guarantee is your A5 + two-sided reference. The web shipped by dropping it (404s exist). You're re-adding it — which is fine, because your corpus is closed, and closedness is exactly what makes A5 affordable. The moment you reference out (external citations), you're back in Xanadu's impossible regime — which is why conflict 2's fix (pull external identity in as Source cards) isn't optional polish; it's what keeps you on the shippable side of the line Xanadu died on.
CTS-URN deserves its own paragraph as your model. It identifies a passage by logical citation — work + passage reference — independent of edition or page: urn:cts:greekLit:tlg0012.tlg001:1.1-1.10. Citation identity is logical (work:passage), never physical (page). That is A3 (identity not address), N2 (survives re-layout), and the FRBR Work-binding, all in one deployed scheme from classics that has survived exactly the reorganizations you're worried about. If you read one thing off this list, read CTS.
6.4 — plugin vs bespoke, and killing the child processes
The honest limits, because they decide the boundary:
Babel plugin: one file's AST, syntactic only, no cross-file knowledge, no evaluation. It can do the [[]]/[] → Mention-node transform (pure syntax) and nothing that needs a value or global state.
TypeScript transformer: has the type graph across files but not values; your catalogue entries are runtime values (print() output), so a transformer can't build the catalogue. Type-level only.
Vite plugin: the right host — but for its machinery, not its model. Vite gives you the module graph, transform hooks, and crucially ␀1␀, the hook where you decide precisely what to invalidate on a change (N4). That's where your salsa engine plugs in. The catch: Vite's own invalidation is module-granular and importer-directed — it invalidates a module's importers, not its name-dependents. A rename that flips a distant reference from passing to failing lives in a module that doesn't import the renamed one, so Vite's default HMR won't invalidate it — you'll get stale-green, the reference is broken and the editor says fine. So: use Vite for dev server, transform, and HMR transport, but drive invalidation from your query engine through handleHotUpdate, not from Vite's module graph. No existing plugin does global non-monotone name-validation; that stays bespoke.
And the concrete escape from per-page child processes: Vite's SSR module runner (ssrLoadModule, or the newer environment/ModuleRunner API) evaluates your modules in-process with HMR support. That is "evaluate, don't parse" (6.4's premise) without a Node process per page. Combine it with scoped DI (so books don't need isolation) and, if you still want a blast radius, vm.createContext per book inside the one warm process. That collapses the 28-of-42 seconds and keeps the salsa cache hot across edits — the two wins are the same move.
6.6 — the grammar restructure
"Composition stops at the paragraph; below it, strings" is defensible and correct to do — with one carve-out that you must not collapse. A paragraph is not a leaf string, because your mentions live inside it. [[great]] occurs mid-prose; if the paragraph is opaque, the mention is trapped inside the string. So the honest leaf is:
text
paragraph → (string | mention | reference)*
a sequence of text-runs and inline anchors — still vastly smaller than word/letter objects (you drop the 33,158-walk because words, letters, and sentences-as-structure vanish), but you keep the one sub-paragraph object that earns its place: the inline mention/reference, because that is the thing the entire system is about. Don't over-collapse and lose the mention as an addressable inline node — Doug already said the prose mention "isn't casual… a reference should be able to go there," which means it's a declared anchor, not text.
What you lose without sentence/word objects is sub-paragraph citation granularity — you can't say "sentence 3 of paragraph 2." But you don't need sentence objects to recover it; you need a selector (the Web Annotation TextQuoteSelector: quote + surrounding context, resolved at build). CTS, legal pincites, and scripture verse-refs all show deep addressing is occasionally needed — and all of them addressinto a text without making every sentence a first-class node. Systems that pushed structure to the word and regretted it: densely-tagged TEI/XML where every token is an element becomes unmaintainable and slow — your 33,158-walk is a taste of that regret. Systems that stopped too coarse and regretted it: Markdown — no stable anchor below the heading, which is why every docs site bolts on heading slugs and why deep-linking a Markdown paragraph is perennially painful. The sweet spot is declared-anchor granularity, which is exactly what mentions give you. So: stop at paragraph, but let the leaf be text-with-inline-anchors, and add a selector for the rare deep citation rather than a sentence class.
6.9 — where this is most likely wrong
In rough order of how much it will cost you:
The assumption that evaluation is pure over tracked inputs. Everything incremental depends on it and the substrate currently violates it three ways: props bypass the bond, DI is captured at construction, and per-page isolation implies global state worth isolating from. Any untracked input makes early cutoff serve stale output silently — N7 violated invisibly, the single worst failure in your value system. This is both the most likely to be wrong and the most expensive. It's why "settle the dependency model first" is item 1.
A5 applied to external citations. Sound inside the corpus, unsound the moment a reference points out. Until Source cards exist, either the build breaks on things you don't control or A5 is quietly partial and you can't say which references are exempt.
The ToC as the hole in refuse-by-membership. Membership works for declared anchors; the ToC references "own parts" positionally. If a part is unnamed, the ToC binds to position, and position is not a catalogue member by identity — so the one place your guarantee leaks is exactly the derived views (ToC, Cover). Check whether ToC entries are catalogue members or a positional side-channel; if the latter, "all links guaranteed right" (A1) has an exception you haven't named. This is the TEI-XPointer lesson biting your own model.
The FRBR/call-number collision. Until identity (Work/card) and address (Manifestation/call number) are separate objects, N2 is aspirational — you'll keep finding references that broke on layout change, and the catalogue will keep carrying an address it shouldn't own.
Stale-green under non-monotone HMR. Vite's importer-directed invalidation won't catch a rename that breaks a name-dependent in a non-importing module. Lean on Vite HMR naively and the dev loop will show green over a broken reference — N7 at the exact moment N7 matters most, during editing.
One connective note, since this .public design is the same object as the type hierarchy from earlier in this thread: reference there was "the first relation over the node-operators — its validity is global, not local." The catalogue is that global relation materialized, and incrementality is the entire fight to make a global relation checkable locally again (the firewall query, the per-entry dependency, the negative-dependency tracking). That's why the catalogue and the incremental engine are not two systems — they're the same claim ("references are edges, and edge-validity is global") answered at two levels. If the dependency model in item 1 is right, that global relation becomes locally checkable and the whole thing holds together. If it's wrong, no amount of catalogue discipline downstream will save it.
Where I'd most want to be corrected: I've assumed the reason for per-page process isolation is shared mutable state. If it's something else — native module crashes, memory pressure per book, genuine untrusted content — then the "kill the child processes" recommendation weakens and the isolation ladder (vm → workers) matters more than scoped DI. That premise is worth checking before you commit to it, because a lot of the speed story rests on it.

Before the three asks: the headline is that Doug is right more often than not here, and on one point — mention-as-annotation — he's handed you something better than what I proposed, which reshapes the whole incremental story in your favor. I'll concede cleanly where my mechanical fix was solving a problem he's chosen not to have, and hold ground in the two or three places where a ruling has a hidden cost that his own method, turned on itself, exposes. Cathy asked for the disagreement over the concession, so where I think the domain answer is worse I'll say so plainly and show my work.
1. Where the rulings move the analysis
Title-as-call-number — I hold ground, but via his method, not against it. The functional claim is sound: one globally-unique, frozen string that identifies a book and seeds the address, with the URL derived. That binds to the Work and survives re-layout — N2 holds. But watch the tell. The library domain has two words here, and it invented the second one for exactly the reason that will bite you: title is a descriptive access point that catalogues explicitly refuse to make unique, and call number (class + cutter) is the unique, frozen, address-seed. The cutter number exists precisely because titles collide and titles change. So "globally-unique title" is fighting the domain at the one spot the domain already solved — and Doug's own "later: subject + title = class + cutter" is him rediscovering the call number under pressure. By his own rule — when the design has no domain word it has drifted; when the domain has a word, use it — the object he's missing is the call number, and the honest move is to name it now: freeze the call number, keep the title editable and non-unique. Reclassification is famously painful in real libraries (frozen call number ✓); fixing a title typo in a record is routine (mutable title ✓). Fusing them means freezing the reader-facing name, and that's the cost — the first time a book title has a typo or wants rephrasing, you either can't fix it or you edit the whole corpus. And you already have the fix in your own hands: [[This is Important]](important) already separates display from key — display varies, only important freezes. Book titles are the one place you didn't apply your own split. Apply it. That's not new machinery; it's the mention syntax generalized to books.
Frozen keys — I concede, and it's the cleaner call. My alias/redirect synthesis was solving rename-ergonomics, and Doug is choosing not to have that problem. Freezing is genuinely better for correctness: it kills the hardest incremental case outright (renames are non-monotone identity changes; without them your interned-key table is immutable, which is the salsa ideal handed to you free), and meaningful-but-frozen keys degrade gracefully — when the-semantics-of-books#the-mention moves essays, the key stops being self-documenting but still resolves, so it decays into an opaque id rather than breaking. My alias layer would have added exactly the rot he's avoiding (A→B→C chains). So: frozen wins. The cost is not in the freezing — it's in the namespace, and that's the real first break (see §3). One caveat that survives: freezing is right where the frozen thing is not reader-facing. The title is reader-facing. That's the single seam where freeze is worse, and it's the same seam as the call-number point above.
Citations-out-are-not-references — right, and cleaner than my Source-card patch. Making it a different object with weaker guarantees (well-formed + reachable, not semantic) dissolves the conflict instead of patching it, and it's the same eukaryote move you like: keep the strong guarantee inside the closed corpus, don't extend it to what you don't control. One leak, and it's a real one: reachability is not a build-stable property. If you check reachability in the build, you've imported the network's current state into a deterministic compiler — an offline build or a transient 502 now fails code that is correct, which is a false-red exception (bad under N7, since the loud failure must be a true failure) and network I/O in the hot loop (bad under N5). BibTeX/LaTeX don't check reachability for this reason; link-checkers run as a separate periodic job. So split the split: well-formedness is a build check (deterministic, local, keep it in always-refuse); reachability is out-of-band and non-blocking (warn, don't fail the build). And where a persistent id exists (DOI/Handle/ARK), cite that, not the raw URL — it's the one property raw URLs lack (location-independence), and it keeps citations-as-not-references while giving them the indirection the library domain uses for exactly this.
The ToC leak — agreed, it's your bug, and the design is the better of the two. Only addition: the same discipline has to cover every derived view, not just the ToC. The Cover holds Title/Author/Synopsis/ToC — confirm the Cover reaches its parts by name too, and that a section's synopsis is an authored declared writing (referrable) rather than a generated one (positional, not an anchor). The rule is uniform: derived views derive from declared anchors, never from position.
A card is a writing — fine, and it doesn't harm incrementality; it clarifies it. Cathy's worry is that card-is-writing plus writing-holds-annotations means a card isn't a flat row and the firewall gets harder. It's the reverse. You never depend on "the card"; you depend on the card'sprojected signature — (does key K exist, what's its call number). A fat card behind a thin signature is exactly what the firewall is for; richness behind the firewall costs nothing to dependents. Editing a card's annotation only ripples if it changes the projected signature; irrelevant card edits cut off. "Horizontal gene transfer" is the right image and it's load-bearing: a card is genetic material inserted laterally, present in the genome without being born through the render lineage — which tells you precisely where cards cost and where they don't. Cards participate in specification (they're writings; the spec pass walks them) but never in rendering (never in the DOM). So cards are O(referrable things) ≈ N×M work in the spec pass and zero in render — which is the right place to pay, given the spec pass is what you're making incremental. One type-hygiene note: forbid a card containing a card, or the catalogue-that-catalogues-books becomes catalogue-in-catalogue.
The leaf — this is the gift, and it makes your two worries answerable. writing ≈ (string | writing)* followed by annotation*, mention-as-annotation, is better than my (string | mention | reference)*, because it tells you exactly what the graph-relevant surface of a writing is: the annotation list is the entire graph surface; the prose is graph-inert. A writing's declarations (inbound keys it provides) and its references (outbound keys it needs) both live in the annotation list. So every edit partitions cleanly: touched an annotation → graph-relevant, run the query engine; touched only prose → graph-inert, skip the graph entirely, re-render just that one writing. That partition is the single biggest incremental win available to you and it falls straight out of Doug's ruling. So — Cathy's second question — annotations-as-signature is real, not pattern-matching: it's the true signature-vs-body cut. A reference pointing at this writing depends on which keys it declares (its annotations), never on its prose; prose edits leave inbound references stable by construction. That's the firewall, defined rather than approximated.
But — Cathy's first question, and it's sharp — yes, it's the same *class* of leak as the ToC, one level down, and it bites unless you anchor the annotation to its span with a declared marker rather than a computed offset. Here's the danger in Doug's exact wording: annotations come after the content ("a sequence of strings or writings followed by a sequence of annotations"). Separating the annotation from its locus forces a locator, and if that locator is an offset or "sentence 3," it drifts the instant prose is edited — the mention silently points at the wrong words (key resolves fine, span is wrong: a quiet semantic break, the worst kind). If instead the annotation's target is a declared inline marker placed in the content stream — …string, ⟦m⟧, string…, and the annotation says "I annotate m" — then the marker moves with the text, survives edits elsewhere, and only breaks if you delete the span it marks. That's the TEIxml:id-inline-anchor discipline versus the XPointer-offset trap you already learned to fear, and it's the W3C-Annotation distinction between a RangeSelector anchored to markup and a TextPositionSelector anchored to char offsets — the offset kind is the fragile one. So keep Doug's outer "content then annotations" shape; make the inner linkage marker-based, not positional. Do that and the leak closes; skip it and you've reopened the ToC bug at sub-paragraph scale, where it's harder to see.
Author — the relator gap is real, and it's the same shape as your earlier Author type. "Author = autobiography, unique to the library, variants handled as different books" is fine for authorship and fine at this corpus's scale — the place it breaks is when one human uses two name-forms and someone later wants their works collated (that's what VIAF/ISNI exist for), and for a library authored by Doug, Ana, and AI collaborators that day is far off. Low priority, name it, move on. But the gap Cathy flags is not that — it's roles. Ana illustrates; Doug writes. "Author = autobiographical subject who wrote this" has exactly one person↔work relation and can't say "Ana illustrated." The domain word is the statement of responsibility / relator: author, editor, illustrator, translator are siblings, a role-tagged attribution. In your earlier type sketch Author was specialize(Reference) — a reference in the attribution role; the honest generalization is that attribution is a family of roles specializing Reference, and Author is one of them. So keep author-as-autobiography for the primary author, but the person↔book edge needs a role tag, or Ana is either miscredited as an author or uncreditable. That's a real gap and it's cheap to close in his own type language.
2. The shortest correct path to the dependency model — and the four fixes shorten it
The keystone I under-weighted is Doug's "find out in the VS Code Problems panel." That doesn't add a surface beside the compiler — it is the dependency model wearing the editor's face, and it converges with "settle the dependency model first" rather than competing with it. What the editor needs (incremental diagnostics on edit) and what the dev server needs (incremental invalidation on edit) are the same computation: given this edit, what changed in the graph, and is anything now broken? That's the query engine. So the architecture is one long-lived process holding the evaluated, incremental library model, exposed over two transports — LSP publishDiagnostics to the Problems panel (N4/N7, the editor), and Vite handleHotUpdate to the browser (N4, the page). It is one job (maintain an incremental evaluated model and answer "what changed / what's broken") with two protocols, not one process doing two jobs. The failure to avoid is two engines — a tsserver plugin computing one answer, a Vite plugin another — that drift, so the editor says green while the browser says red. A pure tsserver plugin can't be the engine anyway: it has the type graph but no values, and your facts are values behind print() and 126-deep getters. So the engine must evaluate, which means it must be long-lived and in-process (the same reason to kill the per-page child processes — pending ruling 5), because that's what keeps the warm cache the incrementality needs. Everything converges on the one process: the dependency model, the death of the child processes, the LSP surface, and Vite HMR are one long-lived incremental query engine with several faces.
And the four fixes make that engine smaller, because each one removes a hard case:
Frozen keys remove renames — the non-monotone identity churn that is the nightmare of incremental systems. What's left is add and delete, no rename. Intern each key once, immutably; that interned table is the card catalogue's spine.
Mention-as-annotation makes dependency extraction trivial and prose inert: read a writing's annotation list to get both its inbound signature (keys declared) and its outbound deps (keys referenced). The engine never reads prose.
Citations-out-not-references keep the graph closed — only intra-library edges inside the engine, external reachability shoved out-of-band. A closed graph is what makes salsa-style early cutoff sound; the moment external non-determinism is inside the core, cutoff lies.
Title/call-number as frozen address-seed makes the firewall signature stable: signature(writing) = (keys-declared, call-number) changes only when a key is added or removed, never on a prose or display edit.
So the path, mostly by subtraction:
One long-lived process; evaluate in it (Vite's SSR module runner / ModuleRunner gives you in-process evaluation with HMR — that's your escape from a Node process per page). 2. Intern keys once, immutably. 3. Extract each writing's graph surface from its annotation list alone. 4. Firewall: references depend on the target's signature (exists + call-number), never its body — so prose edits invalidate only that writing's render, annotation edits invalidate the graph locally. 5. Track negative dependencies — "referenced K, K absent" is a recorded dep on K's absence — so adding K re-runs exactly the references waiting on it; this is the one non-monotone case freezing leaves you. 6. Two transports over the one engine, and drive Vite's invalidation from the engine's changed-set, not from Vite's module graph — Vite invalidates a module's importers, but a rename that flips a name-dependent lives in a module that doesn't import the renamed one, so Vite's default HMR won't touch it and you get stale-green. 7. Purity/containment so re-evaluation is deterministic — scoped DI, all inputs tracked including props, no clock/global reads in print(). That last is the precondition, and the LSP surface raises its stakes: an untracked input now serves stale-green live in the Problems panel as you type, which is N7 violated at the exact moment N7 matters most.
This is the point from the earlier thread cashed out: reference is the one global relation over your local node-operators, and incrementality is the whole fight to make that global relation locally checkable again — the firewall query, the per-entry dependency, the negative-dependency tracking. The catalogue and the incremental engine aren't two systems; they're that one claim answered at two levels.
3. What breaks first — and what breaks worst
They're different, and you should track both.
First (earliest, most certain, from ordinary authoring): the key namespace. Frozen + meaningful + referrable-from-anywhere, taken together, force a decision you haven't visibly made — is the key namespace flat-global or scoped per book? If flat, then two authors independently choosing a common short key — intro, overview, note, def, important — collide, and this starts at tens of books and is constant at hundreds. It's loud (the build refuses the second declaration — good, N7-consistent), but the loser must pick a worse name, and because keys are frozen and meaningful, the namespace degrades toward important-2, semantics-important — which is the exact obscurity Doug forbids, produced by the collision-avoidance. Three rulings interacting manufacture the thing his naming rule prohibits. Here's the resolution, and it's a domain argument he should find congenial: real library references are always qualified — you cite "Rubino, Semantics, p. 41," never a bare "p. 41." The un-library-like move is the bare cross-book reference; qualification is the norm. So scope keys by book/subject, and your syntax already has the slot — [Doug](MY Library Log) puts the qualifier in the paren. A bare [great] means "great in this book"; [great](otherbook) qualifies. Scoping makes collisions intra-book (one author's own namespace, manageable), and it'smore in-domain, not less. So the thing to settle before you build references: keys are book-scoped, cross-book references qualify, and the flat-global reading — which is what makes the collision fatal — is a misreading of a syntax that already carries the qualifier. Pin that and the first break doesn't happen.
Close behind it: the frozen title as frozen display name (§1). First time a title has a typo. Fix now with the display/key split you already use for mentions.
Worst (silent, dangerous, but requires the engine to exist first): stale-green. Two forms. (a) Vite-driven invalidation missing a name-dependent in a non-importing module — the editor and browser say fine, the reference is broken. (b) An untracked input (a prop bypassing the bond, a service captured at construction, a nondeterministic read in print()) making early cutoff serve stale output. Both surface as green over red, now live in the Problems panel, which is N7's quiet-falsy-return failure — the one you spent a day proving out in the other codebase — reborn at the substrate level. You notice (a) by testing rename/add-that-flips-a-distant-reference explicitly in your HMR harness; you notice (b) by making evaluation deterministic and asserting it (same input, same output, or throw). These are why the dependency model is item 1 and why the LSP surface makes getting it right non-optional rather than merely nice.
And third, lower but real: annotation-to-span drift if the linkage is offset-based (§1) — the mention resolves but highlights the wrong words, a quiet semantic break, avoidable by marker-anchoring.
Where I'd still want correcting: the whole "one long-lived in-process engine, kill the child processes" recommendation rests on the isolation reason being shared mutable state. If ruling 5 comes back as memory pressure per book, a native-module crash, or genuine untrusted content, that recommendation weakens and the isolation ladder (scoped-DI → vm.createContext → worker_threads) matters more than I've let it. Read that before anyone acts on it — it's the one premise under the speed story I haven't been able to check.
