A correction, and I want you to push back on it rather than accept it — I read the substrate today and the thing we both called "correctness-fatal untracked input" appears to be narrower than either of us said. I would rather find out I am wrong now than build on this.
What I actually found
You said, and I relayed, that props bypassing the bond is an untracked input and therefore fatal to early cutoff. Doug then asked the question that made me go read it: "could the bond constructor, in theory, be called on render? Is there a way to call it over and over every render without breaking everything, perhaps using cached DOM? If not, should I imagine props as the source of real reactivity that doesn't require rerender?"
The bond constructor is already called on every render. Our React function component's body, unconditional:
js
p[$rendering$] = true;
p[$apply$](props);                                 // props written as fields, EVERY render
if (bond) withAsker(p, () => p[$bond$](), true);   // the bond, EVERY render
const output = augment(withAsker(p, () => p[$renderView$](), true), react, p);
p[$viewCache$] = output;
and [$bond$]() is this[$synthesis$].bond({ children }). So the call happens every time. What is guarded is one level deeper, inside the synthesis:
js
if (this._lastBondArgs && sameArgs(newArgs, this._lastBondArgs)) {
    // Children unchanged — skip bond constructor
}
And the retention Doug called "the cached DOM" already exists. On first render the factory derives the instance; on every render after it looks the instance up by id and gets the same object back. React re-renders the component; the chemical object persists across renders and across the whole mount.
Why I think we were both too broad
If the view re-runs on a prop change — and it does, because React re-rendered and $renderView$ is called unconditionally — then the rendered output is a function of props. Props are reactive through React's own render. What they do not do is re-run the bond constructor's BODY.
So the precise statement seems to be: props bypass RECONSTRUCTION, not rendering. And the untracked input is not "props" but the much narrower derived state computed in the bond body from a prop.
I can name one instance. Our writing base ends its bond constructor with:
ts
if (this.$print !== undefined) this.parenthetical = !this.$print;
$print is a prop. parenthetical is derived from it in the bond body. So change print without changing children and parenthetical is stale — the view re-runs, but against a value that did not update. I have read this path, not executed it.
What I want from you — bounded, three things
1. Is my correction right, or am I now being too narrow? Specifically: for an incremental compiler's early cutoff, is "the rendered output is a function of props because the view re-runs" actually sufficient, or does a memoised object that outlives the render still poison the graph in a way I am not seeing? I am suspicious of my own relief here.
2. What breaks if we simply remove the ␀0␀ guard and let the bond body run every render? My reading: any bond constructor that MUTATES rather than derives would re-apply its mutation. Ours appear to be written defensively already — one guards with if (this.heading() === undefined), another with if (this.path() === undefined && …) — which suggests whoever wrote them already felt this pressure. Is "make every constructor idempotent and run it every render" a known-good position, or a known trap? Who has done it, and what did it cost them? React's own StrictMode double-invocation is the nearest thing I can think of and it was introduced precisely to force idempotence — is that the right analogy?
3. Doug's fallback, which I no longer think he needs but want judged: "should I not view the children as being mutable, and instead imagine props as the source of real reactivity that doesn't require rerender?" That is a genuinely different architecture — children become static structure, props become the reactive channel, and reactivity happens without reconstruction. Signals-without-VDOM, roughly. Is that a better model for what we are building than "run the constructor every render"? What does each cost at the scale of a compiler that evaluates hundreds of books?

Your correction holds at the mechanism level, and I was too broad. But the safety argument you're reaching for — "props are reactive because the view re-runs" — is the wrong reason to feel safe, and if you build onthat rather than on the narrower true statement, it will hurt you exactly where you can't see it. So: yes on the mechanism, no on the relief. Here's the split.
The correct statement is narrower than "derived state computed in the bond body from a prop." It's: any state the bond body writes to the persisting object from a non-children input. Your parenthetical = !$print is the pure case, but the class is wider than derivation — it includes anything the bond allocates or registers from a prop, not just anything it computes. And the reason the object persistence matters — your suspicion is right to persist — is that the poison isn't in the object's own view. It's in dependents. If X's bond caches a prop-derived value and Y reads that value through the reactive graph, a prop change on X updates neither X's cache nor Y, and the staleness propagates one or more hops away from the edit. Your parenthetical example is the mild version because parenthetical is read by X's own view, which re-runs. The dangerous version is the one where the bond-cached-from-prop value is read by another writing — there the "view re-runs" argument gives you nothing, because it's the wrong object's view. So the memoized object does poison the graph, but only through that one write pattern; children-derived state is safe (it recomputes exactly when the bond runs, which is when children change), and props-as-fields read live by the view are safe. Narrow the poison to the write pattern, don't absolve the object.
Which turns the safety condition into a layering rule, not a tracking fact: graph-relevant data flows through children → through the bond → tracked; props carry view-time display state, read live by the view; and the bond body must never read a prop. Under that discipline early cutoff is sound because the graph surface is bonded — and notice this is the same convergence you and Doug already found: [[great]](important) puts the key in children (bonded, tracked), <Mention as="great"> puts it in props (display, not graph). The design already routes graph identity through the tracked channel. parenthetical = !$print is the design's own rule being broken — a prop consumed by the bond — and the fix is not to track props but to forbid the bond from reading them: make parenthetical a view-time getter over $print, or compute it in the view, never cache it in the bond. Go audit for the pattern "bond body reads a$-prop and writes a field"; every hit is a latent stale-green, and the ones read by other writings are the ones that will actually bite.
Now the push-back you asked for, and it's under everything above: you have not verified that a prop change triggers a React re-render of that component. "The view re-runs on a prop change" is true only if the prop change flows through React's props path — parent re-renders, passes new props, React re-renders the child. If props are instead written imperatively onto the persisting object (looked-up-by-id, field assigned directly, outside React's knowledge), then React does not re-render, the view does not re-run, and props aren't reactive at all — they're mutable fields nobody re-reads. You said you read the path but didn't execute it. This is the load-bearing line. Execute it: change a prop, confirm the view actually re-runs. If it does, your correction stands (modulo the bond-reads-prop hole). If it's an imperative write, the relief is misplaced and the original broad worry was closer to right — for the opposite reason we both first said.
On removing the ␀0␀ guard (2): your reading is right, and the tell you spotted is the whole answer. Those if (this.heading() === undefined) guards are hand-rolled dependency arrays — useEffect(fn, []) written by hand. Whoever wrote them already felt exactly this pressure and solved it per-constructor. So removing the guard is safe for the currently-defensive constructors (their guarded inits no-op on re-run) and unsafe for any that mutate, accumulate, or allocate identity without a guard. The StrictMode analogy is exact and worth taking literally: React double-invokes precisely to surface non-idempotent bodies, because React's entire model is "the body runs every render, make it pure." So "run every render, be idempotent" is known-good — but it's known-good because React quarantines side effects out of the body into effects that run on a different schedule. The trap is not idempotent derivation; it's that your bond body mixes derivation with identity-allocation (creating children, registering things), and "run every render" then forces you to makeside effects idempotent by hand, across hundreds of constructors, where one missing guard is a silent per-render leak or a duplicated child. Plus the scale cost: running every bond body on every re-evaluation is O(all bonds), which is the exact opposite of the incremental cutoff N4/N5 demand — fine for a UI (React eats it), wrong for a compiler evaluating hundreds of books. So don't remove the guard globally. Split the bond intopure derivation (cheap, run always, no guard needed) and identity-allocation (must run once, guarded) — the render/effect split imported — and make the guard automatic (dependency-tracked), because a hand-rolled guard is the surface stale-green breeds on.
On Doug's fallback (3): it isn't a fallback. It's the better model, and the reason is that it's the same partition the rest of your design already committed to. "Children static, props reactive, no reconstruction" is signals-without-VDOM — Solid's model. Structure is built once; a signal that changes notifies only the exact reactive reads that depend on it; reconstruction happens only on a structural (children) change. Map that onto the domain: the containment tree is static after construction (a display edit doesn't restructure a book), display edits update only the fragments that read them, and reconstruction fires only on a genuine edit to the tree. That is precisely the incremental compiler's partition — structural edits reconstruct and re-run graph queries; display edits update fine-grained with no graph work — and the fact that Solid's reactivity model and your early-cutoff model are the same partition is a strong signal it's the right endpoint rather than a coincidence. The decisive difference from "run the constructor every render": in the React model cutoff ismanual (the sameArgs guard, the if undefined guards) so stale-green is the default failure and correctness is opt-in; in the signal model cutoff is automatic — a value that didn't change notifies nobody — so stale-green becomes structurally hard rather than vigilance-dependent. Given that stale-green is the thing you most fear and the thing the LSP surface makes most costly, automatic cutoff is worth a lot.
The costs, honestly: it's the larger substrate change (moving off re-render-plus-reconcile is not a small refactor), and it only pays if the reactive reads are genuinely fine-grained — the view must read signals lazily at the point of use, not compute eagerly and cache, or you've bought signals and still recompute broadly. And it demands the same layering discipline from the top: what's a signal (reactive, no reconstruction) versus what's structure (children, reconstruction on change) has to be a clean line, which is the same line as bonded-versus-view above. So the two viable paths are "run-every-render + idempotence + manual cutoff" (familiar, correct-able, wrong perf profile for a compiler, stale-green by default) and "signals + build-once + automatic cutoff" (bigger change, matches the partition you already chose, stale-green by construction hard). For a system whose whole spine is incremental validation under a human attention budget, the second is the coherent choice — Doug's "fallback" is the architecture the rest of the design has been implying.
One thing I can't check and won't pretend to: everything in (3) assumes the reason for the current re-render model isn't load-bearing elsewhere in $Chemistry — some other feature that needs the view to re-run wholesale. If there is one, the signal migration costs more than I've priced. That's worth knowing before committing, same as the process-isolation premise still open from before.

13:30 UTC, 17 September 2026
Names first, reasoning under each. And one correction up front, because it's the highest-value thing here: on question 3 you already have the answer in your own numbers and are about to walk past it.
1. The technique, named — and where the regular/CF line falls
What you're building is a two-phase island/injection parser: a host tokenizer decides which spans are yours (the JsxText regions), and a tokenizer-per-island scans each span. The standard names for the parts: your inner grammar is a delimited construct with an optional trailing argument, and the right lexical technique for it is a scanner with escape-aware longest-match, not a parser. The term of art for "the opener decides the closer" is a mode or lexer state — you were right, it's one state variable, no stack.
Now the regular/CF line, which is Doug's actual push. Your reasoning ("regular is sufficient, so use regular") and his ("regular has context-free options") aren't in conflict, and the resolution is precise:your syntax is regular, and you should keep it regular, but you should recognize it with a *tokenizer* (a lexer that emits typed tokens with offsets), not with a *regex*. Those are two different things people conflate. A regex over the region is regular and brittle — it's where escape handling and error location go to die. A hand-written or generatedscanner is also regular but gives you (a) precise error offsets, (b) clean escape handling as a lexer transition, and (c) the "unterminated construct" failure you want, at the exact byte. So "regular" is the right class; "regex" is the wrong tool; "scanner/tokenizer" is the right tool for the same class. That's most of what his comment buys you without going CF at all.
What context-free would actually buy you is exactly one thing: nesting. A CFG's power over a regular grammar is recursion — balanced, arbitrarily-deep structure. So the real question collapses to "do I want nesting," and here I think you're right and Doug's caution, read as 'go CF,' is wrong for this grammar — but there's a narrow reason to want one bounded level that you haven't named, so let me give you the case against yourself before I agree with you.
The case for nesting: a reference inside a mention's copy — $[the theory of [[reference]]](key) — a mention whose display text itself contains a link. That's not nonsense the way $[a $[b]] is; it's a mention that mentions. And a reference inside a title — a book titled after a linked term. If those are things authors will write, you want one level of nesting (references inside the copy of the outer construct), and that single level is still regular-ish if the inner set is restricted, but is cleanest expressed as a tiny CFG: construct → sigil '[' (text | reference)* ']' key?. That's the CF option worth its cost — not arbitrary recursion, reference-inside-copy, one level, asymmetric (a reference nests in a mention; a mention does not nest in a reference).
The case against — and why I'd still forbid it initially: you don't need it to be parsed nested, you need it to be resolved nested, and those separate. Scan the outer construct's copy as opaque text in phase one; run the same scanner again over that copy in a second pass to find inner references. Two flat passes give you one level of nesting without a CFG, without a stack, and without giving up the "opener chooses closer, no stack" property you correctly prize. So: stay regular, recognize with a scanner not a regex, and get nesting — if you want it — by re-scanning copy, not by going context-free. The only reason to actually adopt the CFG is if you want unbounded nesting, and for this domain unbounded nesting is meaningless ($[a $[b $[c]]] has no reading), so don't. Doug is right that you shouldn't collapse to the weakest formalism reflexively; he's right that there's a CF option; the CF option here is nesting; and nesting here is best had by re-scanning rather than by recursion. You reached the right endpoint; he's right that you should be able to say why you're refusing the CFG rather than merely that regular suffices.
2. The prior art, and their scars
The systems you named split cleanly into two lessons — region and escape — and different ones got each right.
Region question (which spans are mine), best-to-worst for your purpose:
Astro and the Svelte/Vue SFC compilers got it right by doing exactly what you're doing: a real host parser establishes typed regions, and the micro-syntax is scanned only inside the designated ones. Astro's compiler is the closest structural match to your design — it's a Go-based parser that identifies template regions and treats expressions as islands. Svelte and Vue SFCs use@vue/compiler-sfc and Svelte's compiler to carve <template>/<script>/<style> into regions first, then parse each with the right grammar. The lesson they all embody: never regex the whole file; establish regions with a real parser, then scan regions. You've already done this with JsxText. This is the single most important thing and you got it right.
MDX is the cautionary tale on regions, and its scar is directly relevant. MDX embeds JSX-and-expressions inside Markdown, and the hard, years-long problem was exactly the boundary: where does Markdown stop and a JSX expression begin, especially with {} which means one thing in Markdown text and another as an expression. MDX v1→v2 was substantially a reimplementation of the boundary rule (they moved to a real MDAST/micromark-based parser precisely because the ad-hoc region detection couldn't be made correct). The lesson: the region boundary is the whole game, and if you get it from a real grammar you win, and if you get it from heuristics you rewrite. You're getting it from the TS parser — right side of that line.
Markdoc (Stripe's) is your closest inner-syntax analog and the one to actually read. Its {% tag %} / {% /tag %} syntax with []-ish attributes is a sigil-delimited construct with typed arguments, and crucially Markdoc runs its own tokenizer (it's a markdown-it plugin, so it rides an established tokenizer rather than regexing). Its attribute/annotation syntax is the direct precedent for your optional (key). Read Markdoc's tokenizer for how it handles the construct-with-trailing-attributes shape — that's your [copy](key) almost exactly.
Handlebars-in-JSX is the worst case and worth one sentence: {{ }} inside JSX collides with JSX's own { }, and there is no clean region rule, which is why it never became a real pattern. The lesson is the anti-lesson: don't pick sigils that collide with the host's active syntax. Yours (.[, $[, [[) don't collide with JSX's {} — good — but verify against MDX-style ␀6␀ expressions if you ever allow them, and against the fact that [[ is legal TS in a JsxExpression (arr[[0][0]]), which is why scanning only JsxText and not JsxExpression is load-bearing, not incidental.
Escape question, best-to-worst:
Backslash (\]) is what almost everyone uses — Markdown, MDX, Markdoc, JS strings — and its virtue is that it'sthe escape convention, so authors reach for it without being taught. Its scar: backslash inside.tsx string-adjacent contexts fights the host's own escaping, and in JSX text (where you are) backslash is not special, so you'd actually be safe — but authors' fingers assume it is, which causes confusion the other direction (they write \] expecting magic where none is needed elsewhere).
Doubling the delimiter (]] to mean literal ]) is the other common choice (it's how quotes escape in CSV, SQL, and many template languages). Virtue: no escape character at all. Scar: it collides directly with your [[ ]] reference closer — you cannot both use ]] as "literal ]" and as "reference close." So doubling is out for you, structurally.
Your dot-escape (␀0␀) is unusual, and its one real risk is exactly the case you named and accepted — .[The Title.] unterminated — but there's a second-order scar you haven't hit: the dot is also your sigil. .[ opens a title; .] escapes a bracket; so a title whose copy ends with a sigil-like sequence, or any prose where .] appears for non-escape reasons (a sentence ending in a bracketed aside: "see the appendix.]" — unlikely in prose but not impossible), becomes ambiguous to a reader even if not to the scanner. The deeper issue: you're overloading ␀5␀ across three jobs — title sigil (.[), subject/author sigil (.. ...), and escape (.]). A scanner disambiguates them by position (leading vs. before-]), so it's decidable, but it's cognitively loaded for authors, and author-facing ambiguity is where your "obscurity" rule bites. If you want the escape maximally teachable, backslash is the safer choice precisely because it carries no other meaning in your syntax, whereas the dot carries three. I'd weigh "one escape convention everyone knows and that means nothing else here" (backslash) against "consistency with the dot-sigil family" (your .]), and I lean backslash — not because .] fails to parse, but because the escape character should be the one character that has no other role, and the dot has three roles already. That's the reason you asked for and hadn't hit.
3. The cold pass — you already beat 16.6 s and are looking at the wrong number
Here's the correction. You will never pay 16.6 s more than once, and you've already said why: you persist a per-book digest between builds. The cold pass over 8000 files is a first-run-ever cost, amortized to zero across every subsequent build, and the warm edit cost — the number that actually meets N5's "from when I ask to when it happens" — is 2 ms for the one file that changed. So rank the options by that framing:
Persist + re-parse only changed files: this is the real answer, and you already built it. The cold pass is once-ever; steady state is 2 ms × (files touched this edit) ≈ 2 ms. Content-hash each file (you have the digest); on change, re-scan that file, update its rows in the interned table. This is the salsa/query-cache pattern from the earlier thread, applied to the scan. Nothing else on your list matters if this is in place, because nothing else is on the warm path.
␀0␀ instead of ␀1␀: yes, usable, and it is the fiddly part — but you'd only reach for it to bring the cold pass down, which you just established you pay once. The JSX handling in the raw scanner is real but awkward: the scanner has reScanJsxText and scanJsxToken methods precisely because JSX text can't be tokenized in the default mode — the parser drives mode switches the scanner can't decide alone, so a bare scanner walk has to re-implement the JSX-context state machine (when are you in JsxText vs. an expression vs. an attribute). That's the "fiddly part everyone avoids," and avoiding it is correct unless the cold number becomes load-bearing. It isn't, so don't.
tree-sitter: the right tool for a different problem — incremental re-parse within a file as you type, character by character, in an editor. You don't have that problem; your unit of change is a file (an author saves a .tsx), and file-granular re-scan at 2 ms/file is already under the perception floor. tree-sitter would buy you sub-file incrementality you don't need, at the cost of a second grammar to maintain alongside the TS parser and a second source of truth about "which spans are JSX text." The one scenario where tree-sitter wins: if you move to keystroke-latency validation inside the editor (the LSP surface from before) and 2 ms/file on every keystroke of a large file starts to show. Even then, TS's own incremental language service is the more natural fit since you're already in TS. So: not tree-sitter, because your change unit is the file and file-granular is already fast enough.
The fourth option, which is your real question buried in the last line: should the micro-syntax run as a separate pass over raw text, not through the TS parser at all? Yes — and this is the most interesting thing in your message. You don't need the program, you need the JSX-text regions, and there's a cheaper way to get approximately those than a full parse. But the honest answer is that the cheap way is a trap you already documented: the reason you parse as TSX and walk JsxText is that a raw scan can't tell a sigil in JSX text from a sigil in a String.raw, a comment, a type argument, or an import path — you verified that today. A separate raw-text pass re-opens exactly the false-positive surface the TS walk closes. So the TS parse isn't overhead you can shed; it's buying you the region correctness that a raw pass would sacrifice, and MDX's entire v1→v2 rewrite is the receipt for what happens when you try to get regions without a real grammar. Keep the parser for region-finding; the thing you can separate is the inner scan (which is already separate and already 2 ms). So the fourth option's correct form is: don't separate region-finding from the parser (that's what makes you correct), do keep the inner scan separate and cached (that's what makes you fast). You've already arrived at both.
Net on 3: the number to beat isn't 16.6 s, it's 2 ms, and you already beat it. Persist-and-diff is the answer; scanner/tree-sitter/raw-pass are all optimizations of a cold path you pay once. The only thing I'd actually do here is confirm the digest-diff invalidation is correct under the nasty case from before — a file that adds a key which flips a distant file's reference from failing to passing — because that distant file didn't change, so a naive "re-scan changed files" updates the table but doesn't re-validate the dependent. That's the negative-dependency tracking from the earlier thread, and it's the one place file-granular diffing quietly under-invalidates. The scan is fine; the validation triggered by the scan is where the stale-green hides.
4. Escape — covered above
Short version, since I folded the reasoning into §2: .] parses fine and your unterminated-.[The Title.] failure is loud and acceptable. The reason to reconsider isn't parsing, it's that the dot already carries three jobs (title sigil, author/subject sigil, escape) and an escape character is best assigned to a character with no other role — which is why backslash, boring as it is, is the safer pick. Not a blocker; a papercut you'll feel when you write the author docs and have to explain that . means declare-here, declare-up-one, and not-a-bracket depending on where it sits.
One place I'd want to be corrected: I've assumed authors will occasionally want a reference inside a mention's or title's copy (the §1 nesting case). If they never will — if copy is always plain text — then even the re-scan-for-nesting machinery is dead weight, and your original flat-regular scanner is not just sufficient but complete, and Doug's "CF options" comment resolves to "considered and correctly declined." Whether that case is real is an authoring question I can't answer from here; it's worth asking your actual authors before you build even the two-pass version.

A notation question that turned into a semantics question, and I think we may be about to borrow the wrong half of C. Bounded ask — I want you to tell me where the analogy actually breaks, not to bless it.
The situation
We are designing a two-sided reference system for a library compiler. Declarations and uses are written as sigil-bracket forms embedded in JSX prose, resolved statically at build time, refusing on non-membership. Roughly:
text
.[ The Book Title ](key)      declares a title   — one per file
..[ The Author ](key)         declares an author — one per book, on the cover
...[ The Subject ](key)       declares a subject — one per book, on the cover
$[ The Mentioned Text ](key)  declares an inline anchor
[[ The Reference ]](key)      refers to something declared elsewhere
Two problems with that set pushed us toward pointer notation. First, $ already means something in this project — $Writing, $Book, the $-prefix marks about the representation of, so reusing $ for anchors makes one mark mean two things. Second, [[…]] carries MediaWiki's meaning, which is link — the use side — so using it to declare fights its host, and using it to refer leaves it doing the same job as $[…] from the opposite end with no principle distinguishing them.
So: & to declare, * to refer. Except Doug then pushed on it and I think he found something real.
What Doug said, and where I think he is right
"When you give a title, aren't you inventing a memory address? A subject too, but a memory address to a reference. An author is like subject but the thing is more literal. A mention is inventing a memory address."
I think "inventing a memory address" is exactly right and is the cleanest statement anyone has made about this system. A title does not reference a book — it is what makes the book referenceable at all. In C that is neither & nor *; it is the declaration. int x; is what gives x an address. &x merely takes it afterwards. So title and mention are allocations with names, at two scales.
"I always wanted ␀0␀ to be reference for, ␀1␀ dereference of."
Prefix versus postfix to disambiguate the two roles * plays in C. I know this is a known complaint about C's declarator syntax and that later languages moved on it — Go's var p *int / *p, Rust's &T / *p — but I would like the real history and whether postfix-deref has ever been tried and why it did or did not survive.
Where I think he is NOT right — please adjudicate both
1. ␀0␀ for catalogues. He proposes doubling the star for a thing one level further out — "the subject is a reference to a reference for books."
My objection: in C the count of stars is a property of the type (int**), while & and * are operations that move exactly one level. Those are different kinds of thing, and conflating them is precisely the confusion C's declarator syntax is notorious for. "A subject is a reference to a reference for books" is a claim about the type; ** as a written mark would be a claim about the operation. Which do we actually mean, and does any language successfully write indirection depth as a repeated operator without inheriting that confusion?
2. And the one I think matters most — is our operation a dereference at all?
Doug asked it himself: "when you ask for something aren't you dereferencing it? Or are you referencing it because you get the code."
In C, *p yields the value. In our system, resolving *[P ?= NP] yields a URL — which is itself an address. We never reach a value. We turn one address (a human-written name) into another address (a location). That looks to me like address translation, which is what an MMU or a symbol table or a linker does, and not what * does.
If that is right, then the whole reference operation is &-shaped rather than *-shaped — or it is neither and pointer notation is the wrong family, however appealing the two-sidedness is.
What I want, in order
1. Adjudicate the three above. Especially the third: is name → location a dereference, or is it translation/resolution, and does the distinction have a standard name I should be using? Doug is right about the deep thing and wrong about the notation, and the two are connected: the reason&/* feels like it fits is the same reason it will mislead your readers. Let me take the three adjudications in the order that matters, because the third one dissolves the first two.
The operation is not a dereference. It's resolution, and the standard name is binding/lookup in a namespace.
Doug asked the right question against himself and then didn't trust the answer. Name → location is not dereference. Dereference (*p) is the operation that follows an address to the value it holds — it's the last step, the one that touches the referent. Your operation never touches a referent; it turns a name into a location, and the location is itself a reference. You said "address translation," and you're close, but the honest name is narrower and older: resolution — specifically, binding a name in a namespace to what the namespace has recorded for it. The systems you listed are not equally good analogies; they sort exactly along this line, and the sort tells you which family you're in.
MMU (virtual→physical address): wrong analogy. That's address→address translation with no names — both sides are addresses, the mapping is arithmetic-ish, and there's no membership question. Refusal-by-non-membership is foreign to it. Drop it.
Linker symbol resolution: very close, and probably your truest mechanical analogy. A linker has definitions (a symbol given a location — your declaration) and references (a use of a symbol elsewhere — your reference), and it refuses on non-membership: an unresolved external symbol is a link error, which is your always-refuse (A5) exactly. The linker even has your two-sidedness as first-class vocabulary: .defined vs .undefined symbols. If you want the mechanism named, your compiler is a linker over a library, and "the catalogue refuses by non-membership alone" is link-time symbol resolution, full stop.
Symbol table / lexical binding: the same thing one level more abstract, and the right conceptual name. A declaration binds a name; a use looks it up; an unbound use is an error. This is the vocabulary compilers have used for fifty years and it fits you with zero deformation.
DNS and URN→URL: the closest by shape to what you emit, because your resolved output is literally a URL, and DNS/URN-resolution is precisely "a name that resolves to a location, indirected so the location can change under a stable name." This is your N2 (survives re-layout) named in someone else's system: a URN is stable identity, a URL is current location, and the resolver is the indirection between them. CTS-URN from the earlier thread lives here. If you want the identity-outlives-location property to have a pedigree, it's URN→URL resolution.
So the distinction has a standard name and you should use it: this is resolution (name→binding), not dereference (address→value). The tell that clinches it: dereference can be chained to a value (**p → *p → value), but your chain has no value at the bottom — it's names and locations all the way down, because a library is a graph of references, not a store of values. A system whose leaves are references, not values, is a namespace, and its fundamental operation is lookup, not dereference. Doug's "or are you referencing it because you get the code" is him noticing there's no value at the bottom — and that observation, taken seriously, breaks the pointer analogy at the root.
Therefore ** for catalogues is wrong — but your own objection is also slightly wrong, and the correction matters.
You objected that ** conflates a type property (depth of indirection, int**) with an operation (* moves one level). That's a real C confusion and you're right that it's the notorious one. But here's the sharper cut: in a namespace, "a subject is a reference to a reference for books" is not indirection depth at all — it's a type distinction between kinds of binding, and writing it as repeated * imports the worst possible reading. A subject doesn't resolve to "a reference that you then resolve again to get books." A subject resolves to a catalogue — a different kind of entry — which is itself a namespace you can look up in. That's not **; that's "this name binds to a scope rather than to a leaf." The right prior art is not double-pointers; it's nested namespaces / qualified names: std::vector, package.module.name, a DNS zone that delegates to another zone. A subject is a zone delegation, not a double indirection. So both notations are wrong for it — ** (Doug's) reads as depth; but the concept isn't depth, it's kind of binding, and you want notation that says "this resolves to a catalogue" categorically, not "this resolves twice." Does any language write indirection depth as a repeated operator cleanly? Essentially no — and that's the answer to your sub-question. C's ** is exactly the thing every successor language fixed. Nobody successful repeats an operator to count levels, because level-counting is a type fact and operators are steps; the ones that tried are the ones cited as warnings. So don't adopt the one C wart that has zero defenders.
The postfix-deref history, since you asked and it bears on this: *x for "reference-for" and x* for "dereference-of" — Doug's wish — is the standard C-declarator complaint, and the canonical statement of why C is confusing is "declaration follows use" (Ritchie's principle: int *p means "*p is an int"), which fuses the two roles of * on purpose and pays for it forever. The successors didn't go postfix; they went prefix-and-separated: Go's var p *int puts * in the type (a type constructor, "pointer-to-int") and keeps *p as the operation, so the same glyph means "pointer type" in type position and "deref" in expression position but never collides because positions never overlap. Rust's &T/*p, same move. Postfix dereference specifically shows up in a few places — Pascal's p^ is the famous one (postfix ^ for dereference), and it's well-liked by the people who used it precisely because postfix reads in reading-order ("p then follow-it") and never tangles with the type. So Doug's instinct has a real pedigree: Pascal did postfix deref, and it's cleaner than C. It survived poorly only because C won for unrelated reasons (Unix), not because postfix-deref failed. But — and this is why it doesn't rescue the pointer family for you — Pascal's p^ still bottoms out at a value. It's still dereference. Getting the postfix ergonomics right doesn't make your operation a dereference; it just makes the wrong family more comfortable.
The honest risk, which is the real answer: &/* reads as noise to your readers, and worse than noise — it makes a false promise.
You're suspicious that you find it elegant because you know C. Trust that suspicion; it's correct. Three costs, ascending:
To a non-C reader, ␀0␀/␀1␀ is noise — arbitrary sigils with no intuition, exactly as opaque as ¤ would be. That's the mild cost.
To a C reader — and Doug is one — it makes a promise the system doesn't keep. * means dereference-to-value, and your operation is resolution-to-another-address. So the one audience the notation "speaks to" is the audience it actively misleads: they'll import the value-at-the-bottom intuition and be wrong about what the system does. Notation that's opaque to novices and misleading to experts is the worst of both.
The deepest cost, and it's Doug's own method turned on the notation: by his rule, if the design reaches for a mark from the wrong domain, the design has drifted. Pointers are a systems-programming domain; your domain is a library, and the library already has the words. A declaration that makes a thing findable is a catalogue entry / an accession (the library literally calls "adding a work so it can be found" accessioning). A use that reaches a declared thing is a citation or a call (you look a book up by its call number). The two-sided pair in the domain you're actually in is entry / citation, or accession / call — not &/*. Borrowing pointer syntax is precisely the "reaching outside the domain for a mark because it feels elegant" that his catalogue argument was built to catch. The elegance you feel is the pull of a neighboring domain, and his own principle says resist it.
So: pointers are the wrong family, for the reason in §1 (no value at the bottom → namespace, not memory) and the reason here (wrong domain → drift). The two-sidedness is real and worth keeping; the pointer clothing for it is not.
The right family, and the best-earned notation in it
You want three marks: declare-a-reachable-name, reach-a-name, and a-name-that-resolves-to-a-catalogue. Ranked by how well-earned the notation is:
Assembly label/reference — label: to define, bare name to use. Best-earned conceptually (it's the ur-form of "definition here, use there, linker refuses if unmatched") but its notation is too weak for you: a bare name as the use-side is invisible in prose, which is your MediaWiki-unlinked-mention problem again.
BibTeX/LaTeX ␀0␀/␀1␀ — explicit, verb-named (label / ref), and the failure story you already know (?? in the output when unmatched — the bad refusal, quiet). Good vocabulary, bad refusal ergonomics. Steal the verbs, not the silence.
XML ␀0␀/␀1␀ — the schema-level version, and the one with the cleanest account: ID is a typed attribute meaning "this is a definition point, unique in the document"; IDREF means "this must match an existing ID or the document is invalid." That is your always-refuse, as a datatype. The account is the best on the list; the angle-bracket notation isn't yours to borrow, but theconcept (one type says "I am reachable," a paired type says "I reach, and I must resolve") is exactly your two sides.
RDF subject/predicate/object — overkill, and it drags in a whole graph-triple ontology you don't want, but it names the thing a catalogue mention is: a subject is a node that is also a namespace of further triples. If you ever formalize the catalogue-vs-work distinction, RDF's "a resource can be both a node and a subject-of-statements" is the account for your subject-resolves-to-catalogue case.
URN/URL — the winner for your specific N2 property, as above: stable-name/current-location with a resolver between. This is where "identity, not address" comes from as prior art.
The synthesis I'd actually reach for: your operation is linker-shaped (definition/reference, refuse-on-non-membership) with URN-shaped indirection (stable name, derived location), expressed in library vocabulary (entry/citation). Notation should follow the domain, per Doug's own rule — which means the mark should evoke catalogue, not memory. I won't pick your sigils for you, but the selection criterion is now sharp: the declare-mark should read as "I am entering this into the catalogue" and the use-mark as "I am calling for a catalogued thing," and neither should promise a value at the bottom. That criterion rules out * (promises value) and rules out anything that reads as arithmetic or memory. It does not rule out a bracket family, which is why your original [[…]]/$[…] instinct was closer to the domain than &/* is — the problem with the originals was collision ($ overloaded, [[ = MediaWiki-link), not family. You may be one glyph-swap away in the bracket family from what pointer notation was pulling you out of.
The cheap practical, which is not cheap
* is Markdown emphasis and & opens an HTML entity, and you said both sit in JSX prose — but the earlier thread established you parse your own markup and scan only JsxText nodes, so the question is whether these collide in your pipeline, not in Markdown-in-general. Two different hazards:
␀0␀ in JSX text is genuinely dangerous, and not because of your parser — because of everything downstream. & begins a character-entity reference in HTML/XML/JSX (&amp;, &lt;), and JSX itself will try to interpret &foo; as an entity. Even though you scan JsxText, the host TSX parser sees that text first, and a bare & followed by certain characters is at best a warning and at worst silently transformed before you ever see it. & is the one character on your list that the host language has an active claim on inside the exact node type you scan. That's a real collision, not a cosmetic one — ␀8␀ is close to fatal for an in-JSX-text sigil, and it's the concrete reason (beyond the semantic ones) to drop it.
␀0␀ is safe in *your* pipeline but unsafe in *readers' heads and downstream tools*. JSX text doesn't treat * specially, so your scanner is fine. But every author who's touched Markdown will see emphasis, every preview tool and every future "let authors write a little Markdown" feature will fight it, and any pipeline stage that runs a Markdown pass (many static-site setups sneak one in) will eat your stars. It's not fatal to the parser; it's fatal to coexistence, and coexistence with Markdown-shaped expectations is exactly your authoring context.
How did shippers handle this? The ones who survived chose sigils the host and Markdown had no claim on: Markdoc uses {% %} (percent-brace — nothing else wants it); MDX uses { } but only because it fully owns the parse and paid years of boundary-bugs for it (the cautionary tale from before); Handlebars' {{ }} in JSX is the one that didn't survive, precisely because it collided. The lesson converges with everything above: pick marks no neighboring system has an active claim on — which & (HTML entities) and * (Markdown emphasis) both fail, in the very contexts you'll render into.
So the practical answer isn't "escape them"; it's that this collision test agrees with the semantic test and the domain test: &/* is the wrong choice three independent ways — it promises a value it never delivers, it's borrowed from the wrong domain, and both glyphs collide with the render targets. When the notation, the semantics, and the pipeline all say drop it, that's not three problems, it's one wrong turn seen from three sides.
Where I'd want correcting: I've treated "no value at the bottom" as decisive for namespace over pointer, but if your $[mention] anchors are meant to eventually resolve to rendered content that gets transcluded — actual text pulled in at the reference site, Xanadu-style — then there is a value at the bottom (the transcluded prose), and the dereference analogy comes partly back to life for that one operator while staying dead for title/subject/author. Whether mentions transclude or merely link is the fact that decides it, and it's an authoring-intent question I can't settle from here.

A narrow, decidable question with measurements attached. I have a working answer and I want to know whether I am missing a reason to prefer the other one.
What we are building
A compiler for a library of books written as TSX. We add a micro-syntax to prose inside JSX text — declarations and citations — resolved statically at build time, refusing on non-membership. The transform: find the sigil forms, splice by absolute offset, leave everything else byte-identical.
I have proven the scanning half. Parsing with the TypeScript compiler API (ScriptKind.TSX) and walking JsxText, the scan is linear — 0.91 steps per character, flat across sixteen doublings, and every adversarial input I could build sits at or below 1.00 steps per character. Splicing by offset leaves the file identical either side. 112 of our 132 .tsx files are in scope.
What I have chosen, and why
A Vite plugin with ␀0␀, so what @vitejs/plugin-react compiles afterwards is ordinary markup. We already have exactly this shape in production for a different feature — a plugin that finds <Resource>foo.ts</Resource> in a chapter's source, swaps it for the file it names, and throws by name and by chapter when the file is not there.
Measured on a real Vite dev server today, twelve modules importing into one:
text
COLD                      13 transforms in 153 ms
EDIT one chapter          transforms re-run: ["chapter-7.ts"]   23 ms
EDIT, ask only for it     transforms re-run: ["chapter-3.ts"]    7 ms
One file changed, one transform re-runs. That is the incremental behaviour we need and we get it for free.
The question
Can this be done with Babel, and is there a reason to prefer it that I am not seeing?
Babel is already in our pipeline — @vitejs/plugin-react runs it with decorators-legacy. So a Babel plugin is available to us at no setup cost, and it would operate on the same files.
My reasoning for rejecting it, which I want checked:
Babel has no module graph. It transforms one file's AST in isolation.
It has no virtual modules — no resolveId/load equivalent, so it cannot produce a module that does not exist on disk.
It has no way to register a dependency. Vite's this.addWatchFile(id) says "this module depends on that file"; Babel has nothing that means that, so it cannot participate in invalidation.
It rewrites and re-prints the AST, where a Vite transform lets me splice text by offset and keep the file byte-identical outside the match. That matters because 52% of our source is JSX text and I do not want it round-tripped through a printer.
Is any of that wrong? And is there a capability Babel has here that I am overlooking — something about JSX handling, source maps, or ordering relative to the React transform — that would make it the better host despite the above?
The part where I am least sure, and it is a real feature we want
The library's owner wants this, later:
text
$$(<Chapter>
   … markup …
</Chapter>)
collapsed so that a book becomes one long file containing all its chapters, rather than a module importing twelve chapter modules. His reason: "This puts everything in one connected compositional object graph again, no more document." The object model has a real cost today from chapters being separate modules, and he wants the whole book to be one composition.
That is cross-file and generative — reading other files and producing a module. I believe that is squarely Vite's resolveId/load plus addWatchFile, and squarely impossible in Babel. But I have never built it, and it is the case I would most like a second opinion on:
Is a virtual module the right shape for "a book assembled from its chapters", or is generating a real file on disk (which is what our binder does today for its route and index modules) actually the better answer despite being unfashionable? Our generated-on-disk approach means git status is never clean after a build and nothing can invalidate on a change to what was generated — but it is simple and it is debuggable.
What do the tools that do this well actually do? Astro's content collections, Nuxt's generated router, SvelteKit's generated manifest, Remix's route module graph, unplugin-pages. These all assemble a module out of a directory of files, which is our exact problem. Which of them got the invalidation right, and which of them produce real files versus virtual ones, and why?
The cost I can see and want confirmed: inlining twelve chapters into one book module means editing any chapter re-transforms the whole book. Today it re-transforms one chapter and invalidates the book's cached result. Is there a shape that keeps the connected object graph without making every keystroke a whole-book rebuild — or is that trade simply the price?
Prose, no documents. Bounded — I care about (a) whether my four reasons for rejecting Babel are sound, and (b) the prior art on assembling a module from a directory, with the invalidation question answered. Concrete names over explanation.

14:37 UTC, 17 September 2026
Your four reasons are sound. Three are decisive, one is right for a subtler reason than you gave — and that subtler reason is the whole of your $$ question, so I'll fix it here and collect the payoff below.
The four, checked
1. No module graph — correct and decisive. Babel is a per-file AST transform by construction; it has no notion of "other files exist." Everything cross-file in your design (resolution against the catalogue, refuse-on-non-membership, the $$ assembly) is outside what Babel can see, not just outside what it's convenient to do. Decisive.
2. No virtual modules — correct and decisive for ␀0␀. Babel has no resolveId/load; it cannot answer "what is module X" for an X that isn't the file it was handed. Producing-a-module-that-isn't-on-disk is definitionally outside it. Decisive for the assembly feature specifically.
3. No dependency registration — correct, and this is the one that matters most, because it's the *incrementality* you measured. this.addWatchFile(id) is how a transform tells Vite "re-run me when that other file changes." Babel has nothing that means this, so a Babel plugin cannot express "chapter-7 changed, therefore re-validate the book that cites it." Your 23ms/7ms numbers exist because Vite tracks that edge; Babel would give you correct output on a cold build and silent staleness on every incremental one — the stale-green failure from the earlier threads, now sourced to the tool rather than the substrate. Decisive, and it's the reason the whole thing works.
4. Byte-identical splice vs. AST re-print — right conclusion, wrong reason, and the right reason is important. Your stated reason (don't round-trip 52%-JSX-text through a printer) is real but soft — Babel's printer is lossy in ways that matter (it reflows, it can perturb JSX whitespace, which issemantically significant in JSX — a space between elements is a text node — and it invalidates source-map fidelity), so avoiding it is genuinely good. But the hard reason to prefer offset-splicing isn't cosmetic fidelity; it's that offset-splicing is what makes your transform composable with the React transform that runs after it. With enforce: 'pre' you hand @vitejs/plugin-react a file that is byte-identical outside your matches — ordinary TSX it has never heard of your syntax in. If instead you re-printed the whole AST, you'd be handing the React transform Babel's idea of your file, and now two AST-rewriters are composing, with all the ordering and whitespace hazards that implies. So reason 4 is correct, and the correct form of it is: splice-and-stay-pre keeps you a preprocessor; re-print makes you a co-transform, and preprocessor is the position you want. Hold that thought — it's the answer to the assembly question too.
The capability you asked me to look for — is there something Babel has that beats this? Honest sweep: JSX handling (Babel's JSX support is mature, but you're scanning JSX text, not transforming JSX elements, and the TS compiler API already gives you correct JsxText regions — Babel offers nothing extra here); source maps (Babel generates them, but offset-splicing that leaves bytes identical outside matches barely needs one, and Vite's transform can return a map anyway); ordering relative to the React transform (this is the one place Babel could theoretically matter — running inside the same Babel pass as the React transform, sharing one parse). That last is the only real "Babel advantage," and it cuts against you: sharing the React transform's Babel pass means running after or entangled with JSX compilation, when you need to run before it on pristine text. So the single capability Babel has that Vite doesn't — co-residence with the React transform — is a capability you specifically don't want. Nothing overlooked. Reject Babel.
One caveat so this isn't overstated: Babel isn't useless in your pipeline — it's the right tool for the syntactic half if you ever split it out (a pure [[…]]→node text transform with no cross-file knowledge could be a Babel plugin). But the resolving half — catalogue, refusal, assembly — is Vite-plugin-shaped, and since the two halves share a scan, keeping them together in the Vite plugin is correct. Babel's ceiling is exactly the region-scan you've already solved; everything you actually need is above that ceiling.
The $$ assembly question — and the trap in it
Here's the thing I most want you to see before you build it: "assemble a book from its chapters" and "keep incremental invalidation" are in direct tension, and the tension is not incidental — it's the same identity-vs-composition tension from the very first thread, now wearing a build-graph costume. Doug wants "one connected compositional object graph, no more document." A virtual module that inlines twelve chapters gives him the connected graph and destroys the property your measurements prove: right now editing chapter-7 re-transforms chapter-7 (23ms); inline all twelve and editing chapter-7 re-transforms the book (all twelve, every keystroke). You named this cost exactly. It is real and it is the price of inlining. So the question is whether you can have the connected object graph without paying whole-book re-transform, and the answer is yes, but only if you're precise about what is connected.
The move is: the book module should compose *references to* the chapter modules, not *inline copies of* them. A virtual book.ts that is import c1 from './chapter-1'; import c2 …; export default assemble([c1, c2, …]) gives you one connected object graph at runtime/evaluation — the composition is real, the chapters are one graph — while keeping twelve separate transform units, so editing one chapter re-transforms one chapter and only re-runs the cheap assemble at the top. That's the connected graph Doug wants (the objects are composed into one structure) without the inlining cost (the source stays twelve units). The distinction is exactly identity-vs-address again: compose by reference (each chapter keeps its own module identity, the book holds pointers) not by value (each chapter's text copied into the book). "No more document" is satisfied at the object level — there's one composed graph — without collapsing the module level that your incrementality lives on. If Doug's "no more document" requires the source itself be one file (e.g. because the object model can't compose across module boundaries for some reason I can't see), then whole-book re-transform is the unavoidable price and you should say so plainly. But I'd bet the requirement is object-graph connectedness, and that's purchasable by import-composition, not inlining. Settle which "connected" he means first — object-graph or source-file — because it's the whole cost question.
Virtual vs. generated-on-disk, and the prior art
Virtual is the right shape, and your on-disk binder's two pains are exactly the two reasons the field moved to virtual:
␀0␀ never clean — generated files pollute the working tree, get accidentally committed, drift from their source. Every tool below moved to virtual partly to stop emitting into the repo.
Nothing invalidates on change to the generated thing — this is the fatal one and it's the same as the Babel point. A file generated on disk has noedge back to the directory it was assembled from, so a new chapter file doesn't invalidate the generated book. A virtual module built in load() can register that edge (addWatchFile on the directory / each chapter), so adding chapter-13 re-runs the assembly. Generated-on-disk cannot express "re-assemble when the directory changes"; virtual can. That's decisive, and it's your own reason-3 one level up.
The debuggability advantage you value in on-disk (you can look at the file) is real but recoverable: Vite virtual modules are inspectable (the dev server can serve them; you can dump the resolved content in the plugin), so you don't actually lose "see what was generated," you lose "see it as a checked-in file" — which is the part you want to lose.
Prior art, by who got invalidation right:
SvelteKit's generated manifest / ␀0␀ — the cautionary middle. It generates into a dir (visible, debuggable) but treats it as derived (gitignored, rebuilt), and wires invalidation through Vite. It's the "generated but disciplined" model; the scar is that the generated dir occasionally desyncs and the fix is always "delete .svelte-kit and rebuild" — i.e. the on-disk copy can still rot even when disciplined. Evidence that on-disk-generated has a rot failure mode virtual doesn't.
Astro content collections — closest to your problem (assemble a typed module out of a directory of content files) and the one that got it most right: it's virtual, it registers per-file dependencies, adding a file to the collection invalidates the collection, and the generated types are the only thing on disk (types, not the module). Study this one first — it's your exact shape (directory → assembled typed module) with the invalidation done correctly.
Nuxt generated router / ␀0␀ / ␀1␀ — virtual module for the route table assembled from a pages directory; unplugin's whole reason to exist is registering the directory-watch edge so adding a page rebuilds the table. The unplugin family is the generic form of your problem ("assemble a module from a directory, invalidate correctly") and is worth reading as the abstracted pattern.
Remix/React-Router route module graph — composes by reference not inlining (routes are separate modules, the manifest points at them), which is precisely the import-composition answer to your $$ cost above. It's the working proof that "one connected route graph" and "per-route incremental transform" coexist when you compose by reference.
Vite's own ␀0␀ convention (the \0-prefix resolveId idiom) is the mechanism under most of these — worth knowing as the primitive even though you'll likely use it directly rather than via a framework.
The pattern across the ones that got it right: virtual module + explicit per-source-file watch registration + compose-by-reference. The ones that generate real files either gitignore-and-discipline them (SvelteKit, survivable) or generate only types to disk and keep the module virtual (Astro, best). Nobody who got invalidation right inlines-and-generates a real source file, because that's the combination that both pollutes the tree and can't invalidate — your binder's two pains, which is why they're pains and not quirks.
So, the three answers you asked for, tight: (a) your four reasons are sound — 1/2/3 decisive, 4 right-for-a-deeper-reason (preprocessor-not-co-transform); (b) virtual module is the right shape, Astro content collections is the closest correct prior art, on-disk-generated is dispreferred for the two exact reasons your binder already hurts; and (c) the whole-book-rebuild cost is avoidable — compose the book from chapter imports (by reference), not chapter inlining (by value), and you keep Doug's connected object graph while keeping your one-chapter-per-edit incrementality. The one thing to settle before building: which "connected" Doug means, because object-graph-connected is cheap and source-file-connected is the expensive one, and only he can say which the object model actually needs.

So Astro confirms your store shape and your skip are right, not novel. But the important finding is the negative one: Astro does not track cross-entry absence. Adding entry B does not automatically re-validate an entry A that referenced B while B was missing — Astro leans on a full rebuild for that. And its documented failure mode is exactly the stale-green you fear: a package/config change that isn't in the digest leaves the cache "fresh" but wrong until .astro is wiped by hand. So Astro gives you the store and the skip, and explicitly cannot give you the absence-tracking — that has to come from the salsa side.

The fix is that absence must be a tracked read of a real keyed input — look up declaration(K), get None, and that records a dependency on declaration(K) specifically, so when declaration(K) is later set, that dependency fires and the citation re-runs. If absence is instead checked against something untracked (a side table, a global), the missed lookup memoizes forever.
That is the receipt on Part 5's line "dev never needs global invalidation, because a proxy re-resolves on the next edit of its own file." That's the hand-rolled negative-dependency edge, and it's the difference between "sound and automatic" and "sound but you have to remember to poke the citing file."

A — where the catalogue lives, when it is built, and how absence is recorded
The family, named. What you're describing is demand-driven, query-based incremental computation. The canonical members: salsa (the engine under rust-analyzer), rustc's query system, Adapton (the academic root), Skip, and the Build Systems à la Carte paper (Mokhov–Mitchell–Peyton Jones), which is the one that gives you the clean vocabulary. Deliberately not in the family for your purpose: Bazel/Buck and Nix — they assume inputs are declared before a target runs, and they cannot express "rebuild this because a name that didn't exist now does." Your dependencies are discovered by scanning and include absence, so the static-DAG builders are the wrong shelf. Turbopack's engine (turbo-tasks) is demand-driven and in-family, but it's a Rust engine you can't adopt piecemeal.
The vocabulary you asked for, mapped to your system:
Query — a memoized function K → V. "resolve the citations in file F" is a derived query; "the declaration for key K" is an input query.
Input vs derived — inputs are set from outside (file texts; the set of files); derived queries are pure functions of inputs. Your catalogue is a derived query over file texts; your citations are derived over the catalogue.
Revision — a global counter bumped on every input change; how the engine knows what's potentially stale.
Discovered dependencies / instrumentation — as a query runs it records every input it read. This is the property Bazel lacks and you need: the dependency set is found by running, not declared up front.
Red-green / early cutoff / backdating — after an input changes, a memo is "maybe-dirty"; re-run it, and if the output is byte-identical, backdate it so downstream doesn't re-run. This is the firewall that keeps a prose edit from re-validating every citation pointing at that chapter.
Durability — partition inputs by volatility so a volatile change doesn't force checking stable data. Your three tiers fall out naturally: file bodies (volatile — every keystroke), the file set (add/remove — rare), config (rarest). A real salsa project, gdscript-db, states exactly this split: the project's file set is "a salsa input so project-wide queries iterate the files incrementally. It changes only when a file is added or removed, never on a body edit… so a keystroke never invalidates project-wide derived data." That is your catalogue, described by someone else's code.
Now the crux — how absence is recorded — stated precisely, because this is where your runtime failed and where Part 5 is quietly wrong.
The salsa-correct mechanism: a citation to key K does not read "the whole catalogue." It reads a keyed input, ␀0␀, which currently returns None. The act of reading declaration(K) — even though it was absent — records a dependency on declaration(K). So "absence" is not the lack of a dependency; it is a dependency, on a cell whose value is presently None. When a declaration for K is later added, setting declaration(K) None→Some bumps the revision and marks every query that read ␀4␀ as maybe-dirty — including the citation that read it while it was empty. That citation re-runs, resolves, and flips from proxy to link. Depending-on-absence is depending on a keyed input that happens to be empty.
The failure mode when you get this wrong is documented almost verbatim in that same gdscript-db: "a query memoized while it was still absent … would otherwise return that stale empty result forever." The fix there was to make the absent thing a tracked input; when it was an untracked side-handle, the miss memoized permanently.
That is the receipt on your Part 5 line: "dev never needs global invalidation, because a proxy re-resolves on the next edit of its own file." That sentence keys the citation's re-run to its own file's text changing — but the thing that changed is declaration(K) in a different file. So the negative dependency is registered against the wrong input. Sequence: chapter A cites "The Foobar," not yet catalogued → proxy, logged. You add the declaration in chapter B. A's text is untouched → nothing re-runs A → the proxy survives even though the catalogue now resolves it. Then your other settled rule — "publish refuses if any proxy survives" — blocks the build on a reference that is actually resolvable, and the only fix is "go touch A." Those two settled rulings cannot both stand without manual re-touch. This isn't re-opening an anchor; it's showing that two things you filed under "settled" contradict, and the contradiction is exactly the negative-dependency problem you already know defeated the runtime.
The verdict on "is the salsa machinery worth it at six books." Refuted for the machinery, confirmed for the idea. You do not want salsa-the-engine (it's Rust; the JS ports are toys; and it buys its keep through multi-level early cutoff, which you don't have — your dependency graph is depth-1: citations over declarations, and nothing cites a citation, so there's no transitive red-green to save you anything). What you want is eager scan for building the table + exactly one piece of salsa: a reverse index. Concretely, the resident catalogue holds two maps:
declarations: Map<key, DeclSite> — the forward card catalogue. Built by one eager scan at server start (~150ms at your scale, under your own 250ms bar), patched per file change (~2ms, one file).
readers: Map<key, Set<file>> — for every key any file looked up, the files that looked it up. Hit or miss, same edge — a file that cited K wants re-running if K's declaration is removed or moved (hit case) or if K appears (miss case); all three are "K changed," so you don't distinguish. This map is the negative dependency, hand-rolled.
The engine, in full:
On file change: re-scan that one file → its new declarations and its new reads. Diff declarations: for each key this file added/removed/moved, re-run readers[key] (that's the insert-heals-distant-citation path — add K here, the missers of K re-run and heal). Update readers for this file's reads. Re-run this file's own transform.
On create/delete: same; a created file's declarations are all "added" (heal everything waiting), a deleted file's are all "removed" (its dependents flip back to proxy, correctly refused).
That's ~40 lines. It's O(edit), not O(corpus). It records absence correctly because readers includes missers. And it dissolves the contradiction above: if the reverse index runs live in dev, adding B's declaration re-runs A immediately, so no stale proxy ever survives to block publish — "refuse on surviving proxy" and "no manual re-touch" become simultaneously true. So my recommendation on the dev-vs-publish question I left you: build the reverse index live in the resident dev catalogue. It's cheap, it's the N4/N7 property ("add a title, the distant citation heals as I type"), and it's the only version where your two settled rules stop fighting. (Persist it into .graph.json too, so the publish gate has it without a cold rebuild — that's the Astro data-store.json shape you already mirror.)
The one precondition, and it's load-bearing — flagging it because you told me to say where Parts 1–5 look wrong. Anchor 5 (parse, never evaluate) is sound only if every card field and every sigil's copy/key is literal ␀0␀. The scan reads JsxText. The instant a <Title>, <Author>, <Subject>, or sigil copy is an interpolated {expression}, it's a JsxExpression — invisible to the scan — so that title silently never enters declarations, and a citation to it refuses forever, a false refusal, while the rendered page shows it fine. Your "101/101 are print(), 0/101 use this" tells me about this, not about whether the text inside print() is literal. This is not a reason to reopen anchor 5 — it's the input condition anchor 5 requires, and the in-frame fix keeps the anchor: a parse-time lint that refuses a computed card field loudly (N7), forcing the author to write it literal, rather than an evaluation fallback that would violate the anchor. And there's a free safety net: proof.ts already reads the rendered HTML back — have it cross-check that every rendered anchor/title exists as a catalogue key. If render produces an anchor the parse-built catalogue lacks, that's a computed-field leak caught at the gate. That turns proof from "keep" into "keep, and it now guards the precondition."
The probe that settles it is at the very end. Run it first next round; its answer is the one thing I'd most regret designing around unseen.

=== 2 · WHAT THE PROBE ACTUALLY FOUND, WHICH IS NOT WHAT YOU ASKED ===
You asked whether authors write computed card fields. Essentially they do not — one instance in a frozen library, and it is a formula-as-title rather than sloppiness.
What the probe found instead is that (c)/(d) are not an author error at all. That file is the MASTHEAD: generic apparatus that stands on every page of every book. Its links point at whatever book THIS book is about and by, so they are necessarily computed — this.$about and this.$by are values the book already holds.
Which means [copy](target) is currently carrying two different jobs:
an AUTHORED CITATION in prose, which names a thing and needs catalogue resolution; and
a PROGRAMMATIC LINK built by apparatus from an address already in hand, which needs no resolution at all.
That distinction is a ruling Doug owes and I am not going to invent it. But note what it does to your lint.ts: if the two jobs are separated, lint.ts refuses a computed CITATION and has nothing to say about apparatus, and your precondition holds cleanly. If they are not separated, lint.ts would refuse the masthead, which is wrong. So the design question is upstream of the lint, and I would rather settle it than guard it.
Your proof.ts cross-check (rendered anchors ⊆ catalogue keys) is a good idea either way and I am taking it, with one note: under the separation above it must not flag apparatus links, or it flags the masthead on every page.

// WHAT IS READ OFF A LIVE BOOK, ONE MEMBER PER FACT. Loading a book is what costs; once it is // loaded, another fact costs a member here and nothing else — no second pass, and no change to the // graph it is written into. A library that copied this binding adds its own facts by extending // this class. Every member reaches through the framework's reflection, by TYPE and never by class, // because a library writes its own kinds: a cover of its own and a title of its own still answer. // A FACT THAT IS A LIST ANSWERS A LIST. Names are written the way a person writes them, so a // joined string could not be taken apart again — and a structure encoded in a string and parsed // back out is the tell that a mechanism is being used for something it is not for. export class Reading { $name(book: $Book): string { return book.name; } $title(book: $Book): string { return html.text(book.title?.heading()?._block); } // WHAT A MENTION NAMES, NOT WHAT IT SAYS. An author written [Doug](MY Library Log) says Doug // and names the log, and it is the NAME a library is connected by — so the reading asks for the // name and never for the copy, which is the same reading whether a display form was used or not. $author(book: $Book): string { return this.cover(book)?.author()?.name ?? ''; } $subject(book: $Book): string { return this.cover(book)?.subject()?.name ?? ''; } $types(book: $Book): string[] { return reflection.types(this.cover(book) ?? book).flatMap(type => reflection.names(type)); } $chapters(book: $Book): string[] { return book.chapters.map(chapter => chapter.name); } $catalogued(book: $Book): string[] { return (book.tableOfContents?.chapters ?? []).map(mention => mention.name); } // WHAT A CATALOGUE SHELVES, which is a different question from what a book holds. A synopsis says // the book it is FOR, and a catalogue is a book of synopses — so the books it shelves are the // canonical names written into its chapters. It reads the PRINTED documents rather than the block, // because a chapter writes its document in print() and nothing an author wrote is in the book. $shelves(book:Book): string[] { return book.chapters.flatMap(chapter => chapter.parts()) .flatMap(document => reflection.within<Canonical>(document, $TypeOfCanonical)) .map(named => named.name); }
protected cover(book: $Book): Cover | undefined { return book.cover?.searchPartsForOne<Cover>($TypeOfCover); } }
// THE MEMBERS, GATHERED THROUGH THE PROTOTYPE CHAIN, the way the framework gathers a specification's // rules — so a library's own reading extends this one and both sets answer. const members = (held: Reading): string[] => { const names = new Set<string>(); for (let held_: object | null = Object.getPrototypeOf(held) as object | null; held_ !== null && held_ !== Object.prototype; held_ = Object.getPrototypeOf(held_)) for (const name of Object.getOwnPropertyNames(held_)) if (name.startsWith('$') && typeof (held as never)[name] === 'function') names.add(name); return [...names].sort(); };
export const read = (book: $Book, held: Reading): Record<string, string | string[]> => Object.fromEntries(members(held).map(name => [name.slice(1), (held as never as Record<string, (book: $Book) => string | string[]>)[name].call(held, book)]));

LITERAL JsxText inside <Title>. $author the NAME a mention names, not its copy — so the TARGET of [Doug](My Library Log). LITERAL, and note this is already exactly a catalogue key. $subject same shape as author. LITERAL. $chapters each chapter's own name, i.e. each chapter file's title heading. LITERAL, per file. $catalogued the mentions in the table-of-contents chapter. LITERAL, inside one chapter.
$types NOT JsxText. It is reflection.types() over the cover's CLASS, flattened to names — the type hierarchy, not prose. A TS parse of the class declarations could reproduce it (extends chains), but that is a second kind of static analysis, not the JsxText scan. I want your view on whether scan.ts should do both or whether $types should be dropped from the parsed catalogue. $shelves NOT JsxText, and this is the hard one.
