The Card Catalogue
author:[Arthur](../../../../.claude/library/..teamsmanship/..team/arthur/arthur-or-the-shape-of-everything/.cover.md)
coauthor:[Cathy](../../../../.claude/library/..teamsmanship/..team/cathy/cathy-and-the-reactive-canvas/.cover.md), [Libby](../../../../.claude/library/..teamsmanship/..team/libby/libby-and-the-tended-garden/.cover.md), [Adam](../../../../.claude/library/..teamsmanship/..team/adam/adam-between-the-wires/.cover.md)
*The chapter name is Doug's word; the section names are PROXIES.*
*THE DESIGN SESSION OF 2026-09-17, recorded as it was decided rather than after.␀1␀ —read that first; this chapter is what the thesis turns into when it is built.␀2␀the binder is not being rewritten so a stylesheet can be edited faster.␀3␀
<a id="found"></a>What was already there, which is most of it
*Seven things were found in the code rather than designed, and they decide how much of this is new work.*
1 · THE CATALOGUE EXISTS, ONE DRAWER DEEP. [␀0␀](../../package/.binding/assembly/routes.ts) generates ␀1␀ on every bind. That is a card catalogue with exactly one query — a book by its name — whose cards hold addresses rather than identities.
2 · A TITLE IS ALREADY A DOCUMENT MENTION. [␀0␀](../../package/src/library/Title.tsx): ␀1␀, and ␀2␀ returns the mention class. *So a document's card is produced by its title, and "mentions get assembled into a catalogue" is a walk over titles rather than a mechanism to invent.* This is the largest piece of good news in the session.
3 · A CARD IS ALREADY A MENTION PLUS WHAT STANDS WITH IT. [␀0␀](../../package/src/library/CatalogueCard.tsx) specifies ␀1␀ — a composition holding a title.
4 · THE PARSER IS OURS AND SAID SO IN ADVANCE. [␀0␀](../../package/src/utilities/Parser.tsx): "it's not markdown, WE should be parsing that… One expression, and the syntax is free to move without asking another language's permission." One catch: ␀1␀ is anchored ␀2␀, so it only reads a link when the WHOLE writing is one. Mentions stand inline, so they must be found inside a string and split out — the shape ␀3␀ already performs at every level, but new work at each.
5 · NON-MEMBERSHIP DOES NOT REFUSE. IT GUESSES. One line, in ␀0␀, ␀1␀, ␀2␀, ␀3␀ and ␀4␀:
ts
protected override address(): string { return this.standing() ?? super.address(); }
*␀0␀ is the catalogue lookup; ␀1␀ is "unless it is missing, then".␀3␀ —not a broken link a reader reports, a silent one that lands somewhere plausible.* It was deliberate — "a name for a book that is not here yet" — and the thesis reclassifies it rather than discovering it.
6 · THE SHELF IS ADDRESS-BOUND AND BOOK-ONLY. ␀0␀ maps a name to an address STRING, which is the topology-binding the thesis forbids; and it holds books, so every chapter and heading falls through to ␀1␀, a guess, unconditionally.
7 · ␀0␀ NAMES TWO NODE KINDS. In ␀1␀ it is a mention; in ␀2␀ it is a book that catalogues books. The comment beside it manages the collision by export discipline — "the two never meet because only that one is re-exported by ␀3␀." *One word, two kinds, kept apart by module plumbing rather than by meaning — which is exactly what a vocabulary carrying a membership test may not do.*
<a id="rulings"></a>What Doug ruled
<a id="syntax"></a>The two sides, and which bracket is which
*Doug:* "[] and []() would be refers to · [[]] and [[]]() would be referred to as (mentioned as)"
*DOUBLING DECLARES. SINGLE REFERS.␀1␀,and right here because declaring is the rarer, more deliberate act and doubling marks deliberateness.*
writtenreads as
[[great]]this is referred to as great — the key is the copy
[[This is Important]](important)says This is Important, keyed as important
[great]refers to whatever is referred to as great
[Doug](MY Library Log)says Doug, refers to MY Library Log
One doubling rule, learned once, and it reads aloud correctly in both directions. It is also ␀0␀ — the expression the parser already holds — with the brackets doubled to mean *mention instead of link,so nothing new is learned twice.* And every markdown link already written in these libraries is the use side, which gives the migration a direction.
*A mention in prose is therefore never casual.␀2␀"That isn't casual. That will get converted into a mention by the compiler, and a reference should be able to go there."* ␀0␀ plants a target in the prose that a reference elsewhere can land on.
<a id="surface"></a>What is referrable
*NAMED MENTIONS LIVE BELOW THE CHAPTER LEVEL.␀1␀Above and at chapter level the catalogue's spine is structural and derived from titles; below it, a thing is referrable because somebody named it.␀2␀ —"yes let's have standard section ones."*
<a id="queries"></a>What the catalogue is asked
*Doug:* "The catalogue would have subject, title, author queries because each one has a unique book — we need to make unique the author one. And then from those you should be able to query chapter and mention, from chapter to section."
Three entry drawers — SUBJECT, TITLE, AUTHOR — each naming a unique book, and author is the one whose uniqueness has to be manufactured. From a book: its chapters and its mentions. From a chapter: its sections. *A comprehensive catalogue, and its size is N books × M chapters.*
Every card at section scale and above carries a SYNOPSIS — written, or made where nobody wrote one. A direct mention carries none. Doug: "everything at section scale should have a summary or has one made. I don't think the direct mention should carry one of those."
<a id="static"></a>Static references are substituted in; the catalogue serves the dynamic
*Doug:* "if we are careful, all the static links could be validated at build time and even substituted in. We still want a catalogue abstraction, and we want to find a way, at build time, for the system to be able to request parts of the catalogue, so it can provide dynamic services. No API needed."
*This is the ruling that makes the thing scale, and it should be said plainly: THE CATALOGUE IS NOT SHIPPED AND LOOKED UP.␀1␀ —a resolved reference is just a link.␀2␀He raised generating it against a GitHub API and talked himself out of it in the same breath; nothing external is needed.*
<a id="refusal"></a>Always refuse
*A reference that does not resolve fails the bind.␀2␀Which is what the thesis demanded and what DocBook, XML's IDREF and Sphinx's nitpicky mode have each demanded before us.*
<a id="grammar"></a>The restructure — composition begins at the paragraph
*Doug:* "Maybe we have to give up on some of composition. At the bottom, just let things be strings. A composition comes at the paragraph level. But the document still requires either other documents or sections, and they require other sections or paragraphs, and they don't have to be structured."
text
document   →  documents | sections
section    →  sections  | paragraphs
paragraph  →  strings
*Nothing is required to be structured, and below the paragraph there are no compositions at all.␀2␀,and it deletes the levels where the cost lives — specify walks 33,158 writings, and sentences, words and letters are most of them.*
<a id="types"></a>The type compression
*Doug:* "We currently make an interface and a typeof and all of that… We should compress everything just to the ␀0␀ types. The type system can then be used to specify the sort of multiple inheritance that it affords by adding types to add validation, but it doesn't need us to create types for everything."
*The ␀0␀ interface plus ␀1␀ plus ␀2␀ triple collapses to ␀3␀.␀6␀ —which is what the type system is actually for: multiple inheritance by annotation.* The loose coupling the interfaces were buying is bought instead by dependency injection.
<a id="di"></a>Dependency injection, and what it is for
*Doug:* "Full ␀0␀ DI, but the DI container just works anywhere. It just needs to inherit the scoping. And I think we need bond-constructor scoping — if something happens in a bond constructor of a certain type it gets the service requested there if this type of registration is required. We'll have to see how that feels."
A chemistry FEATURE, therefore pitched and not taken. It carries two jobs at once: it is how the card catalogue exists as a service in ␀0␀, and it is what makes the type compression above possible. **Doug: "I think it mostly needs to exist at build time, but we should build it so that it can exist at runtime too."*
<a id="naming"></a>The name, and the rule that found it
*The service that answers a request for part of the catalogue is the CARD CATALOGUE. It is not a new organ.A reference desk was proposed and withdrawn — the closer word was already in the domain.*
The rule it was tested against, which is a correction to how this team had written the naming principle down:
*Doug:* "If any one obscures by being short, you have failed. But if you make something that has no short name, you are deviating from the domain! Naming is a semantic constraint satisfaction problem, and the answer isn't obscurity. It is allowing your design to change to accommodate the missing semantics to stay IN the domain."
*And the reason the domain is load-bearing rather than decorative, in his own demonstration:␀1␀ —real and digital libraries do not carry a catalogue by accident.* Canonical semantics convert design speculation into an argument that can be checked against something that already exists and already works.
<a id="second-round"></a>The second round of rulings, 2026-09-17
*Given after the design went out for an outside reading and came back.* Three of them answer a proposed fix by refusing it and naming the domain's own answer instead, which is the method working rather than a disagreement.
<a id="a-card-is-writing"></a>A card is a writing that is never mounted
*Doug:* "In a world where everything is writing, this doesn't exist in that context at all. I would prefer it be a chemical, though we should consider just using writing as a base and making it a regular piece of writing that we ␀0␀ and assign things to, and it can be viewed but we make them like POJOs. *Like horizontal gene transfer, it's a piece of writing that isn't created in the DOM.*"
*So the catalogue is not a compiled table beside the library; it is made of the library's own material.␀1␀ —which is why it costs nothing at render time and why everything the library already knows how to do to a writing applies to it unchanged.* The alternative — a row of data with no existence in the library — would mean nothing in the library could point at a card or say anything about one.
<a id="frozen-keys"></a>A key is frozen, and it is not a bond
*Doug:* "Catalogue keys are not dynamic. Freeze the thing. These are non-reactive properties."
*Two rulings in one sentence and the second is the load-bearing one.␀1␀And a key is* *non-reactive:in a substrate where every field is a bond, a reactive key would make every card an edge in the graph and a write to one would diffuse through it.*
<a id="the-title"></a>The call number is the title
*The outside reading said the design was missing a call number—a card holds identity, a call number says which shelf, and re-shelving the stacks does not reprint the cards* — *and proposed splitting identity from address into two objects.*
*Doug:* "No that's the title. Book titles have to be unique in the library. If it gets more complicated, in the future we can do the subject and the title, but for now, globally unique titles."
The finding was right and the new object was not needed: the domain already carries it, and the word for it is one we have. And the shape of the deferral is itself canonical — subject plus title is how a call number is actually built, a class followed by a cutter.
<a id="citations-out"></a>A citation out is not a reference
*The same reading found that always-refuse cannot survive a reference pointing at something we do not control,and proposed pulling external works in as cards for things the library does not hold — the union-catalogue record.*
*Doug:* "Then it isn't a reference in the sense of the library. This is why we can point in by having the catalogue build from everything we can know. If we are building the thing, we can validate all the external links at compile time, we just can't validate that they are right."
*The conflict dissolves rather than being patched.␀1␀An external link can be checked at build time for being well formed and reachable, and cannot be checked for saying what the citing text claims it says — and that limit is honest rather than a hole.*
<a id="mention-is-annotation"></a>A mention is an annotation
*The reading agreed composition should stop at the paragraph and warned that the leaf cannot be a plain string, because a mention stands inside prose and would be trapped in it.It proposed a content sequence of strings, mentions and references.*
*Doug:* "Mentions will be annotative, and annotations are associated with writing. A piece of writing is approximately a sequence of strings or other pieces of writing followed by a sequence of annotations and we should make that more explicit."
text
writing  ≈  (string | writing)*  followed by  annotation*
*The prose stays prose. The referrable surface is the annotation list hanging off the writing that holds it.␀3␀ —it makes the existing model explicit, which is what was asked for.*
<a id="author-is-autobiography"></a>An author is an autobiography
*Doug:* "Authorship has to live in an autobiography and we only allow one subject to have that in the library. But autobiographical works can be in a chain… We imagine that like Subject, which has to be unique to a subject, Author has to be unique to a library. Doug versus Douglas M. Rubino might be different ones, and I will handle them with different books."
*So author uniqueness needs no authority file: it comes from the library's own closure.␀1␀Autobiographical works may chain — a team and its members, a person and a professional face — and two forms of one name are simply two books, decided by a person rather than by a mechanism.*
*One gap the outside reading named and this does not close:␀1␀ —what cataloguing calls a* *relator,and we have one word where the domain has many.*
<a id="where-it-surfaces"></a>A fault surfaces in the editor
*Doug:* "I would like them to find out in the VS Code errors possibly — which is why plugins and surfacing exceptions and using those APIs might be best."
*Not the browser, and not the build log — the editor's problem list.␀1␀ —a transformer has the type graph and no values, and our facts are values.*
<a id="the-table-bug"></a>And the table of contents was our bug, not the design's
*The reading found the one place refusal-by-membership leaks: a table addressing a book's own parts by POSITION, which is not membership by identity.* It is the lesson TEI learned when it retreated from XPointer to declared anchors only.
*Doug:* "Right and I said not to. I said by chapter name so that's on you guys. Good bug."
*The ruling was given and not built.* A table names its chapters by name, and no positional path survives anywhere.
<a id="speed"></a>What fast means, ruled while fixing something else
*These were given on 2026-09-17 about a different tool — the driver that reaches Claude Desktop — and they are recorded here because the binder is held to the same standard(␀1␀).They are quoted rather than generalised, because the generalisation is Doug's to make.*
*Doug:* "Running is from the time I ask to the time it happens."

*Doug:* "1 second of blink and 10 seconds of wait is a whole universe." "I shouldn't be waiting noticeable amounts of time for anything so if you HAVE to wait, wait 250." configure → survives, once at server start and once at build. Shared. (configuration/.)
inventory → survives as a directory watch in dev, full walk in build. Pure, kept whole. It's also the front half of the catalogue (finding what's there). (inventory/.)
assemble → becomes resolveId/load virtual modules (D). Bodies kept, file-writing dropped. Dissolves the bootstrap rot (4.6). (assembly/ → hooks in server.ts.)

And D11's last premise — "specify's local checks can run in a transform" — is now movable, and the answer is: mostly yes, with one real catch I can see in ␀0␀. The catch isn't localness — live.specify() runs a book's own specification, which is local by construction once referential checks leave for the catalogue. The catch is ␀2␀ evaluates the book (ssrLoadModule → open[folder]() → read(live, held) + live.specify()). That evaluation is exactly what anchor 5 deletes for facts — but live.specify() is not fact-gathering, it's validation, and validation of local well-formedness is precisely what the thesis (18, §division) says stays dynamic and portable: "the same ␀9␀ can fire in the binder, in the prerender, and in a development browser at the moment a writing is constructed." So the local checks don't run in the transform (a transform has source text, not a constructed writing); they run where the writing is constructed — at render, in the browser, and could fire in dev. The transform's job is referential refusal (does this key resolve), which is the catalogue's; the local checks stay @specify firing at construction. So D11's row "specify (local checks only) → transform" is slightly miscast:local checks → ␀11␀ at construction; referential checks → the catalogue at transform. C makes it package-shaped. A single host that exports a plugin, a config factory, and a resident catalogue is exactly a dependency's export surface. A copied folder "wants to be a program" (your words, and 01-the-unit-of-code.md's compiler column agrees — a phase is a function, and a set of exported functions is a package).

The cost, honestly: the copy's one real virtue is that it's vendored — a library carries its exact compiler, and you can edit ␀0␀ in place to debug a build without touching a published package. D9's proxy anchor — the constraint, not the spelling
You asked for a constraint for Doug to rule the spelling against. Here's what a proxy anchor must satisfy, derived from what D9 needs it to do:
Unique per (file, key, offset) — so two unresolved keys, or the same key cited twice, never collapse onto one anchor. D9'sassumed names exactly this ("two unresolved keys cannot collapse onto one").
Greppable in the built HTML — a single literal substring that means "unresolved," so the publish gate finds every survivor with one scan, no parse. (proof.ts already reads HTML back; this is one more grep in a pass that exists.)
Structurally a real anchor — a link that renders as a link, so the dev page is structurally identical to the built page (D9: "a proxy cannot leak… a link is still a link"). It must occupy the same shape a resolved reference will, so nothing shifts when it later resolves.
Carries its own key back — so the log entry (file, key, offset) is reconstructable from the anchor alone, since the logis the diagnostics and shouldn't need a side table.
Spelling that satisfies all four is Doug's — but the constraint says: a unique, self-identifying, greppable, real-anchor token that embeds its key. (My instinct is something like a reserved fragment scheme carrying the key, but that's a spelling and it's his.)
What a mention's lowered target must satisfy — the actual open question
This is the one you flagged as the real hole, and 04 + the vocabulary let me sharpen it rather than answer it. Doug's question: a mention returns nothing, so when it lowers, what goes in the parens?
Here's the constraint set, derived from what's now settled, framed for his ruling:
It must be the KEY, not an address — because D6/thesis forbid an address below book level, and a mention is below book level. So a mention's lowered target is the thing resolution looks up, not the thing it produces.
It must be what ␀0␀ returns FALSE for — because the runtime already routes on that predicate: addresses(copy) true → it's a ref, gets a $Path; false → it's a mention, named by the target. A mention's lowered target must therefore be arelative form (no scheme, no //, no /, no #, no ?), or the runtime will mistake it for a ref and try to path it. This is the sharp constraint and it's already enforced by code that exists. The mention key must be spelled so Url.addresses says false.
It must be unique enough to be a catalogue member — the key is what membership is tested against, so two different mentions must not lower to the same key unless they mean the same target. This is where "author uniqueness must be manufactured" (still open in 04) and "what a card holds" (still open) actually bite: the key's shape is the catalogue's primary key.
It must be frozen-able — 04's frozen-keys ruling means once a mention lowers to key K, K is a permanent commitment. So the lowered target can't encode anything that changes (not position, not a slug of a renameable display name) — it must be the stable identity.
So the honest statement back to Doug: a mention's lowered target is a relative, ␀0␀-false, unique, frozen key — and the open sub-question is whether that key is authored (the ␀1␀ the author typed) or derived. 04 leans authored ("the key is the copy" when no explicit key is given; an explicit key when written), which means the answer is probably the key is literally what the author put in the doubled brackets, and its only constraint is that ␀3␀ returns false for it — i.e. a mention key may not look like an address. That's a constraint I can state; whether it'scomplete depends on the heading-referrability ruling that's out with him, because that decides whether every heading needs a key (universal, must be generated-unique) or only mentioned ones (authored, bounded). The two rulings are coupled, and I'd want them together before saying the key shape is closed. Until then: the constraint is items 1–4; the spelling and the authored-vs-derived call are his.
One place I'll flag I might be wrong: I'm reading Url.addresses-false as the definition of "is a mention" at the lowered layer. If a mention key is ever legitimately address-shaped (a mention whose key happens to contain a /), then the runtime's own predicate misclassifies it, and the transform would have to mark mentions explicitly rather than relying on the target's shape. The corpus (2254 literal links, the fork clean) suggests keys aren't address-shaped, but that's the assumption under item 2, and it's worth a grep before it's load-bearing: do any existing mention targets contain a ␀2␀, ␀3␀, ␀4␀, or ␀5␀ — anything Url.addresses would catch? If zero, the shape-based split is safe and the transform needs no mention-mark. If nonzero, mentions need an explicit lowered mark and item 2 becomes a design change.

All four have verdicts now, and three of them touch units — I'll name which. Research round, delivered as findings-with-consequences, no structure.
(a) The two Vite surfaces — and a correction to D11's addWatchFile line
␀0␀ does not do what D11 says it does, and this is the most important finding in the round. D11's RESTS-ON line reads: "␀1␀ plus ␀2␀ on the directory can [supply the edge]." That is wrong as written, and it's wrong in Vite's own words. Vite's addWatchFile does not mirror Rollup's contract. Rollup's docs promise that addWatchFile from within transform re-runs that transform when the watched file changes; Vite's implementation, per the tracking issue that's been open since 2021, "does nothing special in this case and just tracks the new file independently." So addWatchFile('the directory') will notice the directory changed and it will not re-run your virtual book module's load(). The edge you need — chapter changes → virtual book re-assembles — is not what addWatchFile alone gives you.
The working idiom — and this is a checkable correction, because it's the pattern vanilla-extract and the "hidden virtual-module dependency" discussion both ship — is three parts, not one:
configureServer(server) → server.watcher.add(directoryGlob) — register the chapter directory with the chokidar watcher.
handleHotUpdate({ server, file }) → when file is a chapter in that directory, reach the virtual module by id (server.moduleGraph.getModuleById(resolvedVirtualId)) and manually server.moduleGraph.invalidateModule(it), then return [it].
resolveId/load as normal for the virtual module.
The person who documented this named the dragon precisely: "we are introducing a virtual module which has hidden (in vite's eyes) dependencies on other files… both the modules and server.moduleGraph from the HmrContext are empty" — i.e. Vite doesn't know the virtual book depends on the chapter, so you must aim the invalidation. The newer, cleaner call is server.reloadModule(module) (added for exactly this "invalidate my virtual module when its hidden source changed" case).
This also resolves D9's open caveat — in the direction of "you must do it yourself." D9 honestly flagged: "the importer edge was NOT observed… what is NOT proven is that Vite tracks the edge correctly." The Vite source settles it: watched/glob files are treated differently from static imports in the invalidation walk — a non-statically-imported dependency can only soft-invalidate its importer under conditions a static import doesn't need. So Vite does not track the hidden edge for you; the probe's shallow graph wasn't a probe artifact, it was the real behavior. D9's premise moves from unknown to verified, and the verified answer is: the edge is manual, via ␀2␀ + ␀3␀, not automatic via ␀4␀. That's a correction to two units (D11's RESTS-ON line, D9's caveat), found in Vite's own tracker, and it changes an implementation detail without changing the architecture — the edge still exists, you just build it with the watcher and manual invalidation rather than trusting addWatchFile to imply it.
Build-mode vs dev-mode — two hazards that bear on C. addWatchFile is only legal during the build graph phase: calling it after the build finishes throws "Cannot call addWatchFile after the build has finished" (a live issue), and in plain vite build without --watch the established idiom is to skip it entirely (if (config.command === 'build' && !config.build.watch) return). So the watch edge is a dev-only concern by construction; the build path re-assembles everything anyway. That's clean for you: the resident-catalogue-with-watch-edge lives in the dev host, and the build driver just runs the phases. Second hazard, for the long-lived host specifically: addWatchFile (or any watcher add) after server close hangs the Node process — it sets a watcher that prevents exit. Matters for your teardown, and it's a known footgun (an open issue about exactly this in a Vitest-hosted-Vite setup).
␀0␀ as a long-lived host — who does it and what breaks. It's a supported, documented pattern (middleware mode, server.transformRequest/ssrLoadModule to drive resolve→load→transform programmatically without HTTP — which is what your specify.mjs already uses today via ssrLoadModule). The catalogue stays resident as plugin state across edits; it does not survive a config reload — Vite responds to a config change by restarting the server (server.restart()), which tears down the module graph and re-runs configureServer, so your resident catalogue rebuilds. At 150ms that's a non-event; the design point is just don't assume the catalogue survives a ␀7␀ edit — rebuild it in ␀8␀, which runs again on restart. The one gotcha the JS-API docs call out explicitly, and it bites C directly: "when using ␀9␀ and ␀10␀ in the same Node.js process, both rely on ␀11␀." So a single process that owns both dev (createServer) and build (build()) must manage NODE_ENV deliberately between them — the shared-process design is fine, but that env var is the sharp edge, and it's the concrete answer to "what breaks" when one process owns both modes.
Net for C: one process owning both modes is standard and supported; the watch edge is dev-only and manual; the two things to get right are NODE_ENV between modes and not-adding-watchers-after-close.
(b) How other systems spell an unresolved reference — three spellings, three failure stories
Your four proxy constraints are good; here's who's lived with theirs, and the verdict is that your design should be linker-at-the-gate, Sphinx-in-the-log, and never LaTeX-in-the-output.
The linker (undefined symbol) — the model your thesis already invokes, and it's the strictest. Default behavior on an unresolved reference: terminate the whole link, produce no output. ld: fatal: Symbol referencing errors. No output written to prog. A broken reference doesn't yield a broken program — it yields no program. And the report satisfies your attributable-refusal obligation exactly: it names the symboland the file it was first referenced in (foo / main.o). The escape hatch (-z nodefs, "allow undefined") carries a warning in the docs that turning off refusal moves the failure to aruntime relocation error later — which is the argument for always-refuse stated by the linker itself: the only thing worse than refusing at build is not refusing and failing somewhere later. This is your A5, and it's the spelling for the publish gate: any surviving proxy → no site written.
LaTeX ␀0␀ — the anti-pattern, and the one your proxy must not resemble. An undefined \ref renders a literal ?? in the output and emits a warning buried in a multi-thousand-line log. Papers ship to print with?? in them constantly, precisely because the placeholder is renderable and shippable and the warning is quiet. This is the N7 death you already fear, at document scale. The lesson for your proxy: it must be greppable and self-identifying so it can never ship silently — the opposite of ??, which is neither attributable (which ref?) nor safely greppable (?? collides with real content, e.g. s?? in code samples).
Sphinx nitpick — the attributable-warning spelling, with an auditable escape valve. Missing reference → a warning naming file and line: glossary.rst:144: WARNING: py:meth reference target not found: __await__. Not fatal by default, but -W makes warnings fatal (CI-standard), and — the interesting part — nitpick_ignore is a declared allowlist of known-missing references. That's a middle path you should know exists: refusal stays total except for an explicitly enumerated ignore-list, so "known missing" is itself a declared, reviewable set rather than a silent tolerance. You likely don't want it (always-refuse is cleaner for a closed corpus), but it's the prior art for "refuse, unless the miss is on a list someone signed."
Verdict for the proxy anchor, satisfying your four constraints and informed by these three: the log is Sphinx-shaped (file + offset + key, one line per survivor, greppable), the gate is linker-shaped (any survivor → no output), and the anchor token is defined against LaTeX — a unique, self-identifying, greppable string that embeds its key, so a single grep over built HTML finds every survivor and each names its own (file, key, offset). The spelling is still Doug's; the constraint the prior art adds to your four is a fifth: the token must not collide with real content (LaTeX's ?? fails this), so it should be a reserved form that cannot occur in authored prose — which, conveniently, your sigil namespace already guarantees is clean.
(c) How other systems spell a stable content key — the authored-key family, and the duplicate verdict
This is the one you most wanted five examples for. Here they are, ranked by what happens on the two things that break a frozen key: rename and duplicate.
Obsidian block IDs — the closest match, and it's authored. A caret ^ then alphanumerics-and-dashes, either generated (^37066d) or authored (^quote-of-the-day). The ID is a stable pointer that survives content change — the block's text can be rewritten and the ID persists, which is exactly your frozen-key-over-mutable-display split. The shipped design criteria (from a plugin author who built one) name your item 4 almost verbatim: "line-of-sight stable — not time-encoded; rearranging notes doesn't reshape IDs." And the failure modes have names that map onto your reverse index: an ID no longer linked is orphaned (declared-but-unread — your readers[key] empty), a link to a missing ID is broken (read-but-undeclared — your proxy case). There's an entire plugin genre for finding orphans and broken links, which is your reverse index sold as a product. Duplicate behavior: an ^id must be unique within a note; write it twice and links resolve to the first — silent, and the reason Obsidian's generated IDs are hex (collision resistance) while authored ones are the user's problem.
XML ␀0␀ / ␀1␀ — the strict end: duplicate = reject the document. An ID-typed attribute must be unique per document; a validating parser refuses the document on a duplicate. This is the safest duplicate behavior on the list and it matches always-refuse: a colliding key is a build failure, not a silent miswire. Rename survival: the ID is opaque-by-convention and independent of position, so it survives reflow — but XML gives you no authored-meaningful guarantee, it just enforces uniqueness.
BibTeX cite keys — the worst duplicate behavior, and a hidden collision-widener. Raw BibTeX, on a duplicate key in one .bib: "compares keys case-insensitively and silently keeps one of the colliding entries." Two failures in one sentence — silent (no error, one entry just vanishes) and case-insensitive (so Turing1936 and turing1936 collide, which no one expects). This is the spelling to design against: a frozen key store must be case-sensitive and must refuse duplicates loudly, or it does what BibTeX does.
Sphinx labels — the dangerous middle: duplicate = warn + miswire. A duplicate label emits a warning naming both locations ("duplicate label examples, other instance in c-api/typeobj.rst") but still resolves, to one of the two, silently wrong. The Python docs carried a real bug where text meaning to link to one section linked to the other because the label was duplicated. The lesson: a warning that still resolves is worse than a refusal, because the link works and points at the wrong thing — the exact silent-wrong-target failure the whole catalogue exists to prevent.
The verdict, and it's the one finding in (c) that touches an open question. sphinxcontrib-bibtex spent years (issues #199, #243, #271, #365, and a backward-incompatible change in the May 2026 release) arriving at the design you already want: they split the duplicate check into ␀0␀ (same document — an error, not acceptable) versus ␀1␀ (across documents — fine, when keys are prefixed by scope), and the rule became "resolve locally first." That is your book-scoped keys, discovered by someone else the hard way. A mention key that collides within a book is the error; the same key in two books is fine because the scope differs. This directly informs the still-open items in 04 ("how author names are made unique," "what a card holds"): key uniqueness is per-scope, not global — subject/title/author are unique per library (the three drawers), but a mention key need only be unique within its book, because resolution is scoped. That's not mine to rule, but it's the constraint the prior art hands you, and it converges with the qualified-reference syntax you already have ([great] = this book, [great](otherbook) = qualified).
So the mention-key constraint set, now with prior art behind each:
Authored (Obsidian ^quote-of-the-day, not generated hex) — Doug's heading ruling settled this.
␀0␀-false (relative, no / # ? :) — your grep confirmed zero violations, so shape-based classification is safe.
Unique per scope, refused loudly on within-scope duplicate (XML-strict, not BibTeX-silent, not Sphinx-warn-but-resolve) — the sphinxcontrib-bibtex verdict.
Frozen, position-independent (Obsidian's "not time-encoded, rearranging doesn't reshape IDs") — your item 4, shipped by someone.
Case-sensitive (the BibTeX anti-lesson) — a new constraint the prior art adds.
The .latex corpus you found — a mention keyed mathsf-p-stackrel-mathsf-np, a slug of the formula title — is constraint 4 being violated by default when nothing forbids it: a slug of a display form became the identity, so if the display changes the key lies. It's the exact fault, sitting in a frozen library, proving the constraint is load-bearing rather than theoretical.
(d) Prerendering — the verdict converges on D2/D3, no new tool
The honest 2026 answer: React's own prerender / prerenderToNodeStream (react-dom/static) is the current SSG-to-string API, and it waits for Suspense/data before resolving — but it's for React's render-to-string model, and you don't have that; you draw a class-based reactive substrate through a DOM. For "a DOM in Node without a browser,"happy-dom is already the standard lighter-than-jsdom choice — you're not using a workaround, you're using the tool. So there's nothing to adopt there.
The thing that isn't standard is one child process per page, and (d) converges exactly on what D3 already found. Two confirmations from the research: React 19'srenderToString from the browser build hangs the Node process after completion (an open facebook/react issue) — the kind of post-render hang that makes per-process isolationfeel necessary when the real cause is elsewhere; and the standard SSG pattern is unambiguously render-many-routes-in-one-process, not fork-per-route. Your D3 already established the real reason you can't do that today — a book registers its theme against the shared Book component at module load, last-writer-wins — and D2 supplies the fix (register against the book's own lifted component). So (d)'s verdict is: the child-process-per-page is not the prerender pattern; it's the D3 collision wearing a performance cost, and the standard one-process equivalent becomes available precisely when D2 lands. No tool to adopt, and this is a fourth confirmation of the D2-unblocks-everything finding rather than a new axis — the prerender question and the process-isolation question are the same question, which is what D3 already said.
One thing I'll flag as a possible future correction rather than a current one: if you ever move off the child process after D2, the happy-dom-in-one-warm-process path will surface React's post-render hang and the NODE_ENV-shared-between-modes gotcha from (a) together, because they live in the same process. Not a problem now — the child process sidesteps both — but worth knowing they're waiting there, so "kill the child processes" (post-D2) should be tested for exit-cleanliness specifically, not just correctness. That's a probe for later, not a finding for now.
That's the round. The load-bearing corrections: D11's ␀0␀ line and D9's importer-edge caveat both resolve to "the edge is manual — watcher + ␀1␀, not ␀2␀," and the mention-key uniqueness is per-scope, refused loudly within-scope, which is the sphinxcontrib-bibtex verdict and which bears on 04's two still-open key questions. The proxy spelling and the mention-key spelling both now have five prior examples behind their constraints for Doug to rule against — which was the thing nobody in the conversation had seen.

This is stated by a Vite maintainer tracing the call chain in PR #22188: "handleHotUpdate is only invoked when ␀1␀, so it is never called from the 'add'/'unlink' paths at all." Confirmed independently by a user report (discussion #4580, "HMR not triggered on creation/deletion of files") and by the rollup-plugin-pages maintainer ("Adding a new markdown page in the directory doesn't trigger anything"). So the directory-membership change — the thirteenth chapter appearing, which is the entire reason D11's RESTS-ON says the book must go virtual ("adding a thirteenth chapter invalidates nothing") — is exactly the case handleHotUpdate cannot see. D11's edge, as written, handles the case the virtual module doesn't need (content edit, which idiom A already covers) and misses the case it exists for (membership change).
The correct edge is therefore split by event, not unified under handleHotUpdate:
Chapter content edit → native, via the real imports idiom A already gives you (Vite re-runs the imported chapter; the book re-renders). No manual work.
Chapter add / delete → handleHotUpdate is silent; you must catch it at the chokidar level — server.watcher.on('add', …) and server.watcher.on('unlink', …) registered in configureServer — and on either, regenerate the virtual book's import list, invalidateModule it, and patch the catalogue (a new chapter's declarations enter; a deleted chapter's leave, and its keys' readers re-run — your reverse index). This is also where the D9 reverse-index heal fires on add.

This is the same shallow-graph fact your own D9 probe hit — a module Vite hasn't analyzed doesn't propagate. In prerender/publish it's moot (the build loads everything); in dev it means the heal is reliable for chapters that have been served, and the add/unlink watcher path is what covers the rest. So the honest statement for D11: idiom A (real imports) for content, raw ␀3␀ for membership, and ␀4␀ is the wrong hook for the membership case it was assigned.

So the whole watch-edge apparatus is dev-only by construction — the build re-assembles from scratch and needs no edge. This matches your anchor that publish is a full build().

That's the disposal point for your watcher and resident catalogue, and the reason is exactly what lets you distinguish a config reload ('restart' — dispose, and configureServer will re-fire and rebuild the catalogue) from a shutdown ('close' — dispose for good). So "keep the catalogue resident across a config reload" resolves to: don't — dispose on 'restart', rebuild in the re-fired configureServer (150ms), which also sidesteps the "watcher-added-after-close hangs the process" hazard, because disposal is tied to the lifecycle event rather than left dangling. (Flag: I read closeServer's reason param from the current v8 docs; verify it exists in your pinned Vite 7 — the hook is older but thereason discriminator may be newer. If it's not in 7, the configureServer-returned-cleanup-function is the 7-era equivalent.)
(2) The Vite hook verdict, so you write it once — and it's exactly the sentence you offered
Your predicted honest answer is the correct one, and I'll give it back verbatim so you can write it today, plus the one sharpening the source forces.
Write ␀0␀. It is not deprecated. The current stable docs say: "The deprecation of handleHotUpdate is planned for a future major. We don't recommend moving away from handleHotUpdate yet." The main plugin API page documents handleHotUpdate and does not even mention hotUpdate — hotUpdate lives only in the Environment-API section. So handleHotUpdate is the canonical hook today.
The exact difference in what each is handed and may return:
␀0␀ — HmrContext = { file, timestamp, modules, read, server }. modules is the affected-module array with mixed Client+SSR information. Called once, for all environments. May return a filtered ModuleNode[] (narrow the HMR), or [] + custom handling. Only ever fires on ␀5␀.
␀0␀ — HotUpdateOptions = { type: 'create' | 'update' | 'delete', file, timestamp, modules, read, server }, and this.environment is the current one. Called per environment (so it runs multiple times — once per env). modules are that environment's nodes only. May return EnvironmentModuleNode[].
The one concrete reason ␀0␀ matters for you — and it's sooner than "someday." Its type: 'create' | 'delete' is the add/delete signal ␀2␀ structurally lacks, and add/delete-of-chapters is your directory-membership case from piece 1. So the migration trigger isn't hypothetical: the moment you want the thirteenth-chapter heal to run through the hook system rather than through a raw watcher.on('add'), hotUpdate is the hook that carries it. Two viable shapes, and you can defer the choice cleanly: (a) handleHotUpdate for content + raw server.watcher.on('add'/'unlink') for membership — works on Vite 7, no Environment API; or (b) hotUpdate for all three event types — Environment-API-aware, the future-facing form. D11's correction already says "keep the invalidation decision in a plain function"; that's what makes (a)→(b) a one-line rewire.
␀0␀ vs ␀1␀ — is it the same work behind a nicer name? Nearly, with a real difference. server.moduleGraph.invalidateModule(mod, seen?, timestamp?, isHmr?) marks a module (and, per the four-arg form in the docs, walks importers) as needing re-evaluation but is a graph-bookkeeping call; you typically pair it with return [mod] or a ws.send. server.reloadModule(mod) (added in PR #10333 for exactly the "invalidate my virtual module when its hidden source changed" case) is the higher-level "invalidate and trigger the HMR for it" — it does the reload propagation you'd otherwise assemble by hand. For your virtual-book case, reloadModule is the more honest call: it's the one written for a virtual module with hidden deps. So the verdict:invalidateModule is the primitive, reloadModule is the primitive + the HMR trigger, and for the manual membership edge you want reloadModule.
One landscape fact to know but not act on: current Vite is 8, Rolldown-powered (this.meta.rolldownVersion detects it); the plugin interface now extends Rolldown's, not Rollup's. You anchored Vite 7, and every hook above (configureServer, handleHotUpdate, apply, closeServer, resolveId/load/transform, \0 virtual ids) is stable across 7→8, so nothing you build on 7 breaks the reasoning. I flag it only so "Vite 7 stays" is a chosen pin rather than an unnoticed one — the Rolldown transition is the kind of thing that's cheap to know now and expensive to discover mid-migration.
(3) The two parsing paths — and createScanner is disqualified on capability, which resolves D9's last unknown
This is the one where the detail decides it, exactly as you said, and the answer is: do not measure ␀0␀ — it cannot provide your prose-only guarantee, and that's a capability fact, not a speed fact. Here's the evidence, from Microsoft's own compiler notes and scanner.ts.
The scanner has two modes, Standard and JSX (setLanguageVariant), but — and this is the load-bearing sentence, from the TypeScript-Compiler-Notes scanner doc —"the more complicated aspects of JSX support is mostly handled back in the parser." Concretely, in scanner.ts the JSX tokens are produced only by dedicated methods the parser calls: scanJsxToken(), reScanJsxToken(allowMultilineJsxText?), scanJsxIdentifier(), scanJsxAttributeValue(). The default scan() — the one a raw createScanner loop calls — is Standard mode and never emits ␀8␀. A bare scanner walking a .tsx with scan() tokenizes the JSX children as ordinary JS (identifiers, <, >, /, strings) and has no way to know it's inside JSX children versus inside a String.raw template versus a type argument — because that distinction is grammatical, not lexical. The scanner emits JsxText only when something with grammatical context calls scanJsxToken() at the right position, and the only thing that knows those positions is the parser.
So your prose-only guarantee — that the scan saw Scott Aaronson and the reference URL but not the String.raw LaTeX formula, not the 3 imports, not the 5 comments — is precisely the guarantee a raw scanner cannot give, because "is this run of characters JsxText or a template body or a comment" is the exact question the scanner delegates upward. To get it from createScanner you would have to re-implement the parser's JSX context tracking — i.e., write a JSX parser to avoid calling the JSX parser. Disqualified. Not slow — incapable.
The other candidates, briefly:
␀0␀ (full parse) → builds the AST including JsxText nodes with pos/end offsets. This is the source of your prose-only guarantee. It's what you already run with setParentNodes: false (which skips parent-pointer wiring — the one cheap trim available on a full parse). There is no lighter full-parse that still yields JsxText with positions. Keep it; it's the floor.
␀0␀ → produces JS output, not a walkable positioned tree. Wrong artifact — you can't get JsxText byte-spans out of it. Disqualified for a different reason than the scanner: it gives you the transpile, not the structure.
tree-sitter → would work (it has a real grammar), but it's a second grammar to maintain beside the TS parse, and it reintroduces exactly the "two engines that can disagree" risk D7 killed for the editor. At six books it's all cost, no benefit. Disqualified on the same principle D7 already ruled.
This resolves D9's remaining ␀0␀. D9 lists: "whether the cold pass wants ␀1␀, a persisted table, or tree-sitter." Two of the three are now eliminated on capability/principle (createScanner can't see JsxText; tree-sitter is a second engine), leaving ␀3␀ + a persisted table — which is what the design already has (parse once, cache by digest, the .graph.json shape). So D9's last world-premise doesn't need a /think; it needs createSourceFile and persistence, both already chosen. The unknown collapses to the answer you're already building.
Which of these changes if the numbers were 10× worse (your calibration): none of the disqualifications. createScanner is out on capability at any speed; tree-sitter is out on principle at any speed. What changes at 10× (20.7ms/file; 166s cold on 8000; 20ms warm) is only the emphasis on persistence: the warm edit at 20ms is still comfortably under your 250ms ceiling, so the interactive loop survives 10×; the cold pass at 166s becomes genuinely painful and makes the persisted table load-bearing rather than merely nice — and possibly worth a worker-pool across files for the one-time cold build. But that's a refinement to a mechanism you already have (the digest-skip), not a change of path. So the honest answer to "what would you re-decide at 10×": nothing architectural — you'd parallelize the cold pass and lean harder on the digest cache, both already in the design. Measure only ␀1␀ variants (with/without setParentNodes, and whether pre-reading the file yourself beats letting TS read it); everything else is out before the stopwatch.
That's the round. The three load-bearing findings, each with its evidence: ␀0␀ never fires on add/delete (Vite PR #22188), which corrects D11's edge sentence and means the membership case wants watcher.on('add'/'unlink') or hotUpdate, not handleHotUpdate; ␀4␀ is current, ␀5␀ is the migration whose create/delete types are your membership signal (Vite changes docs), which is the sentence you offered, confirmed with the sharper "sooner than you think" reason; and ␀6␀ cannot identify JsxText without the parser (scanner.ts: JSX tokens come only from scanJsxToken/reScanJsxToken, never from scan()), which disqualifies it on capability and collapses D9's last unknown to the createSourceFile-plus-persist path already built.

Let me hold the whole shape and look at it from as far back as I can, because that's the job now — not to improve the milestones but to find where they'll hurt. Four things, in the order you asked, and I'm going to lead with your M4 worry because you're right, and being right about it exposes a deeper ordering fault than the one you named.
1. The order — M4 is misplaced, and it's worse than you think
You caught the real thing: M3's gate ("parsed cards equal the evaluated ones, book for book") pins equality to the evaluated cards, and the evaluated cards are keyed by #slug(name) because no id was ever planted. So M3 as written certifies the slug. Then M4 removes it. You'd be making the slug the definition of correct in one milestone and deleting the definition in the next — and any test you wrote for M3's gate becomes a test you must rewrite in M4, which means M3's gate was never testing the thing you actually want.
But here's the part underneath your worry. The equality gate is the wrong gate, not just wrongly ordered. "Parsed cards equal evaluated cards" assumes the evaluated cards are the ground truth. They're not —reading.ts produces them by running the book, and some of what it reads is exactly what you're removing (the slug guess) or what the thesis calls a fault (address-bound shelved). So equality-to-evaluated bakes the faults into the acceptance criterion. You'd pass M3 by reproducing the slug faithfully, which is the opposite of progress.
The fix isn't to reorder M3 and M4. It's to change M3's gate from equality to equality on the fields that are already correct, and divergence-by-design on the fields that aren't. Concretely: the parsed cards must equal the evaluated ones on name, title, author-key, subject-key, chapters, catalogued, shelves-as-identities — the facts the thesis says are sound — and must not reproduce address()/#slug, because address is a derived late pass (D6) and doesn't belong in the card at all. If you keep the naive equality gate, M3 either fails on a difference that is correct (the parsed card rightly lacks a slug the evaluated card wrongly has) or passes by copying a fault. Either way the gate lies. So:
Split the id out of M4 and pull its *front half* before M3. The "mention plants an id" work is really two things wearing one number (see §2), and the half that matters for ordering is: the card carries an identity, not an address. That has to be true before M3's gate can be honest, because M3's gate is about what a card is. Planting the id in the rendered page (the writing/ kind that draws a target) can stay late — the page doesn't need it until references resolve to it (M5). But the card holding an identity instead of a slug is a precondition of M3, not a consequence of M4.
So the ordering fault is: M3's gate depends on the identity/address split that M4 is scheduled to perform. Move the identity-in-the-card half of M4 to before M3, restate M3's gate as field-wise-equality-on-the-sound-fields, and leave the page-side id-planting where it is. Your instinct was "M4 after M3 pins equality to the thing we're removing" — correct, and the resolution is that M3's gate was never the right gate, because it made a fault the standard.
One more ordering note, smaller: M1's gate ("bind and preview unchanged") and M7 are the same claim at two ends of the project, and M1 can't actually prove it. M1 promotes createServer out of the child process. But the reason the child process exists (D3, verified) is theme-registers-against-shared-Book, last-writer-wins — and that collision is a framework fix (D2), not in your seven milestones at all. So M1 puts all six books in one dev process, and if any two books register a theme against the shared component at module load, the last one wins and M1's gate (".me serves all six books") passes visually while the theme is silently wrong for five of them. M1's gate as written ("serves all six books") won't catch it — you need the gate to be "serves all six books with each book's own theme," and you need to know whether D2 has landed in the framework before M1, because if it hasn't, M1 can't be honest either. This is the same shape as the M3 gate problem: a gate that passes on the visible thing while the invisible thing is wrong. Check the D2 dependency before M1, not during.
2. What's hiding two — M5 hides four, and M4 hides two
M5 is the one that will hurt, and it's not hiding two, it's hiding four, each with a different failure mode and a different gate:
The transform — find the five forms in JsxText, splice by offset, emit the lowered [copy](target). Pure, per-file, no catalogue needed. Its failure mode is splice correctness (byte-identical outside matches).
Resolution against the catalogue — turn a citation's key into the address it resolves to. Needs the catalogue (M3) and the id (M4). Its failure mode is wrong address / non-membership.
The proxy path — a miss emits the address-it-would-have-had and writes a log line. Its failure mode is the log missing a survivor or a survivor not blocking publish.
The reverse index — record (key → files that read it), heal on later declaration. Its failure mode is the negative-dependency one you already know: heal doesn't fire, or fires too broadly.
These have different gates and different prerequisites, and bundling them means M5's single gate can pass while one of the four is silently broken. The tell is that your M5 gate tests items 3 and 4 (cite-a-missing-title, then declare-it-elsewhere-and-heal) and says nothing about item 1 (splice) or item 2 (correct resolution of a present key). So the gate as written could pass with a transform that mangles a paragraph's whitespace or resolves a present key to the wrong address, because neither is exercised. Split M5 into at least two, ideally three:
M5a — the transform alone. Gate: every one of the five forms, spliced, leaves the file byte-identical outside its match; the lowered form round-trips through the runtime Parser.link() (which already exists and is ^…$-anchored — see the collision in §3). This is testable without the catalogue, which is exactly why it should be its own milestone: you can prove the splice before resolution exists.
M5b — resolution + proxy. Gate: a present key resolves to the right address (the positive case your current gate omits); a missing key emits the would-be address and one log line with key/file/offset. This needs M3 and the id.
M5c — the reverse index / heal. Gate: your current M5 gate (declare-in-another-file, heals with no edit to the citing file). This is the one genuinely hard thing and it deserves to not share a milestone with the splice, because when it fails you want to know it's the index and not the transform.
Splitting M5 isn't bureaucracy — it's that the reverse index is the single highest-risk thing in the whole project (it's what defeated the runtime; it's the negative-dependency problem), and burying it in a four-part milestone means its failure arrives tangled with three other possible causes. Isolate it so that when the heal doesn't fire, the transform and resolution are already known-good.
M4 hides two, as above: card-holds-identity (must precede M3) and page-draws-a-target-with-an-id (can stay before M5, since M5 resolves to it). Same number, two jobs, two positions in the order.
M2 might hide two, and it's worth checking before you start it. M2 says three artifacts go virtual "via the real imports (content) and the watcher (membership)." But the three artifacts aren't symmetric. The per-book module has real chapter imports (idiom A works). Thebook index (books.ts) and route table — do they? If books.ts is a generated map of folder → () => import(...), its dependencies are the set of books, which is a directory-membership fact, and idiom A (real imports) only covers content, not membership. So books.ts going virtual is entirely a membership-watcher problem with no native-import half — which is a different, and harder, case than the per-book module. M2's gate ("add a thirteenth chapter, it appears") tests the per-book membership but you should confirm it also tests add a thirteenth *book*, because that's the books.ts case and it's the one more likely to be wrong. I'd flag M2's gate to add: "add a new book folder and it appears in routing with no bind."
3. The collision — two settled things will fight, and one is load-bearing
Collision 1, and it's real: the runtime ␀2␀ is ␀3␀-anchored, and your lowered mentions are inline. You sent me this yourself, and it's now a collision because of what M5 emits. Parser.link() is /^␀0␀]*)\]␀1␀$/ — it matches only when the whole writing is a single link. A reference lowers to a whole-writing link, so it's fine. But a mention stands mid-prose — [[great]] inside a sentence lowers to [great](key) inside a paragraph, and the anchored link() will not see it, because it isn't the whole writing. So the lowered form is bivalent (ref vs mention) but the runtime parser that reads the lowered form only handles one valence. The 04 chapter even flags this: "␀10␀ is anchored ␀11␀, so it only reads a link when the WHOLE writing is one. Mentions stand inline, so they must be found inside a string and split out — the shape ␀12␀ already performs at every level, but new work at each." So this is known but it's filed as "new work," and it's actually a cross-milestone collision: M5's transform emits inline lowered mentions, and nothing in the runtime reads them until that "new work at each level" is done. If M5 emits inline mentions and the runtime still only reads whole-writing links, M5's page renders the mention as literal text [great](key) — the MediaWiki-red-link failure, except silent. Where it bites: M5a's gate ("round-trips through Parser.link()") will pass for refs and fail for mentions, and if you only test a ref you won't see it. So the collision is: the inline-mention parse is a prerequisite of M5 that lives in the framework (␀15␀/␀16␀), not in the binder, and it's not in any milestone. Name it, and put it in M5a or before.
Collision 2, softer but worth stating: the ␀0␀-separated key grammar and ␀1␀. The new reference grammar keys are Book Code > Chapter Code > Mention. Your grep verified that no mention target today contains / # ? : — so shape-based classification (mention vs ref) is safe. But > is a new character in the key space, and the classification predicate is Url.addresses, which tests for scheme//////#/?. > isn't in that set, so a >-bearing key correctly classifies as a mention (relative, address-false) — good, that's consistent. The thing to verify: > (and the spaces around it in Book Code > Chapter Code) must survive the lowered form and the emitted URL without being percent-mangled or treated as an address delimiter downstream. This is a small probe, not a redesign, but it's the kind of thing that passes every unit test and breaks on the one book whose chapter code has a > in a way you didn't expect. Probe: does a ␀15␀-and-space key round-trip through the transform → lowered form → ␀16␀ → the emitted ␀17␀ unchanged? If the browser or the HTML serializer touches > (it can, in attribute context), the key is corrupted at the last step.
A third, quieter one you should log even though it's not in these seven: the check mode (M6) and dev share ␀0␀ but must not share its evaluation. M6 is "the check, which is not dev." But specify.ts today evaluates books (ssrLoadModule + live.specify()). If M6's cross-library pass reuses specify.ts, it re-imports the evaluation you spent M3 removing from the critical path — and now evaluation is back, just wearing "check mode." That may be fine (local @specify checks are the thesis's portable, construction-time checks, and running them deliberately-and-incrementally is legitimate). But the collision is: M6 must run the *local well-formedness* checks (construction-time, portable) and must NOT re-run the *referential* checks (those are the catalogue's, already done at transform). If M6 re-does referential validation by evaluation, you've rebuilt the thing M3 deleted. So M6's gate needs a negative clause: "the check pass evaluates a book's own well-formedness and never resolves a cross-book reference — that's the catalogue's job, done." Otherwise M6 quietly re-couples the library.
4. The scars — what I've read someone get exactly wrong, per milestone
M1 (one process, ␀0␀ hosted). The scar is the one from your own (a)-round source, and it's specific: renderToString from react-dom/server.browser hangs the Node process after completion in React 19 (facebook/react#32965 — the render finishes, the process won't exit). You're promoting rendering into a long-lived host. A long-lived host that can't exit cleanly is worse than a child process that always did. Cost to them: the process hangs on teardown, CI times out, and it looks like a test problem. Guard: M1's gate should include the process exits cleanly on ␀3␀/close, not just it serves. This is also why closeServer with reason matters — dispose the watcher there or the chokidar watcher alone will hold the process open (the other hang, vite#18224).
M2 (virtual artifacts). The scar is dolbex's, in the exact discussion thread I read (#15504): they did idiom A correctly — injected real imports into the virtual module — and still couldn't trigger an SSR reload, only client. Their load() returned real imports, HMR worked for the browser, and the SSR module (which is your prerender/specify path) didn't update. Cost: silent staleness on the SSR side specifically, which is the side your build uses. Guard: M2's gate ("add a thirteenth chapter, it appears") must be checked in the rendered output, not just in the dev client — because the SSR path is where D9's "not analyzed → stop propagation" and dolbex's "SSR didn't reload" both live. Test the membership change through a prerender, not just a browser refresh.
M3 (parsed catalogue). The scar is Astro's, read at the PR (withastro/astro#12767, #11591): their content-layer cache is keyed by a digest that excludes parts of the config, so a change that should invalidate doesn't, and the fix is "delete .astro by hand." Your .graph.json digest is sha256(book's files + bases + package hashes). The Astro scar says: the digest must include everything the parsed card depends on, and the thing most likely to be forgotten is the parser's own version. If you change the parse rule (a new sigil, a fix to how JsxText maps to a card) but the digest doesn't include the parser/transform version, every book's card is stale-but-"fresh" and nothing rebuilds — and, exactly like Astro, the only fix is rm .graph.json, which your comment already anticipates ("delete the file to read everything"). Guard: put the transform/parse-rule version into the digest's fixed inputs, next to the package hashes. Otherwise M3 ships a cache that goes silently stale on the one kind of change you'll make most during development — changes to the parser itself.
M4 (plant the id). The scar is Sphinx's duplicate-label, which I read at the source (Python docs bug, sphinx#9707): a duplicate label doesn't error — it resolves to one of the two, silently wrong, and text meant to link to section A links to section B. The moment you plant author-written ids, two writings can carry the same id. If your resolution picks one silently (BibTeX's "keep one," Sphinx's "resolve to first"), you've built the exact miswire. Guard: M4 must refuse a duplicate id within its scope loudly (XML-ID behavior: reject), not resolve-to-first. And the scope is the >-key grammar's scope — same id in two books is fine, same id twice in one book is the error. This is the sphinxcontrib-bibtex verdict (duplicate_local_citation is an error, duplicate_citation across docs is fine) that they reached after years of issues. You can have it on day one of M4 by making within-scope duplicate a hard refusal.
M5 (the transform + resolution + proxy + reverse index). Two scars, one per hidden milestone. For the transform (M5a): LaTeX's ?? — the unresolved ref renders a placeholder and the warning buries in the log, and papers ship with ␀1␀. Doug's ruling ("the address it would have had, and the log is the refusal") is deliberately LaTeX-shaped for the page — a potentially-broken link, no special anchor — which is fine only because the gate refuses on any log survivor (the linker's "no output written"). The scar's lesson: the danger isn't the broken link on the page, it's the log line getting lost. So M5b's gate must assert the log line is machine-checkable and complete — one line per survivor, greppable, and the publish gate greps for zero. If the log is prose a human skims, you've rebuilt ??. For the reverse index (M5c): the scar is the one I read almost verbatim in a real salsa project (gdscript-db): "a query memoized while it was still absent would otherwise return that stale empty result forever" — the immortal-absence bug. Their fix required making the absent thing a tracked input; when it was an untracked side-handle, the miss memoized permanently. Your reverse index is the tracked-input; the scar says the failure is when a miss is recorded against the wrong key or not recorded at all. M5c's gate (declare-elsewhere-and-heal) tests the happy path; add the unhappy path that actually bit them: cite a missing key, then delete a different file entirely — the citation must not heal (it's still missing), and the reverse index must not have spuriously cleared. The immortal-absence bug hides on the deletion side, not the addition side, and your gate only tests addition.
M6 (the check, not dev). The scar is Astro again, the other one from the incremental-builds piece I read: build.concurrency > 1 disables the incremental cache and Astro re-renders every page. The lesson for a "run efficiently, only checks things that change" pass: the incremental check and any parallelism you add to it will fight, and the naive fix (parallelize the check for speed) silently turns off the incrementality that was the whole point. Cost to Astro: people set concurrency for speed and got full rebuilds, slower, and didn't know why. Guard: M6's gate ("change one chapter, only that book re-checked") must be measured with whatever parallelism you ship, because the incrementality-vs-parallelism collision is exactly where it hides.
M7 (backpropagate; resolve the two ␀0␀ owners). The scar is subtle and I read it in the Astro cache-busting thread (kurkle/astro-chartjs-editor#20): when a tool is linked rather than versioned (a file: dependency, which is your copy-template-from-master situation), a change to the master doesn't bump any version, so nothing downstream invalidates, and you develop against a stale copy without knowing — "developing the integration itself via a ␀2␀ install (no version bump between edits) still requires clearing ␀3␀ by hand." This is precisely your M7 setup: the binder is developed in the live library's copy and backpropagated to the master, and copies resolve their own deps. The scar says: the copy can silently diverge from the master with no signal, and your own specifying.ts's fixed() already hashes the resolved package to catch exactly this — so M7's gate should verify that the digest actually changes when the master binder changes, or a stale binder will validate a library against rules it no longer has. You have the mechanism (fixed() hashes @dna-platform/public and chemistry); M7 must extend it to hash the binder itself, or the one thing you're backpropagating is the one thing not in the digest.
The through-line, said once from the back of the room: five of your seven gates test that the visible thing works and not that the invisible thing is right — M1 serves books but doesn't check per-book themes; M3 equals evaluated cards but that includes the fault; M5 heals on add but not on delete; M6 checks incrementally but not under parallelism; M7 copies but doesn't prove the copy sees the master's changes. That's not a flaw in the milestones, it's a flaw in thegates, and it's the same flaw each time: the gate watches the output and not the dependency. Every scar above is someone who shipped the visible thing green while the invisible thing was wrong. The cheapest fix is to make each gate assert the dependency, not the appearance — per-book theme, not six books; field-wise-correct cards, not equal cards; heal-on-add and no-spurious-heal-on-delete; incremental under real parallelism; digest-changes-when-master-changes. Get the gates to watch the edges and the milestones are in good shape — with M4's front half moved before M3, M5 split into three, and the inline-mention parse named as the framework prerequisite it is.

(a) entry, not phase — right, with one seam to watch

That's exactly right, and it's the "one fact, two uses" obligation from the thesis one level down — two readings of .pubconfig are two computations of one fact that can drift.

State Two's gate tests a Title/Author/Subject receiving a reference (whole-writing, so link() handles it) and a cited missing title (also a reference). Neither gate exercises an inline mention, so State Two could pass green while every inline mention is broken. 04 flags this as "new work at each level" but doesn't put it in a state. Restated guard: State Two's work must include the inline-mention parse in Parser/Composition (framework, not binder), and State Two's gate must include an inline mention in prose resolves to its target, not only the three card-field references. The through-line is unchanged from the seven: the gates watch the visible output, and the failures live in the invisible dependency — the slug hiding in "unchanged," the theme collision hiding in "six books served," the inline mention hiding in "a reference works." Regrouping into three states is the right call for seeing progress, but it makes each gate cover more, so each gate has to assert its buried dependency explicitly or it passes green over a wrong edge. For State One specifically, the buried edge to assert before you trust the gate is the D3 theme collision — because serving.ts has already created the exact condition that triggers it, and nothing built or planned fixes it.

Here's the distinction that matters: production isolation comes from one bundle per book plus one runtime per book, and the thing that makes the theme leak impossible in production is the one-runtime-per-book part, not the prerendered-HTML part. Prerendering is a performance and indexability property (the content is in the HTML before JS runs); runtime isolation is the correctness property (book A's module-load registrations can't reach book B). Those are separable, and only the second is what Doug's ruling is protecting. So "replicate what is published" means, precisely: each book gets its own runtime in dev, so that a book's module-scope registrations are scoped to that book and cannot leak — and it does not mean dev must serve pre-baked HTML. The shell can be shared. A shared shell that loads one book's bundle into a fresh runtime per navigation is architecturally the same isolation as production; a shared runtime that swaps books via a client router is not. So the line isn't "prerendered vs live," it's "one runtime per book vs one runtime for the app," and that line lands in State One (it's about how the host serves and how books load), not in a new prerender-in-dev milestone.
