The answer is not none — three answers change, one of them fundamentally, and it's not the one you'd expect to be worst. Let me take your three in order and then the fourth thing, because the fourth (subjective build) is the one that reaches back and changes the shape, not just a parameter.
First — the salsa verdict flips, and I was right for the wrong reason at six books. I refuted the machinery on two grounds: depth-1 graph (no transitive cutoff to save), and "six books, over-engineering." The second ground is now gone. But you should not let me keep the first ground unexamined, because it's doing less work than I claimed. Depth-1 was about the reference graph — citations over declarations, nothing cites a citation. That's still true topologically. But early cutoff's value was never only about depth — it's about fan-out under a global rebuild, and fan-out is exactly what scale creates. At six books, when a declaration changes, re-running everything that read it is cheap because "everything" is a handful. At ten thousand books, a single common title — imagine a conversation everyone's related-works point at — has thousands of readers, and the naive "re-run all readers" is now the expensive operation the reverse index was supposed to make cheap. So the reverse index doesn't just stay necessary at scale, it becomes the thing standing between you and an O(readers) storm on every edit to a popular declaration. And early cutoff earns its keep in a way it didn't at six: when a chapter's prose changes but its declarations don't, backdating means the thousands of citations pointing at that chapter don't re-validate. At six books you'd never notice skipping that work; at thousands, "a prose edit re-validates every reference into this book" is a freeze. So: build the reverse index (you're already doing this), and add the one piece of salsa I said you didn't need — the firewall/backdating discipline, where a reference depends on the target's *signature* (does key K exist, what's its address-identity) and not the target's *body*. That's what makes a prose edit not touch its citers. At six books it was ceremony; at thousands it's the difference between an incremental compiler and a batch one wearing a watcher. I still would not adopt salsa-the-Rust-library — there's no mature JS port and you don't want a second engine — but the disciplines (per-key dependency, negative dependency, signature-not-body firewall, backdating) all flip from "over-engineering" to "load-bearing." My six-books verdict ("hand-roll the reverse index, skip the rest") becomes "hand-roll the reverse index and the firewall query; the rest of salsa's machinery you still don't need, but for a new reason — you're depth-1 so you don't need transitive red-green, just one-level cutoff."
Second — "scan eagerly, it's 150ms" is dead, and persistence stops being the fix — sharding does. At ten thousand files the cold scan is ~20s and you named that yourself. But here's the part that changes more than the number: at six books, "persist and only rescan by digest" fully solved it, because the cold pass happened once ever and steady-state was one file. At thousands arriving via an importer, the cold pass is not a once-ever event — it's what happens every time a batch of conversations imports, and an import of five hundred conversations is five hundred files that were never scanned, so you pay a cold-scan-of-the-batch on every import. Persistence still helps (you don't rescan the unchanged ten thousand), but the new cost is import-batch-sized cold scans, repeatedly. Two things follow. One: the scan must be parallel across files — it's embarrassingly parallel (each file's JsxText is independent until the catalogue merge), and at 20s-cold-serial a worker pool is the difference between a 20s import and a 3s one. At six books parallelism was pointless overhead; at thousands it's mandatory, and it's a real design fact because it means the scan phase must be structured as independent per-file units that merge, not a single walk. Two, and this is the one to internalize: the persisted store itself has to shard. A single .graph.json holding thousands of book entries is a file you rewrite on every import and parse on every cold start — you've moved the "whole table in the critical path" problem from runtime (your third point) into thebuild. This is exactly what Astro hit and fixed: their content layer added experimental.collectionStorage: 'chunked' — content-addressed shards with a manifest — specifically because a single data-store.json didn't scale. I mentioned that in passing as "not relevant at six books." It's relevant now. So: the catalogue store shards (one shard per book or per subject, plus a manifest), the scan parallelizes, and the digest-skip you already have becomes the thing that keeps an import from rescanning the world. My "persistence is load-bearing at 10x" becomes "persistence + sharding + parallel scan, and the unit of persistence is a shard, not the store."
Third — this is the real one, and it's not a compiler problem, it's a runtime problem that your compiler ruling already half-solved. routes.ts holding every book and main.tsx importing it on every page means each page load parses the whole route table and builds the whole shelf before drawing a word. At thousands, that's the entire library's index in the critical path of viewingone conversation. And note what it collides with: the subjective-runtime ruling from your last message. You already ruled that dev must replicate production's one-runtime-per-book. But one-runtime-per-book with a global route table means every one of those isolated runtimes still loads the global table — you get the isolation andkeep the scaling problem. So the two things have to be solved together: the route table cannot be a single artifact every page loads. The fix is the same identity-not-address discipline from D6, applied to routing: a book needs to resolve its own references to addresses, and it needs the addresses of the books it actually references, not all books. Which means the route table shards the same way the catalogue does — a book carries (or lazily fetches) the address-identities of its referents, not the global shelf. This is precisely Doug's "the catalogue survives as something that hands out PARTS, for the things that genuinely have to ask" — at six books you could ship the whole thing and look it up; at thousands, "hand out parts" stops being an elegance and becomes the only thing that fits in a page load. So my earlier read — "resolved references bake to plain links, ordinary prose costs nothing at runtime, the catalogue hands out parts for dynamic work" — was right and I underweighted how much rides on it: at scale, "bake the addresses in, ship no table" is not an optimization, it's the requirement, because the alternative (ship the table, resolve at runtime) puts the whole index in every view. The links an author wrote must be fully resolved at build into plain hrefs, and the runtime must load zero global index to render a page. If any page loads routes.ts-of-everything, the design doesn't scale, full stop. This is the one where I'd stop and say: this is a change to what State One's "resolve" produces — not a global route table imported everywhere, but per-book resolved addresses baked into each book's output, with the global table (if it exists at all) used only by the build, never shipped.
The fourth thing — subjective build — is the one that reaches back and changes the shape, and it's your sphinxcontrib-bibtex verdict arriving from the other direction, exactly as you said. Here's what it does to the three above. If the same book bound against two libraries produces two link graphs, then the resolved address of a reference is not a property of the book — it's a property of (book, library). That breaks a quiet assumption under everything: I've been treating a card's identity as global and its address as a late derivation. Now the derivation is per-library. Which means: the parsed identity (the key, Book Code > Chapter > Mention) is still global and library-independent — that's what makes cross-library referential integrity possible at all — but the resolution (identity → address) is scoped to whose library you're standing in, and the same key resolves to different addresses, or resolves in one library and refuses in another (the referent isn't in this user's library). This is the sphinxcontrib-bibtex scoping verdict from the other side: they scopeduniqueness per document; you're scoping resolution per library. And it lands cleanly on the three: (1) the reverse index is now per-library — "who read key K" is answered within the library doing the build, because a citation in user A's library missing a key user B has is correctly a miss for A; (2) the shards are naturally per-library-composable — a book's identity shard is global, its address shard is per-library; (3) the "hand out parts" runtime becomes the mechanism, because a subjective build means the parts handed out are the ones this user's library contains. The thing to protect, and it's the whole reason Doug is scoping resolution rather than identity: keys must be global and frozen so that two libraries can agree on what a reference *means* even when they disagree on where it *lands*. If you ever let the key become library-scoped, cross-library referential integrity dies — a reference from a related work into user A's conversation can't be validated against user B's copy. So the ruling sharpens the identity/address split you already have rather than replacing it: identity global, resolution subjective. My mention-key constraint set gets a fifth member it didn't need at six books —the key must be library-independent — and the address-derivation pass (D6's late resolve) gets a parameter it didn't have: which library.
So, plainly, which answers change: the salsa verdict (machinery was refused on scale grounds that are gone; the firewall/backdating discipline is now required, not the full engine), the eager-scan verdict (persistence alone is insufficient; sharding + parallel scan, with the store as shards not a file), and the runtime-route-table (was a non-issue, is now the load-bearing scaling constraint, and it must be solvedwith the per-book-runtime ruling, not after it). What does not change: the parse-not-evaluate architecture, the notation, the reverse index existing, the always-refuse gate, and the identity/address split — those were right and scale sharpens them rather than bending them. And the one I'd flag hardest, because it's the intersection of your third point and the subjective build and it's where a wrong move is expensive to undo: decide now that no page ever loads a global index to render itself. Everything else is tuning; that one is a shape decision, it contradicts what main.tsx does today, and it's cheapest to commit to before State One resolves, because State One's "resolve stops waiting on evaluation" is exactly the step that decides whether resolve produces a global table (fatal at scale) or per-book baked addresses (correct at scale). That's the sentence I'd put in front of Doug: at thousands, resolve must emit per-book addresses, not a global route table — and dev must replicate that too, or dev is testing an application that scales differently from the one that ships.

So this round is that question. Here is what I found, then what I think, then where I want you to break it.
=== WHAT THE MECHANISM ACTUALLY IS TODAY, AND IT IS ONE SENTENCE ===
I inventoried every place an address is manufactured. Eight sites, three mechanisms.
ONE — SLUG A NAME INTO AN ANCHOR. Catalogue.address() -> #${reflection.slug(this.name)} every mention Chapter.tsx:43 -> #${reflection.slug(<title text>)} a chapter's anchor Heading.tsx:27 -> <Level id={reflection.slug(<own text>)}> A HEADING'S ID
TWO — LOOK IT UP IN THE SHIPPED SHELF. Catalogue.shelved / shelve() / standing(), plus five overrides — $Book, $Subject, $Author, $Canonical, $Participant — each this.standing() ?? super.address().
THREE — SLUG A NAME INTO A ROUTE SEGMENT. resolution/addresses.ts:36 and rendering/place.ts. Build-time, recorded, not a guess.
And I had told you earlier that NOTHING in the framework emits an id. That was wrong — Heading does. Seeing both ends together is what makes the mechanism legible, so here it is in one sentence:
A HEADING MAKES ITS ID BY SLUGGING ITS OWN TEXT. A MENTION MAKES ITS HREF BY SLUGGING THE NAME IT WAS GIVEN. THEY MEET IF AND ONLY IF THE TWO STRINGS HAPPEN TO SLUG THE SAME.
No catalogue, no membership, no refusal. Two slugs agreeing. That is the entire reference system, and it is exactly why the thesis calls it a guess.
=== WHAT I THINK THE ANSWER IS ===
THE ID IS THE KEY. Not derived from the copy, not slugged from anything: the anchor's id is the authored key, the same string the citation names. The failure today is that two ends derive independently and meet by luck; if both ends carry the same authored string, they cannot drift, and renaming the prose cannot break a link. That is your constraint 4 (frozen, position-independent) and constraint 1 (authored, not generated) doing their job at the DOM.
AND THERE IS A CONVERGENCE THAT MAKES ME THINK IT IS RIGHT. HTML ids must be unique per DOCUMENT. A page is one BOOK (measured — one runtime per book, in dev and in the built site). Keys are unique per BOOK, which is the sphinxcontrib-bibtex scoping you found. So the scope rule and the DOM rule are the same rule, arrived at from two directions. If that is a coincidence I want to know.
WHO PLANTS IT: the notation already answers it. PREFIX ALLOCATES. *[ X ]( Y ) declares — that is where the anchor goes. $[ X ]( Y )* only stands in and plants nothing. So a mention does not blanket-plant ids; an ALLOCATING mention does, which is Doug's by-mention ruling expressed in the markup rather than enforced beside it.
HOW IT IS DRAWN: the compiler should not emit raw HTML. The precedent is in production — the resources plugin finds <Resource>foo.ts</Resource> and emits a FRAMEWORK ELEMENT, letting the kind draw itself. So the transform lowers an allocating mention to a framework kind, and that kind draws the span carrying the id. Doug: "maybe mention just puts a span with an id and it can be DI'd to do cooler things" — the DI lives in the kind, which is only possible if the compiler emits a kind rather than markup.
=== WHERE I WANT YOU TO BREAK IT ===
THE ID-IS-THE-KEY CLAIM. An HTML id has a grammar — it cannot contain a space, and historically could not begin with a digit. Our keys are written the way a person writes them: "My Library Log", "Claude & Our Projects", "Semantics of Types & More". Those are not valid ids as they stand. So either the id is an ESCAPED key (and now there IS a derivation, and the thing I said cannot drift can drift), or keys gain a grammar (and Doug's "you NEVER write urls, names aren't actually kebab cased" is under pressure). Four things to break, and I want to lead with the fourth, because it's the one you ranked worst and you're right that it is — but it's worse than you framed it, and seeing why changes the answer to the first three. So let me break them in the order that makes each one inform the next, not the order you listed.
Break 4 first, because it's the load-bearing crack
You said: the id is planted by one parser at build, and the DOM is built by another parser at draw, and what guarantees the anchor survives. Here's the sharper version, and it's not a survival question — it's a provenance question. Your build-time transform sees source text and splices by offset. The draw-time framework sees a composed object tree — prose parsed into found levels, mentions lifted into annotations (D5), the whole thing drawn through view()/print(). These two parsers do not agree on what the units are. The build parser knows "there is a mention sigil at byte 4,213 in this file." The draw parser knows "there is a $$Chapter annotation on this $Paragraph." The id has to be carried from the first ontology to the second, and the offset is meaningless in the second. So the guarantee you're looking for isn't "does the anchor survive" — it's "is the id attached to a thing that exists in both ontologies, so that the draw parser can't fail to carry it."
And that is exactly why your own instinct — "lower to a framework kind, don't emit raw HTML" — is correct, and it's correct for a reason deeper than the resources-plugin precedent you cited. If the transform emitted raw <span id="...">, the draw parser would have to preserve HTML it doesn't understand through a compose pass that reparses prose into levels — and it won't, because the compose pass operates on the framework's kinds, not on arbitrary spans. Raw HTML injected at build is precisely the thing the second parser is entitled to reflow, drop, or reparse, because it isn't one of its kinds. But if the transform lowers the mention to a framework kind that already exists in the draw ontology (the ␀0␀Chapter, $$Document, etc.), then the id isn't riding on a foreign span, it's riding on a first-class citizen of the second parser's world. The draw parser can't drop it because it's not foreign to it. So the answer to "what guarantees survival" is: you don't inject an anchor and hope it survives — you lower to a kind that the draw parser constructs natively, and the kind draws its own id at ␀4␀ time. The id's provenance is the key (authored, in the source, parsed out at build), and its carrier is a framework kind (native to draw). That's the only design where the two parsers can't disagree, because the thing carrying the id is a thing both of them recognize.
Now the gate. "Rendered-ids superset-of catalogue-keys" is necessary but the wrong direction to catch the failure you care about. Superset checks that every key has an id somewhere — it catches a missing anchor. But the integrity failure at scale is worse: an anchor that exists but is attached to the wrong writing, because the build parser's offset and the draw parser's composed tree diverged (a mention inside aString.raw, a mention whose surrounding prose got reflowed into a different paragraph). Superset-of-keys passes that, because the id is present — it's just on the wrong element. So the gate has to be bidirectional and positional: every catalogue key appears as an id (superset, your version), and every emitted id traces back to exactly one catalogue key at the source position the parser claimed (injective, and position-checked). The prior art for the positional half is the W3C Web Annotation model's own self-check — a TextQuoteSelector (the quote) validated against a TextPositionSelector (the offset): if the quote at the offset isn't the quote you recorded, the anchor drifted. Your D5 mention already stores both key and quote and start/end — that pairing was chosen for re-anchoring, and it's also your build-vs-draw integrity check: after draw, the text inside the planted anchor must equal the quote the parser recorded. If it doesn't, the two parsers disagreed, and you've caught it. So the gate is not "ids ⊇ keys" — it's "ids ⊇ keys, ids injective into keys, and each anchor's drawn text equals its recorded quote." The third clause is the one that catches the expensive failure, and you already store what it needs.
This reframes the whole thing: the id doesn't need to survive a hostile second parser; it needs to be carried by a kind native to the second parser, and verified by the quote you already store. Hold that, because it's what makes break 1 tractable.
Break 1 — id-is-the-key is right in spirit and wrong in mechanism, and the fix is already in your model
You found the real hole: "Claude & Our Projects" is not a valid HTML id, so either you escape (and now there's a derivation that can drift, killing the claim) or keys gain a grammar (and Doug's "you never write URLs" is under pressure). Both horns are real. Here's the way through, and it's not a compromise — it dissolves the dilemma.
The id is not the key. The id is the key's *identity*, and the human-readable key is a label over it. This is exactly the opaque-vs-meaningful split from the Wikidata/Obsidian finding, and you're being pushed onto it by the DOM the same way Wikidata was pushed onto it by reorganization. But — critical — this does not mean generating an opaque Q42 and losing authored meaning. It means: the authored key "Claude & Our Projects" is the label; the thing that goes in the id= attribute and in the citation's resolved href is a canonical form of that key; and — this is the part that saves the no-drift claim — the canonicalization is frozen at declaration time and stored in the card, not recomputed at each end.
That's the whole trick, and it's why it doesn't drift. Escaping drifts when both ends escape independently — the same failure you already have (two slugs meeting by luck), just moved to escaping. But if the canonical form is computed once, at declaration, and stored as the card's identity, then both the anchor and the citation read the same stored canonical form — they don't each derive it, they both look it up. The derivation happens exactly once, is frozen (your constraint 4), and both ends carry it by reference, not by recomputation. So: authored label → canonicalize once at declaration → freeze in card → both anchor-id and citation-href read the frozen canonical form. The label stays human ("Claude & Our Projects", written the way a person writes it — Doug's rule holds); the id is valid HTML; and nothing drifts because nothing is derived twice.
The prior art naming, since you asked how systems that use authored keys as DOM anchors resolve exactly this: DocBook/DITA ␀0␀ faced precisely this — human-meaningful ids that must satisfy the XML NCName grammar (no spaces, no leading digit, restricted punctuation). Their resolution is the one above: the author writes a constrained id, and a separate <title> carries the human phrase. They split label from id at the point of authoring. Sphinx labels do the same — .. _my-label: is the id (constrained), the section title is the human text, and the two are explicitly different fields. AsciiDoc auto-generates an id from the title and lets you override it, and its scars are instructive: auto-generation drifts (retitle → id changes → links break — your exact failure), which is why every mature docs system that started with title-derived ids added explicit, frozen id overrides. The lesson from all three: nobody who has lived with this uses the display string as the id. They carry a frozen id and a separate label, always. So id-is-the-key is right if "the key" means the frozen canonical identity and "the label" is the human string — and your model already has both slots (D5's mention stores key and quote; the card stores identity). You are not adding a concept; you are refusing to collapse two slots you already have into one.
One thing this forces you to rule, and it's Doug's: what is the canonical form, and is it reversible enough to stay legible? Obsidian's answer (^ + alphanumerics-and-dashes, lowercased) is legible-ish and lossy (& → dropped or -and-). CTS-URN's answer (percent-ish but domain-specific) is precise and ugly. The one to avoid is slugging, because slugging "Claude & Our Projects" and "Claude and Our Projects" to the same thing is a silent collision — and at scale, silent collisions in the identity space are the referential-integrity failure you're building the whole system to prevent. So the canonical form must beinjective (two different keys never canonicalize to the same id), which rules out lossy slugging and points at a reversible encoding. That's the constraint; the spelling is Doug's, and I'd hand him exactly that framing: the id is a frozen, injective, once-computed encoding of the authored key, stored in the card, read by both ends — not a slug, because slugs collide, and a collision here is the thing we're preventing.
Break 2 — the scope convergence is real, but it's real for a reason that can break, so name the reason
"Keys unique per book" = "ids unique per document" is not a coincidence today, and it's not a deep law either — it's a coincidence that is currently load-bearing because of a fact you measured: one runtime per book, one book per page. So the convergence holdsexactly as long as "a page is a book" holds, and you already listed the three things that break it: a book split across pages, two books on one page, a chapter that is its own page. Here's the verdict on each, because they resolve differently:
A chapter is its own page (the N2 layout change Doug explicitly wants to be able to make): this tightens the convergence, doesn't break it. If a chapter is a page, then ids need only be unique perchapter, which is a smaller scope than per-book — your keys are already unique at a finer grain (Book > Chapter > Mention), so they're still unique within the smaller document. Safe.
A book split across pages: this breaks the DOM half without breaking the key half. Keys stay unique per book (the identity is unchanged), but now the book's ids are spread across multiple documents, and a citation into the middle of the book has to resolve to which page — which is the address-derivation pass's job (identity → address, per layout), and it's why D6 keeps address separate from identity. So this doesn't break the design; it's the exact case the identity/address split exists to absorb. The id (identity) is book-unique; the address (which page + which fragment) is layout-derived. Safe, because you already separated them.
Two books on one page: this breaks it, genuinely, and it's the one to rule out or handle explicitly. Two books on one page means two per-book id namespaces collide in one document — book A's intro and book B's intro are both id="intro", invalid HTML, silent wrong-anchor resolution (the Sphinx duplicate-label failure). So: either the design forbids two books on one page (clean, and consistent with one-runtime-per-book), or the id must carry the book scope (id="bookA>intro" — the > grammar you already have, which makes the id globally unique, not just document-unique).
And notice: the second option is strictly safer and costs almost nothing, which tells you something. If the id carries its full scoped key (Book > Chapter > Mention, canonicalized), then it's unique globally, not merely per-document, and the convergence you're relying on stops being a coincidence you have to protect and becomes a property you have — the id is unique for the same reason the key is unique, at every layout, because it is the key. So the answer to "is the convergence real or coincidental": it's coincidental if the id is the bare mention name (intro), and it's structural if the id is the fully scoped key (bookA>chapter3>intro, canonicalized). Use the scoped key as the id and the coincidence becomes a guarantee that survives all three layout changes — which is the same move as break 1 (the id is the frozen scoped key), arriving from the layout direction. That's your convergence, made non-accidental: scope the id with the full key, and "unique per document" holds because "unique globally" holds, at any layout. The subjective-build ruling reinforces this — resolution is per-library, so the address varies by library, but the id/key must be library-independent (global), and a fully-scoped id is exactly a library-independent identity. Everything points the same way.
Break 3 — the heading is where by-mention meets navigation, and the answer is a ruling, but I can tell you which ruling is coherent
You don't trust that you like "the table of contents is the mention that allocates" for the right reason, and you're right not to — it's attractive because it's tidy, and tidy isn't a reason. Let me give you the actual structure so Doug can rule.
By-mention (Doug's ruling) says: a heading nobody referenced needs no id, and Heading.tsx:27's self-slug goes. The tension you found: a table of contents links to headings, so if headings have no ids, what does it link to? Here's the resolution, and it's not "the ToC is a mention" — it's cleaner than that. A table of contents is not a set of references that need resolving; it is a *derived view of the containment tree*, and containment is local. The thesis says this directly (§topology): "enumeration is local; resolution never is." A bookknows its own chapters — that's local data, not a cross-reference. So a ToC linking to a chapter is not a citation that needs a catalogue key; it's the book addressing its own part, which it can do by position in its own tree without any global id at all. The ToC doesn't need the heading to have caught a global id; it needs the heading to be locatable within its own book, which it always is, because the book contains it.
So the coherent ruling is: a heading is referrable-by-mention for *cross-references* (someone in another book cites it → it needs a global key → an allocating mention plants one), and locatable-by-containment for *its own book's ToC* (no global key needed → the ToC derives the within-book address from the tree). These are two different needs and by-mention only governs the first. Heading.tsx:27's self-slug goes for the cross-reference purpose (it was manufacturing a global-looking id by luck), but the within-book navigation it accidentally also served has to be replaced by containment-derived addressing, not left to fall away. This is exactly the D6 debt you already carry ("an address below book level must come from a key, not a slug") plus its complement ("...unless the address is within-book, where containment suffices"). The failure mode to rule against, and it's the one hiding: if you delete the heading's self-slug and don't replace within-book navigation with containment-addressing, then removing the guess breaks the ToC — you'd have fixed the integrity hole and broken navigation in the same move, and the ToC gate would catch it late. So the ruling Doug needs to make is not "is the ToC a mention" (it isn't) but "within-book navigation is derived from containment, cross-book reference is by mention — two mechanisms, and the heading participates in both differently." That's coherent, it honors by-mention, and it doesn't need the ToC to pretend to be something it isn't.
The prior art that confirms the split: CTS-URN distinguishes exactly this — a citation into a work (global, logical, work:passage) versus navigation within an edition (local, positional). They never conflated "how you cite a passage from outside" with "how you move to it from the table of contents inside," and the systems that did conflate them (early HTML docs where every ToC link and every cross-ref were the same #slug) are the ones with the drift you're removing. Two mechanisms, deliberately. That's the answer, and the reason to trust it isn't tidiness — it's that containment is local and reference is global, which is the one distinction this entire architecture is built on.
The through-line across all four: the id must be a frozen, injective, fully-scoped encoding of the authored key, carried by a framework kind native to the draw parser, verified against the stored quote, and used only for cross-reference — while within-book navigation stays containment-derived. Every break resolved the same way — refuse to collapse identity into display (break 1), refuse to collapse global-id into document-id (break 2), refuse to collapse cross-reference into navigation (break 3), and refuse to collapse build-provenance into draw-carrier (break 4). Four refusals to collapse two things into one, which is the same discipline the thesis calls the soundness of the vocabulary — one thing, one name — arriving four times from four directions. Where I'd want Doug's ruling rather than my inference: the canonical-form spelling (injective and legible, his call), and whether two-books-on-one-page is forbidden or scope-carried (I lean scope-carried because it makes the convergence structural, but it's his layout call). Everything else the model already decides, if you stop collapsing the slots it already has.

Those two paths agreeing is exactly the fidelity check from question 2, and shelves is the first fact where the derivation methods differ enough that agreement is not guaranteed by construction. The name/title facts agree because both read essentially the same string; shelves agrees only if the printed $Canonicals equal the source <For>s, which your grep supports but which the fidelity gate should confirm per-book before you trust it.
So the verdict on "is stopping at five the right stopping place": stopping at five is the right place to stop *parsing*, but it is not a place where resolve can fully leave evaluation, and the reason is ␀0␀. Here's the chain. Resolve reads the graph. If the graph is written by the parsed phase, the parsed phase must produce every fact resolve or any downstream reader needs — or resolve reads a graph missing fields, and something falls back to evaluation to fill them. Does resolve need types/catalogued/shelves? addresses.ts produces book routes from {name, folder} — it needs name, which you parse. So resolve itself is satisfied by the five. But the graph has other readers: running.ts/the specification suite, proof.ts, and whatever consumes types for the Catalogue/Cover/Document distinction. If any of those still needs types and it's only on the evaluated path, then specify (the evaluation phase) cannot be removed — it's still the only writer of types — and "specify leaves the critical path" is false even though resolve is satisfied. So the test for whether State One's third part can close is not "does resolve read parsed cards" — it's "is there any consumer of the graph that still forces evaluation to run." And types is the one still on the evaluated path that is trivially parseable, so the honest move is: parse types too (it's free, same AST), which removes the most likely remaining reason evaluation stays on the path. Leave catalogued and shelves for State Two's mention work only if nothing on State One's critical path reads them — and confirm that, because if proof.ts or the route pass reads shelves (a catalogue book's shelves are its routing-relevant content), then shelves is on the critical path and must be parsed for evaluation to leave.
The one-sentence consistency verdict: you have built the uncertain half of State One's third part and proved it works; the part closes when the parsed phase writes the graph that resolve reads *and* no remaining graph-consumer forces evaluation — which means parse ␀0␀ now (it's free and it's the most likely hold-out), verify nothing on the critical path needs ␀1␀/␀2␀, and then make the wiring change that is the actual deliverable. You haven't drifted; you've built up to the exact edge where the deliverable is a wiring change gated by three facts, and named all three correctly. The thing to not do is call State One's third part done while a parser produces cards nobody reads and evaluation still writes the graph — because that's the "machinery exists" measure Doug collapsed the milestones to avoid, and you'd know it wasn't done the first time you deleted .graph.json and something reached for a running book to rebuild it.
